# Counting integral points in thin sets of type II: singularities, sieves, and stratification

**Authors:** Dante Bonolis Address: Duke University, 120 Science Drive, Durham NC 27708 Email address: dante.bonolis@duke.edu , Lillian B. Pierce Address: Duke University, 120 Science Drive, Durham NC 27708 Email address: lillian.pierce@duke.edu and Katharine Woo Address: Princeton University, Fine Hall, Washington Road, Princeton NJ 08544 Email address: khwoo@princeton.edu

## Abstract

Consider an absolutely irreducible polynomial $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ that is monic in $Y$ and is a polynomial in $Y^{m}$ for an integer $m\geq 1$ . Let $N(F,B)$ count the number of $\mathbf{x}\in[-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ such that $F(y,\mathbf{x})=0$ is solvable for $y\in\mathbb{Z}$ . In nomenclature of Serre, bounding $N(F,B)$ corresponds to counting integral points in an affine thin set of type II. Previously, in this generality Serre proved $N(F,B)\ll_{F}B^{n-1/2}(\log B)^{\gamma}$ for some $\gamma<1$ . When $m\geq 2$ , this new work proves $N(F,B)\ll_{n,F,\varepsilon}B^{n-1+1/(n+1)+\varepsilon}$ under a nondegeneracy condition that encapsulates that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is truly a polynomial in $n+1$ variables, even after performing any $\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ change of variables on $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ . Under GRH, this result also holds when $m=1$ . We show that generic polynomials satisfy the relevant nondegeneracy condition. Moreover, for a certain class of polynomials, we prove the stronger bound $N(F,B)\ll_{F}B^{n-1}(\log B)^{e(n)}$ , comparable to a conjecture of Serre. A key strength of these results is that they require no nonsingularity property of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ . The Katz-Laumon stratification for character sums, in a new uniform formulation appearing in a companion paper of Bonolis, Kowalski and Woo, is a key ingredient in the sieve method we develop to prove upper bounds that explicitly control any dependence on the size of the coefficients of $F$ .

## 1. Introduction

Let $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}]$ be a polynomial, and define the counting function

$$ N(F,B)=\#\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cap[-B,B]^{n}:\exists y\in\mathbb{Z},F(y,\mathbf{x})=0\}. $$

Trivially, $N(F,B)\ll B^{n}$ , and this is sharp in the case that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ has degree at most 1 in $Y$ . If $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ and $F$ is absolutely irreducible, the best known bound (in such generality) is $N(F,B)\ll_{F}B^{n-1/2}(\log B)^{\gamma}$ for some $\gamma<1$ due to Serre [Ser97]. A conjecture of Serre on thin sets of type II suggests that for suitable polynomials $F(Y,\mathbf{X}),$ the trivial bound for $N(F,B)$ may be reduced by a full factor of $B$ , and this is the motivation for the present work. As an illustration, here is a special consequence of our main work:

#### Theorem 1.1.

Fix $n\geq 2$ . Let $H(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be an irreducible polynomial and define $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{d}-H(\mathbf{X})$ for an integer $d\geq 2$ . Suppose there is no $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $H(L(\mathbf{X}))\in\mathbb{Z}[(X_{i})_{i\in I}]$ for a subset $I\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ . Then there is an integer $e(n)\geq 1$ such that for all $B\geq 1$ ,

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}\log(\|F\|+2)^{e(n)}B^{n-1+\frac{1}{n+1}+\varepsilon}, $$

for all $\varepsilon>0$ .

(Here and throughout, $\|F\|$ denotes the maximum absolute value of any coefficient of $F$ . We follow the convention that $A\ll_{\kappa}B$ implies that $|A|\leq C_{\kappa}B$ with the implied constant $C_{\kappa}$ depending on $\kappa$ .) A strength of Theorem 1.1 is that it requires no assumption of nonsingularity for $F$ . Many previous works on bounding $N(F,B)$ in various contexts, such as [Pie06, HB08, Mun09, HBP12, Bon21, BCLP23, BP24] have relied on $F$ satisfying an appropriate nonsingularity condition. A central aim of the present work is to bound $N(F,B)$ for singular polynomials $F$ .

Our main work goes beyond the cyclic structure of the polynomial in Theorem 1.1. Consider any absolutely irreducible polynomial of the form

$$ F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})=Y^{md}+Y^{m(d-1)}f_{1}(\mathbf{X})+\cdots+Y^{m}f_{d-1}(\mathbf{X})+f_{d}(\mathbf{X}), $$

in which each $f_{j}(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ is a polynomial (not necessarily homogeneous) of degree $k_{j}\geq 0$ , and $f_{d}\not\equiv 0$ . If $m=1$ , (1.1) simply specifies that $F$ is monic in $Y$ ; if $m\geq 2$ , this structure imposes that $F$ is a polynomial in $Y^{m}$ . It is natural to require that $f_{d}\not\equiv 0$ (since otherwise $y=0$ provides a solution to $F(y,\mathbf{x})=0$ for each $\mathbf{x}\in[-B,B]^{n}$ and so $B^{n}\ll N(F,B)\ll B^{n}$ ); this certainly holds if $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is absolutely irreducible.

Our most general theorem (Theorem 1.2) bounds $N(F,B)$ with an exponent as strong as Theorem 1.1 under two conditions: (i) a nondegeneracy condition that encapsulates that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is truly a polynomial in $n+1$ variables, even after performing any $\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ change of variables on $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ ; (ii) the condition $m\geq 2$ in (1.1). We furthermore can allow $m=1$ , under the assumption of GRH. Under a stronger nondegeneracy condition, we show the dependence on $\|F\|$ is at most polylogarithmic (Theorem 1.3). In particular, our main theorems require no assumption of nonsingularity. Moreover, we show that in the moduli space of polynomials of the form (1.1) for fixed $m,d,k_{1},\ldots,k_{j}$ (and even among the subspace of singular polynomials), polynomials that satisfy the relevant nondegeneracy condition (i) are generic (Theorem 3.1). We furthermore prove for a certain class of polynomials the stronger bound $N(F,B)\ll_{F}B^{n-1}(\log B)^{e(n)}$ , which is comparable to a conjecture of Serre (Theorems 1.4 and 1.5). We next state these general results precisely.

### 1.1. General setting of new work

The first nondegeneracy condition we require takes the following form. Let $M$ be a finite (nontrivial) extension of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n})=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ . We say $M$ is an n-genuine extension of $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ if for every $G(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ such that

$$ M=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X})), $$

$G(Y,\mathbf{X})$ has nonzero degree in each of $Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ . We say an absolutely irreducible polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ that is monic in $Y$ is $(1,n)$ -allowable if for every linear change of variables $\sigma\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ , the polynomial $F_{\sigma}(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}):=F(Y,\sigma(\mathbf{X}))$ has the property that $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(F_{\sigma}(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ is an $n$ -genuine extension. (In particular, $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ .) Our first main result is:

#### Theorem 1.2.

Fix $n\geq 2$ . Let $F\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ be a $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomial of the form (1.1) for an integer $m\geq 2$ . Then there exists an integer $h=h(n,\deg F)\geq 1$ such that for all $B\geq 1$ ,

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}\|F\|^{h}B^{n-1+\frac{1}{n+1}+\varepsilon}, $$

for every $\varepsilon>0$ . If $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ and the same hypotheses hold with $m=1$ , the same result holds, conditional on GRH.

The proof of this theorem relies on a dichotomy, so that it is a consequence of two main theorems. On one side of the dichotomy leading to Theorem 1.2, we prove a slightly better bound, with a polylogarithmic dependency on $\|F\|$ , under a stronger nondegeneracy condition. The main strategy to prove this result is a polynomial sieve.

Precisely, we say that a finite (nontrivial) extension $M$ of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n})=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine extension of $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ if for all subextensions $M^{\prime}$ satisfying

$$ \mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})\subsetneq M^{\prime}\subset M, $$

$M^{\prime}$ is an $n$ -genuine extension. We say that an absolutely irreducible polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ that is monic in $Y$ is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable if for every linear change of variables $\sigma\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ , the polynomial $F_{\sigma}(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}):=F(Y,\sigma(\mathbf{X}))$ has the property that $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(F_{\sigma}(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine extension. (In particular, $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ .)

#### Theorem 1.3.

Fix $n\geq 2$ . Let $F\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ be a strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomial of the form (1.1) for an integer $m\geq 2$ . Then there exists an integer $e(n)\geq 1$ such that for all $B\geq 1$ ,

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}\log(\|F\|+2)^{e(n)}B^{n-1+\frac{1}{n+1}+\varepsilon}, $$

for every $\varepsilon>0$ . If $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ and the same hypotheses hold with $m=1$ , the same result holds, conditional on GRH.

On the other side of the dichotomy leading to Theorem 1.2, we must consider the case in which $F$ is $(1,n)$ -allowable but not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable. In this case, a completely different argument achieves a stronger exponent, at the expense of the dependency on the coefficients of $F$ :

#### Theorem 1.4.

Fix $n\geq 2$ . Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ be $(1,n)$ -allowable but not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable. Then there exists an integer $e(n)\geq 1$ such that for all $B\geq 1$ ,

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n,F}B^{n-1}(\log(B+2))^{e(n)}. $$

The exponent in this case concurs with a conjecture of Serre, which we review momentarily. In this theorem, the dependence on $F$ in the implicit constant is inexplicit. But we show that within the dichotomy leading to Theorem 1.2, either we can apply the polynomial sieve (leading to the inequality stated for $N(F,B)$ in Theorem 1.3) or we can refine the strategy for Theorem 1.4 to attain $N(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F}\|F\|^{h}B^{n-1}(\log(B+2))^{e}$ for some $e=e(n)$ and $h=h(n,\deg F)$ . Taken together, this ultimately verifies the remaining cases of Theorem 1.2. Note that this result does not require the polynomial to have the form (1.1) for an integer $m\geq 2$ , and hence sidesteps the need to assume GRH when $m=1$ .

### 1.2. Relation to previous results

The special case of Theorem 1.1 in which $H(\mathbf{X})$ is a nonsingular form includes the main theorem of Munshi’s work [Mun09] as formulated and proved by Bonolis [Bon21, Remark 1]. The special case of Theorem 1.2 in which $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=g(Y)-f(\mathbf{X})$ for a fixed polynomial $g$ and a nonsingular form $f$ recovers many cases of the main theorem of [Bon21] (see Example 8.12 and details in Remark 8.13). Theorem 1.3 immediately implies Theorem 1.1, since under the hypotheses of Theorem 1.1, $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{d}-H(\mathbf{X})$ is a strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomial (as proved in Example 8.7). Finally, the special case of Theorem 1.3 in which $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=0$ defines a nonsingular hypersurface in weighted projective space $\mathbb{P}(e,1,\ldots,1)$ (for an integer $e\geq 1$ ) recovers the main theorem of Bonolis and Pierce’s work [BP24] (see Example 8.10 and Remark 8.11).

### 1.3. Relation to Serre’s conjecture on thin sets

Recall Serre’s formulation of thin sets [Ser97, §9.1]: a subset $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ is a thin set of type I if there is a Zariski-closed subvariety $F\subsetneq\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ such that $M\subset F(\mathbb{Q})$ . On the other hand, a subset $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ is a thin set of type II in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ if there is an irreducible projective algebraic variety $Z$ of dimension $n-1$ and a generically surjective morphism $\pi:Z\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ of degree $D\geq 2$ with $M\subset\pi(Z(\mathbb{Q}))$ . Any thin set is contained in a finite union of thin sets of type I and type II. Affine thin sets of each type are defined analogously, with $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ replaced by $\mathbb{A}^{n}$ . One motivation to show a thin set contains few points comes from specialization of Galois groups: as Serre observed, for $\mathbf{x}$ outside of a thin set, $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ has the same Galois group as $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ [Ser97, p. 122].

#### 1.3.1. Projective setting

Let $M\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ be a thin set. Define the height function $H(\mathbf{x})=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_{i}|$ for $\mathbf{x}=[x_{1}:\cdots:x_{n}]\in\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ with $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ and $\gcd(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=1$ , and the associated counting function for the thin set:

$$ M_{H}(B)=\{\mathbf{x}\in M:H(\mathbf{x})\leq B\}. $$

Trivially, $M_{H}(B)\ll B^{n}$ . Serre conjectured in [Ser97, p. 178] that

$$ M_{H}(B)\ll_{M}B^{n-1}(\log B)^{c} $$

for some $c$ . If $M$ is of type I this can be interpreted as a statement of the Dimension Growth Conjecture, which predicts that if $Z$ is an irreducible projective variety in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ of degree $D\geq 2$ then $Z_{H}(B)\ll_{Z,\varepsilon}B^{\dim Z+\varepsilon}$ for all $B\geq 1$ and $\varepsilon>0$ . This has been resolved in many cases by [Bro03b, BHB06a, BHB06b, HB94, HB02, Sal07], and in all remaining cases by Salberger [Sal23]. A uniform version, in which the implied constant depends only on $n,\deg Z,\varepsilon$ is also known, as long as $\deg Z\neq 3$ ; see [Sal23].

For thin sets of type II in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ , the conjecture (1.2) has been proved (with $B^{\varepsilon}$ instead of a logarithmic factor) when $n=2$ , and when $n=3$ if the cover has degree at least 3, by Broberg [Bro03a]. (For $n=3$ and degree 2, Broberg proves $M_{H}(B)\ll B^{9/4+\varepsilon}$ .) It has also been proved for the special case of nonsingular cyclic covers of $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ when $n\geq 10$ , by Heath-Brown and Pierce in [HBP12] (which also obtains somewhat weaker nontrivial bounds for $3\leq n\leq 9$ ).

#### 1.3.2. Affine setting

As Serre describes in [Ser97, p. 122], an affine thin set $M$ of type II in $\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ has a corresponding polynomial $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]$ that is absolutely irreducible (that is, irreducible in $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]$ ) and of degree $D\geq 2$ in $Y$ , for which

$$ M=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}:\exists y\in\mathbb{Q},F(y,\mathbf{x})=0,\text{$y$ not a pole of any coefficient of $F$}\}. $$

If $F$ satisfies appropriate homogeneity conditions, a thin set of type II in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}(\mathbb{Q})$ can be described in an analogous way.

Our study of $N(F,B)$ is thus the study of counting integral points on affine thin sets of type II. Serre made initial progress: if $F\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ is absolutely irreducible and $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ , then by [Ser97, Thm. 1, p. 177],

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{F}B^{n-1/2}(\log B)^{\gamma} $$

for some $\gamma<1$ , and unspecified dependence of the implicit constant on $F$ . An examination of Serre’s original argument (which is done in [BPW25a]) shows that this bound (with $\gamma=1$ ) can be made to have at most polylog dependence on $\|F\|$ if $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is of the form (1.1) for some $m\geq 2$ ; when $m=1$ , this polylog dependence can be established under GRH for reasons similar to why GRH is assumed in Theorem 1.2 for $m=1$ . To prove our main theorems, we require an unconditional version of (1.3) with at most polylog dependence on $\|F\|$ , which applies to any irreducible polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ with constant-leading-coefficient in $Y$ . We prove this in Theorem 2.13.

Serre also attributes to earlier work of Cohen [Coh81, Thm. 2.1] a bound of the strength

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n,D}\|F\|^{c}B^{n-1/2}\log B $$

for all $B\geq\|F\|^{3c}$ for some $c=c(n,\deg F)$ . There is a gap in the method described in [Coh81, Thm. 2.1]; we prove in the companion paper [BPW25b] that this gap can be repaired by using the theory of strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials that we develop in the present paper.

If no further condition is placed on $F$ , the upper bound (1.3) is (essentially) sharp. For example, Serre points to the trivial example $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})=Y^{2}-X_{1}$ , for which

$$ N(F,B)=\#\{\mathbf{x}\in[-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}:\text{$x_{1}$ is a square}\}\gg B^{n-1/2}. $$

But Serre’s conjecture (1.2) for counting rational points on projective thin sets also suggests a question for counting integral points on certain affine thin sets of type II: for suitable polynomials $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ , is there is some $c=c(F)$ such that

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{F}B^{n-1}(\log B)^{c},\qquad\text{for all $B\geq 1$?} $$

And, can the dependence of the implicit constant on $\|F\|$ be controlled? These questions motivate our present work.

Previous works such as [Mun09, Bon21, BP24] (or in the function field setting [BCLP23]) improved on Serre’s bound (1.3), and approached (1.5), but only when $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ satisfies a nonsingularity condition, and has a special shape. Additionally, Pierce and Heath-Brown [HBP12] have proved Serre’s conjecture (1.5) for $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{d}-f(\mathbf{X})$ when $n\geq 10$ (also obtaining stronger results than (1.3) for $n\geq 6$ and than Theorem 1.1 for $n\geq 8$ ), but only under the assumption that $f$ has nonsingular leading form.

In the present work, we make no assumption of nonsingularity. Theorems 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3 provide bounds for $N(F,B)$ that approach (1.5) as $n\rightarrow\infty$ . Moreover, Theorem 1.4 and Theorem 1.5 (stated below) admit the exponent predicted by (1.5).

### 1.4. Singularities, sieves, and stratification:

Our strategy is to count solutions contributing to $N(F,B)$ via a polynomial sieve, as formulated in [BP24]. The unconditional sieve lemma we employ (Lemma 6.1) imposes that $m\geq 2$ in the depiction (1.1) of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ ; under GRH, an analogous sieve lemma also holds true for $m=1$ (Lemma 6.2). Aside from this application of the sieve lemma, the remainder of the paper does not distinguish between $m\geq 2$ and $m=1$ .

After an application of a polynomial sieve lemma, our central concern is to understand for many primes $p$ the local counting function

$$ v_{p}(\mathbf{x})=\#\{y\;(\text{mod}\;p):F(y,\mathbf{x})=0\;(\text{mod}\;p)\}. $$

In particular, it is crucial to estimate for each $\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ the associated complete sum

$$ S(\bfu,p)=\sum_{\bfa\;(\text{mod}\;p)}(v_{p}(\bfa)-1)e_{p}(\bfu\cdot\bfa). $$

A celebrated stratification result of Katz and Laumon [KL85] (see also Fouvry [Fou00]) provides a set of nested varieties that control how large $|S(\mathbf{u},p)|$ can be as $\mathbf{u}$ varies. The version of the stratification we require is as follows: there exists a constant $C_{F}\geq 1$ , an integer $N_{F}\geq 1$ , and homogeneous varieties $\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbb{Z}[1/N_{F}]}\supset V_{1}\supset V_{2}\supset...\supset V_{n}$ , where $V_{j}$ has codimension at least $j$ , such that for any prime $p\nmid N_{F}$ and for $\bfu\not\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ ,

$$ |S(\mathbf{u},p)|\leq C_{F}p^{\frac{n+j-1}{2}}. $$

Thus in particular if $\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\setminus V_{j+1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ , then $|S(\mathbf{u},p)|\leq C_{F}p^{\frac{n+j}{2}}$ . Previous works that employed the polynomial sieve (such as [Mun09, Bon21, BCLP23, BB23, BP24]) only encountered two possibilities: $|S(\mathbf{u},p)|\leq C_{F}p^{\frac{n}{2}}$ ( $\mathbf{u}$ is good) or $|S(\mathbf{u},p)|\leq C_{F}p^{\frac{n+1}{2}}$ ( $\mathbf{u}$ is bad), since in all those works $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ was assumed to be nonsingular. Here we make no such assumption, and we require the full strength of the Katz-Laumon stratification.

To obtain the explicit dependence on $\|F\|$ in Theorems 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3, we require an even stronger statement of stratification, which makes explicit whether (and how) the following parameters depend on the coefficients of $F$ : $C_{F},N_{F}$ , and the degree, number of irreducible components, and defining polynomials of each stratum $V_{j}$ . This uniform stratification is new: it is proved by two of the authors with Emmanuel Kowalski, in the companion paper [BKW25], and recorded here in Theorem 6.3.

Even with such a uniform stratification in hand, an essential difficulty arises when applying the stratification to bound $N(F,B)$ . This occurs if an irreducible component, say $X_{j}$ , of some stratum $V_{j}$ is degenerate, that is, lies in a proper linear subspace of $\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ (and in particular is hence contained in a hyperplane, say $W_{j}$ ). We show that to handle the contribution of a possible degenerate component, it would suffice to prove that aside from a set $\mathcal{E}$ of exceptional primes with $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|$ , for each prime $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ ,

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{u}\in W_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}|S(\mathbf{u},p)|^{2}\ll_{n,\deg F}p^{2n-1}. $$

Since there are $O(p^{n-1})$ terms in the sum, this is a statement that $|S(\mathbf{u},p)|\ll p^{n/2}$ on average over $\mathbf{u}\in W_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ . The proof of the second moment bound (1.6) is delicate: it is precisely where the assumption that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable becomes relevant (in the proof of Theorem 1.3).

Precisely, we are able to prove that (1.6) holds as long as for a certain change of variables $L\in\mathrm{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ with integer entries (determined by the hyperplane $W_{j}$ ), the polynomial $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}):=F(Y,L(\mathbf{X}))$ has the property that aside from an exceptional set $\mathcal{E}_{L}$ of primes with $|\mathcal{E}_{L}|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F_{L}\|$ , for each prime $p\not\in\mathcal{E}_{L}$ ,

$$ \#\{(a_{2},\ldots,a_{n})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}:F_{L}(Y,X_{1},a_{2},...,a_{n})\text{ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$}\}\ll_{n,\deg F}p^{n-2}. $$

In a key step, we show that (1.7) holds as long as $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is “strongly $n$ -genuine.” Here, and throughout, we say an absolutely irreducible polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ is an $n$ -genuine polynomial if $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ is an $n$ -genuine extension. Similarly, we say an absolutely irreducible polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial if $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine extension. That is to say, $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is $(1,n)$ -allowable (resp. strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable) precisely when $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is $n$ -genuine (resp. strongly $n$ -genuine) for all $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ .

This series of ideas leads ultimately to Theorem 1.3 with at most polylog dependency on $\|F\|$ : if $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable then $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is strongly $n$ -genuine for all $L$ , by definition. Thus we can show (1.7) holds, and hence the second moment bound (1.6) can be obtained for all hyperplanes $W$ , and in particular for any hyperplane that contains at least one degenerate component of a stratum $V_{j}$ . Here the full strength of the new uniform stratification provided by the companion paper [BKW25] by Bonolis, Kowalski and Woo is also required to control the size of the set $\mathcal{E}_{L}$ of exceptional primes for which (1.7) may not hold.

On the other hand, if $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine, we do not prove (1.7), and so we do not prove (1.6). Instead, it is possible to exploit the property of not being strongly $n$ -genuine and save a variable, without applying the polynomial sieve:

#### Theorem 1.5.

Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ be $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine. Then there exists an integer $e(n)\geq 1$ such that for all $B\geq 1$ ,

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F}\log(\|F\|+2)^{e(n)}B^{n-1}(\log(B+2))^{2e(n)}. $$

This result concurs with the exponent predicted in (1.5), in relation to Serre’s conjecture. We deduce Theorem 1.4 from this result, but the polylog dependency on $\|F\|$ is degraded, as we explain in §4.1. We combine Theorem 1.5 with the polynomial sieve (in the form of Theorem 6.4) to complete the proof of Theorem 1.2. Here too the polylog dependency on $\|F\|$ is degraded, as we explain in §6.5. See Example 8.2 for infinite classes of polynomials satisfying the hypothesis of Theorem 1.5.

### 1.5. Organization

In §2 we assemble a wide array of counting results and algebraic facts we will call upon, with careful attention to explicit dependence on $\|F\|$ . In §3 we state a theorem that $(1,n)$ -allowable and strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomials are generic (Theorem 3.1, Corollary 3.2), also among singular polynomials (Corollary 3.3), and prove several useful facts about these classes of polynomials. In §4 we focus on polynomials that are $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine, and prove Theorem 4.1, from which we deduce Theorems 1.4 and 1.5. In §5, under the hypothesis that $F$ is strongly $n$ -genuine, we prove second moment bound related to (1.6). In §6 we initiate the polynomial sieve, and the main claim is Theorem 6.4. Theorem 6.4 immediately implies Theorem 1.3, which in turn immediately implies Theorem 1.1 (by Example 8.7). We show that Theorem 6.4 and Theorem 4.1 together imply Theorem 1.2. To prove Theorem 6.4, we introduce the polynomial sieve lemma to bound $N(F,B)$ , dissect the sieve terms using the Katz-Laumon stratification in the new uniform version of Bonolis, Kowalski and Woo [BKW25], and bound all of the resulting terms. In §7 we combine all the estimates for terms in the sieve lemma, and conclude the proof of Theorem 6.4. In §8 we construct examples necessary to verify genericity in §3; examples of classes of polynomials to which each main theorem applies; examples that verify this paper recovers nearly all the previous literature on these problems.

## 2. Preliminaries

We will apply several existing bounds for counting points within our argument, and because the uniformity of these estimates with respect to the underlying polynomial coefficients will play a role, we assemble precise statements here.

#### Lemma 2.1 (Trivial bound).

Let $F\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be a polynomial of degree $e\geq 1$ , and $S\subset\mathbb{Z}$ a finite subset. Then

$$ \#\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in S^{n}:F(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=0\}\leq e|S|^{n-1}. $$

The proof is by induction on dimension, and may be found in many places, such as [HB02, Thm. 1] or [BCLP23, Lemma 10.1]; it is sometimes called the Schwartz-Zippel bound. While the proof given in [BCLP23, Lemma 10.1] is stated in the case where $F$ is homogeneous, it also applies in the nonhomogeneous case via trivial modifications.

We will call upon a result to count the points in a “box” in $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}$ lying on a variety with a given codimension; we quote a special case of a lemma of Xu [Xu20, Lemma 1.7]:

#### Proposition 2.2.

Let $X\subset\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}^{n}$ be a subscheme of codimension $j$ , and let $d$ be the sum of the dimensions of its irreducible components. If $\{B_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ are subsets of $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , consider the “box” $\mathcal{B}=\prod_{i}B_{i}\subset\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}^{n}$ . Assuming $1\leq\#B_{1}\leq\#B_{2}\leq\cdots\leq\#B_{n}<\infty$ ,

$$ \#(X(\mathbb{F}_{p})\cap\mathcal{B})\leq d\prod_{i=j+1}^{n}\#B_{i}=d(\#\mathcal{B})(\prod_{i=1}^{j}\#B_{j})^{-1}. $$

The Lang-Weil bound provides both a main term and an error term with good uniformity:

#### Lemma 2.3 (Lang-Weil [LW54, Thm. 1]).

Let $V\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}$ be a variety of dimension $m$ and degree $d$ defined over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ and irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{F}_{q}}$ . Then

$$ \#V(\mathbb{F}_{q})=q^{m}+E $$

where $E=(d-1)(d-2)q^{m-1/2}+O_{n,m,d}(q^{m-1})$ , in which the implied constant only depends on $n,m,d$ .

See e.g. [Ser97, p. 184] for a formal statement. We apply its consequence in an affine setting:

#### Lemma 2.4.

Let $F\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{k}]$ have degree $d$ (not necessarily homogeneous) and let $p$ be a prime such that the affine variety $V(F):=\{F(\mathbf{X})=0\}\subset\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}^{k}$ of dimension $k-1$ is absolutely irreducible (that is, irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{F}_{q}}$ ). Then

$$ \#\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{k}:F(\mathbf{x})=0\}=p^{k-1}+O_{k,d}(p^{k-1-1/2}). $$

#### Proof.

By homogenizing, we consider the polynomial $\tilde{F}(X_{0},\ldots,X_{k})=X_{0}^{d}F(X_{1}/X_{0},\ldots,X_{k}/X_{0})$ . Then the projective closure of the affine variety defined as the vanishing set of $F$ in $\mathbb{A}^{k}$ is $V(\tilde{F})\subset\mathbb{P}^{k}$ . The projective closure is irreducible if and only if the affine variety is (see [Sha13, §4.5 Ex. 1] or [Rei88, §5.5 Prop.]), so by the hypothesis, $V(\tilde{F})$ is irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ . Thus by Lemma 2.3, $\#V(\tilde{F})=p^{k-1}+O_{k,d}(p^{k-1-1/2})$ . Let $U_{0}=\mathbb{P}^{k}\setminus V(X_{0})$ , where $V(X_{0})=\{X_{0}=0\}$ . Then $V(\tilde{F})$ is the union of $V(\tilde{F})\cap U_{0}$ (the points we wish to count) and $V(\tilde{F})\cap V(X_{0})$ , which can be identified with a subset of $\mathbb{P}^{k-1}$ and hence can contribute at most $O(p^{k-2})$ points over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , and the proposition is verified. ∎

### 2.1. Variants of Noether’s Lemma

We will frequently apply Noether’s Lemma, (for example in Theorem 3.1 and Lemma 5.5), and for Lemma 4.5 we need a refined version, which we now specify.

#### Definition 2.5.

Let $K$ be a field, and $\overline{K}$ a given algebraic closure. Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in K[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ . Let $e$ denote a multi-degree $e=(e_{0},e_{1},\ldots,e_{n})$ with non-negative integral entries, and set $|e|=e_{0}+e_{1}+\cdots+e_{n}$ . For a given multi-degree $e$ with $1\leq|e|<\deg_{F}$ , we say that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ satisfies divisibility condition $\mathcal{D}(e)$ over $\overline{K}$ if there exists a factorization

$$ F(Y,\mathbf{X})=G(Y,\mathbf{X})H(Y,\mathbf{X}) $$

where $G$ and $H$ lie in $\overline{K}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ , $\deg H<\deg F$ , and $\deg_{Y}G\leq e_{0},$ $\deg_{X_{j}}G\leq e_{j}$ for $j=1,\ldots,n$ .

We will later apply this in two settings: $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in K[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ with total degree $\deg F>1$ is absolutely irreducible (that is, irreducible over $\overline{K}$ ) precisely when $F$ does not satisfy condition $\mathcal{D}(e)$ for any multi-degree $e$ with $1\leq|e|<\deg_{F}$ ; this relates to the classical formulation of Noether’s lemma. Second, if $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (see (4.2)) then $F$ satisfies condition $\mathcal{D}(e)$ for some multi-degree $e=(1,e_{1},\ldots,e_{n})$ with $e_{0}=1$ .

To detect when a polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ satisfies a divisibility condition $\mathcal{D}(e)$ , we record a variant of Noether’s lemma, which closely follows the presentation and proof of [Sch76, Ch. V Thm. 2A].

#### Lemma 2.6 (Variant of Noether’s Lemma).

Let $K$ be a field. Fix $D\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $D\geq 2$ .

- (i) Let $\mathcal{D}(e)$ be a divisibility condition for a fixed multi-degree $e=(e_{0},e_{1},\ldots,e_{n})$ with $1\leq|e|<D$ . Then there exist forms $G_{1},...,G_{s}$ in variables $(A_{i_{0},...,i_{n}})_{i_{0}+\cdots+i_{n}\leq D}$ such that a polynomial

$$ F(Y,\mathbf{X})=\sum_{i_{0}+\cdots+i_{n}\leq D}a_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}Y^{i_{0}}X_{1}^{i_{1}}\cdots X_{n}^{i_{n}} $$

(2.1) satisfies $\mathcal{D}(e)$ over $\overline{K}$ or is of degree $\deg F<D$ , if and only if

$$ G_{j}((a_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}))=0,\forall j=1,...,s. $$

The forms $G_{1},...,G_{s}$ depend only on $n,D$ and $e$ , and are independent of the field $K$ in the sense that if $\mathrm{char}(K)=0$ they have rational integer coefficients and if $\mathrm{char}(K)=p\neq 0$ , the polynomials are obtained by reducing the integral coefficients modulo $p$ . Moreover, $s=O_{n,D,e}(1)$ , and $\deg G_{j}\ll_{n,D,e}1$ for all $j=1,\ldots,s$ . If $\mathrm{char}(K)=0$ ,

$$ \|G_{j}\|\ll_{n,D,e}1 $$

for all $j=1,\ldots,s$ .

- (ii) The same result as (i) holds if (2.1) is replaced by: is reducible over $\overline{K}$ or is of degree $\deg_{F}<D$ .

#### Proof.

The result (ii) is the classical statement proved in [Sch76, Ch. V Thm. 2A], so we only prove (i). Let us suppose that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ satisfies $\mathcal{D}(e)$ over $\overline{K}$ . Let us assume that $G(Y,\mathbf{X})\mid F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ over $\overline{K}$ and denote the coefficients as

$$ G(Y,\mathbf{X})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i_{j}\leq e_{j}\\
j=0,\ldots,n\end{subarray}}b_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}Y^{i_{0}}X_{1}^{i_{1}}...X_{n}^{i_{n}}. $$

(Incidentally, to prove (ii) the only change in this argument is to specify not $i_{j}\leq e_{j}$ but $i_{0}+\cdots+i_{n}\leq D-1$ at this step.) We also denote the quotient $F(Y,\mathbf{X})/G(Y,\mathbf{X})$ as $H(Y,\mathbf{X})$ with coefficients:

$$ H(Y,\mathbf{X})=\sum_{i_{0}+...+i_{n}\leq D-1}c_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}Y^{i_{0}}X_{1}^{i_{1}}...X_{n}^{i_{n}}. $$

We note that there exists such a $G(Y,\mathbf{X})$ and $H(Y,\mathbf{X})$ in $\overline{K}[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ , where $G(Y,\mathbf{X})$ satisfies $\deg_{Y}G\leq e_{0}$ and $\deg_{X_{j}}G\leq e_{j}$ for each $j=1,...,n$ , if and only if for some fixed choice of coefficients $\{b_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}\}$ , there is a nontrivial solution to the system of equations in the variables $c$ and $\{c_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}\}$ given by:

$$ \sum_{j_{0}+k_{0}=i_{0}}...\sum_{j_{n}+k_{n}=i_{n}}b_{j_{0},...,j_{n}}c_{k_{0},...,k_{n}}-c\cdot a_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}=0, $$

with one equation for each multi-degree $(i_{0},i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ that can appear in $F$ (of total degree $\leq D$ ). The number of equations in this system is given by $\binom{D+n}{n}$ , as that is the number of $(n+1)$ -tuples of non-negative indices with $i_{0}+\cdots+i_{n}\leq D$ . Let us denote by $K$ the number variables $c$ and $\{c_{i_{0},\ldots,i_{n}}\}$ , so that

$$ K\leq 1+\binom{D-1+n}{n}, $$

which depends only on $D$ and $n$ . In particular, $K<\binom{D+n}{n}$ . Note that the restriction to $G(Y,\mathbf{X})$ satisfying $\mathcal{D}(e)$ does not change the number of equations, nor the number of variables, but how many of the coefficients $b_{j_{0},...,j_{n}}$ are forced to be zero.

Given values for the $\{b_{i_{0},\ldots,i_{n}}\}$ and $\{a_{i_{0},\ldots,i_{n}}\}$ , for the above linear system to have a nontrivial solution in the variables $c$ and $\{c_{i_{0},\ldots,i_{n}}\}$ , it is equivalent to require the determinant of each $K\times K$ submatrix (of the corresponding matrix) to be zero. This is equivalent to a system of (determinant) forms of degree $K$ vanishing, say

$$ \Delta_{i}(\{b_{j_{0},...,j_{n}}\},\{a_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}\})=0,\qquad i=1,...,r, $$

where we denote the number of such $K\times K$ determinants by $r$ , which only depends on $D$ , $n$ , and $e$ . These determinants can be viewed as polynomials with coefficients in terms of $\{a_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}\}$ , evaluated at variables $\{b_{i_{0},\ldots,i_{n}}\}$ .

By [Sch76, Ch. V Thm. 1A], there exist forms $h_{1},...,h_{s}$ in the coefficients of $\Delta_{1},...,\Delta_{r}$ (i.e. in polynomials of $\{a_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}\}$ ) such that $\Delta_{1}=\Delta_{2}=...=\Delta_{r}=0$ is solvable in the $\{b_{j_{0},...,j_{n}}\}$ if and only if $h_{1}=...=h_{s}=0$ when evaluated at $\{a_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}\}$ . These forms $h_{i}$ are moreover of degree $O_{D,n,e}(1)$ ; if $\mathrm{char}{K}=0$ , $\|h_{i}\|=O_{D,n,e}(1)$ for $i=1,\ldots,s$ (see [Sch76, Ch. V Thm. 1D]).

Now for each $i=1,\ldots,r$ we define a form $G_{i}$ by substituting into $h_{i}$ the coefficients of the forms $\Delta_{1},\ldots,\Delta_{r}$ , as polynomials in the $\{a_{i_{0},\ldots,i_{n}}\}$ . We recall that the coefficients of $\Delta_{i}$ , as a function of $\{b_{i_{0},\ldots,i_{n}}\}$ , can be at most linear in $a_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}$ . Additionally, since $\Delta_{1},...,\Delta_{r}$ range over all $K\times K$ minors, there exists a nonempty subset of the polynomials $\{\Delta_{i}\}$ where the coefficients have degree 1 in $\{a_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}\}.$ So, the composition of $h_{j}$ with these linear polynomials in $a_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}$ give us forms $G_{j}(\{a_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}\})$ such that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=G(Y,\mathbf{X})H(Y,\mathbf{X})$ if and only if

$$ G_{j}(\{a_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}\})=0,j=1,...,s. $$

We observe that these forms $G_{j}$ cannot be uniformly zero, as that would imply that any polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is reducible. Moreover, $G_{j}$ has degree and coefficients that are $O_{D,n,e}(1).$ Indeed, Schmidt notes that $\deg G_{j}\leq(K-1)^{2^{K-1}}$ and $\|G_{j}\|\leq 4^{{K-1}^{2^{K-1}}}$ [Sch76, Ch. V Thm. 2A].

We note that the statement of [Sch76, Ch. V Thm. 1A] does not explicitly quantify the size of $s$ in terms of $n,D,e$ . But the functions $h_{1},\ldots,h_{s}$ are a resultant system of $r$ forms in the variables $\{a_{i_{0},\ldots,i_{n}}\}$ . A resultant system for $R$ forms in $S$ variables, when $R\geq S$ , is the set of all $S\times S$ subdeterminants of an associated $R\times S$ matrix, so that the number of forms in the resultant system is $\ll_{R,S}1$ ; see [Sch76, p. 179]. Thus in the statement of the lemma at hand, $s\ll_{n,D,e}1$ . ∎

#### Remark 2.7.

Observe that the divisibility condition $\mathcal{D}(e)$ forces certain entries of the $K\times K$ submatrices to be zero. Nevertheless, we can still view the determinants of the $K\times K$ submatrices as polynomials in $\{b_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}\}$ with coefficients in terms of $\{a_{i_{0},...,i_{n}}\}$ , as we have done above.

One immediate corollary is the following standard fact.

#### Corollary 2.8.

For $D\geq 2$ , let $\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ denote the moduli space of polynomials in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ that are monic in $Y$ and satisfy $\deg_{Y}(F)=D$ and $\deg_{X_{i}}(F)\leq k_{i}.$ In this moduli space, absolutely irreducible polynomials are generic.

Indeed, by Noether’s Lemma 2.6 (ii), for a degree $D\geq 2$ there exist forms $G_{1},\ldots,G_{s}$ such that if $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (or $\deg F<D$ ) then $G_{i}$ vanish when evaluated at $F$ , verifying the corollary.

The following fact is a consequence of Lemma 2.6, just as [Sch76, Ch. V Cor. 2B] follows from [Sch76, Ch. V Thm. 2A] (as initially observed by Ostrowski).

#### Lemma 2.9.

Let $F(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ have degree $D\geq 1$ . (i) If $F$ does not satisfy divisibility condition $\mathcal{D}(e)$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , then there exists a finite set $\mathcal{E}_{e}$ of exceptional primes with $|\mathcal{E}_{e}|\ll_{n,D,e}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ such that for $p\not\in\mathcal{E}_{e}$ , the reduction of $F$ modulo $p$ is again of degree $D$ and does not satisfy divisibility condition $\mathcal{D}(e)$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ . (ii) If $F$ is absolutely irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , then there exists a finite set $\mathcal{E}$ of exceptional primes with $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{n,D}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ such that for $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ , the reduction of $F$ modulo $p$ is again of degree $D$ and is irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ .

#### Proof.

For (i), let $F(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be given, with degree $D$ , and let $\mathcal{D}(e)$ be a given divisibility condition with $|e|<D$ . By hypothesis, $F$ does not satisfy $\mathcal{D}(e)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ (and has degree $D$ ) so among the forms $G_{1},\ldots,G_{s}$ provided by Lemma 2.6 there is at least one, say $G_{j^{*}}$ , such that when evaluated at the coefficients of $F$ , $G_{j^{*}}(\{a_{i_{0},\ldots,i_{n}}\})\neq 0$ . By Lemma 2.6, $F$ satisfies $\mathcal{D}(e)$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ or has degree $<D$ if and only if $p$ belongs the exceptional set $\mathcal{E}_{e}$ of primes such that $p|G_{j^{*}}(\{a_{i_{0},\ldots,i_{n}}\})$ . As a nonzero integer,

$$ |G_{j^{*}}(\{a_{i_{0},\ldots,i_{n}}\})|\leq\|G_{j^{*}}\|\|F\|^{\deg G_{j^{*}}}. $$

By Lemma 2.6 (i), $\|G_{j^{*}}\|\ll_{n,D,e}1$ . For any nonzero integer $t$ , the number $\omega(t)$ of distinct prime divisors of $t$ satisfies $\omega(t)\ll\log t/\log\log t$ . Consequently $|\mathcal{E}_{e}|\ll_{n,D,e}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ , as claimed.

For (ii), suppose $F(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ of degree $D$ is irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . One can argue as above using the forms $G_{1},\ldots,G_{s}$ provided by Lemma 2.6 (ii), or observe that $F$ does not satisfy $\mathcal{D}(e)$ for any multi-degree $e$ with $1\leq|e|<D$ . Let $\mathcal{E}=\cup_{e}\mathcal{E}_{e}$ denote the finite union over multi-degrees $e$ with $1\leq|e|<D$ . Then $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{n,D}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ and for $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ , $F$ does not satisfy condition $\mathcal{D}(e)$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ for any multi-index $e$ , and is hence irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ .

∎

### 2.2. Hilbert’s irreducibility theorem

We record the following version of the Hilbert Irreducibility Theorem, which we use extensively in the next sections; a proof can be found in [FJ23, Ch. 13 and Ch. 14 §3] or in [Lan83, Ch. 9, pp. 233-235].

#### Theorem 2.10 (Hilbert).

Let $F_{1},...,F_{s}\in\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n},T_{1},...,T_{r})$ be irreducible polynomials in $n+r$ variables. There exists a dense subset $U\subset\mathbb{A}^{r}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that for any $(t_{1},...,t_{r})\in U$ , $F_{1}(X_{1},...,X_{n},t_{1},...,t_{r}),...,F_{s}(X_{1},...,X_{n},t_{1},...,t_{r})$ are irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ .

### 2.3. Counting via the determinant method

We will apply a result developed from the Bombieri-Pila determinant method, which has suitable uniformity, and a savings that depends on the degree of the variety:

#### Theorem 2.11 (Pila [Pil95, Thm. A]).

Let $V$ be an irreducible affine variety defined over $\mathbb{R}$ of dimension $m$ and degree $d$ in $\mathbb{A}^{n}$ . The number $N(H)$ of integral points $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ lying on $V$ with $\max_{i}|x_{i}|\leq H$ satisfies

$$ N(H)\ll_{n,m,d}H^{m-1+1/d}\exp(12\sqrt{d\log H\log\log H}) $$

for all $H\geq 1$ . Note that given $\varepsilon>0$ , for all $H\gg_{d,\varepsilon}1$ , $\exp(12\sqrt{d\log H\log\log H})\leq H^{\varepsilon}$ .

### 2.4. Counting with a smooth weight

A smoothed count preserves the upper bound from a sharp cut-off count for “points in a box,” up to a negligible factor.

#### Lemma 2.12.

Let $W(\mathbf{u})=w(\mathbf{u}/B)$ where $B\geq 1$ and $w$ is a non-negative infinitely differentiable function that is compactly supported in $[-2,2]^{n}$ .

- (i) For any $M\geq 1$ ,

$$ \hat{W}(\bfu)\ll_{n}B^{n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+|u_{i}|B\right)^{-M}. $$

- (ii) Suppose an affine variety $V\subset\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}$ has the property that for each $H\geq 1$ , (2.2)

$$ \#\{\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cap V\cap[-H,H]^{n}\}\ll H^{\kappa}, $$

for a given $\kappa=\kappa(V)\in[1,n]$ . Let $A\geq 0$ be fixed. Then for any $Y>0$ and any $\varepsilon>0$ , by taking $M\gg_{n,\kappa,\varepsilon}1$ sufficiently large,

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\cap V}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|}{Y}\right)^{-M}(\log(1+|\mathbf{u}|))^{A}\ll_{n,A,\varepsilon}\max\{1,Y^{\kappa+\varepsilon}\}. $$

- (iii) Suppose an affine variety $V\subset\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}^{n}$ has the property that for any subset $I\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}$ and corresponding “box” $I^{n}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}$ , (2.3)

$$ \#(V(\mathbb{F}_{p})\cap I^{n})\ll|I|^{\kappa}, $$

for a given $\kappa=\kappa(V)\in[1,n]$ . Let $A\geq 0$ be fixed. Then for $Y\geq 1$ , for any sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$ , by taking $M\gg_{n,\kappa,\varepsilon}1$ sufficiently large,

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\ \mathbf{u}_{p}\in V(\mathbb{F}_{p})\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|}{Y}\right)^{-M}(\log(1+|\mathbf{u}|))^{A}\ll_{n,A,\varepsilon}\begin{cases}Y^{\kappa+\varepsilon},&\text{$Y\ll p^{\sigma},$ $\sigma<1$}\\ (Y/p)^{n}p^{\kappa}Y^{\varepsilon}&\text{$Y\gg p$}\end{cases}, $$

in which $\mathbf{u}_{p}\in V(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ indicates that the reduction of $\mathbf{u}\;(\text{mod}\;p)$ is identified with a point in $V(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ .

#### Proof.

The bound for $\hat{W}(\mathbf{u})$ holds because $\hat{W}(\mathbf{u})=B^{n}\hat{w}(B\mathbf{u})$ , and integrating $\hat{w}(\mathbf{x})$ by parts $M$ times in each coordinate proves the rapidly decaying upper bound $\hat{w}(\mathbf{x})\ll\prod_{i}(1+|x_{i}|)^{-M}$ , for any $M\geq 1$ .

For the second claim, if $0<Y<1$ it suffices to observe the left-hand side is bounded above, for sufficiently large $M$ , by

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1+|u_{i}|)^{-M}(\log(1+|\mathbf{u}|))^{A}\ll_{n,A}\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1+|u_{i}|)^{-(M-1)}\ll 1. $$

Thus from now on we assume $Y\geq 1$ . We divide the sum over $\mathbf{u}$ into $\mathrm{I}+\mathrm{II}$ , which denote the contributions from $\mathbf{u}\in C_{\varepsilon}$ and $\mathbf{u}\not\in C_{\varepsilon}$ , respectively, in which we define

$$ C_{\varepsilon}=[-Y^{1+\varepsilon},Y^{1+\varepsilon}]^{n} $$

for a fixed small $\varepsilon>0$ of our choice. Then for any $M\geq 1$ , by the hypothesis (2.2),

$$ \mathrm{I}\ll_{\varepsilon,M}(\log Y)^{A}\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in C_{\varepsilon}\cap V}1\ll(\log Y)^{A}(Y^{1+\varepsilon})^{\kappa}\ll_{A,\varepsilon}Y^{\kappa+(\kappa+1)\varepsilon}, $$

say, using $(\log Y)^{A}\ll_{A,\varepsilon}Y^{\varepsilon}$ . On the other hand,

$$ \mathrm{II}\leq\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\setminus C_{\varepsilon}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|}{Y}\right)^{-M}(\log|u_{i}|)^{A}\ll_{n,A,\varepsilon}Y^{n}Y^{-\varepsilon(M-2)}. $$

(This used the fact that $(\log|u_{i}|)^{A}\ll_{A,\varepsilon}\log Y$ if $|u_{i}|\leq Y^{1+\varepsilon}$ , and that $(\log|u_{i}|)^{A}(1+|u_{i}|/Y)^{-1}\leq 1$ if $|u_{i}|\geq Y^{1+\varepsilon}$ , for all $Y\gg_{A,\varepsilon}1$ .) By taking $M\gg_{n,\varepsilon,A}1$ sufficiently large, this is dominated by as small a power of $Y$ as we like, and in particular by the contribution of $\mathrm{I}$ . We then obtain (ii) by taking $\varepsilon>0$ as small as we like.

For the third claim, we again define the box $C_{\varepsilon}$ as above (for a small $\varepsilon>0$ of our choice) and divide the sum over $\mathbf{u}$ into $\mathrm{I}+\mathrm{II}$ , denoting the contributions from $\mathbf{u}\in C_{\varepsilon}$ and $\mathbf{u}\not\in C_{\varepsilon}$ , respectively. Suppose first $Y\gg p$ . (We ultimately do not require this case, but include it for completeness.) Then the integer points in the box $C_{\varepsilon}$ may be identified as belonging to at most $\ll(Y^{1+\varepsilon}/p+1)^{n}$ copies of $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}$ . Thus by the hypothesis (2.3) and positivity,

$$ \mathrm{I}\ll_{\varepsilon}(\log Y)^{A}(Y^{1+\varepsilon}/p+1)^{n}p^{\kappa}\ll_{n,A,\varepsilon}(Y/p)^{n}p^{\kappa}Y^{(n+1)\varepsilon}\qquad(Y\gg p). $$

If on the other hand $Y\ll p^{\sigma}$ for some $\sigma<1$ , by choosing $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small with respect to $\sigma$ , we may ensure that with $C_{\varepsilon}$ defined as above, $C_{\varepsilon}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ can be identified with a subset, say $I^{n}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}$ , to which the hypothesis (2.3) applies directly. Consequently $\mathrm{I}\ll_{A}(\log Y)^{A}(Y^{1+\varepsilon})^{\kappa}\ll_{A,\varepsilon}Y^{\kappa+(\kappa+1)\varepsilon}$ . In either case, by positivity we may bound $\mathrm{II}$ by summing over all integer tuples in the complement of $C_{\varepsilon}$ as in (2.4). By taking $M$ sufficiently large this is dominated by the contribution of $\mathrm{I}$ . ∎

### 2.5. An estimate with polylog dependency

We prove an unconditional estimate for $N(F,B)$ with polylog dependence on $\|F\|$ . This provides an explicit bound with essentially the same exponent as Serre’s bound (1.3), which we require later.

#### Theorem 2.13.

Fix an integer $n\geq 1$ . Let $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}]$ be irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}]$ of total degree $D$ , with $\deg_{Y}(F)\geq 2$ , and assume that $F$ has constant-leading-coefficient in $Y$ . Then

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n,D}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{e(n)}B^{n-\frac{1}{2}}(\log B)^{e(n)}\qquad\text{for all $B\geq 1$,} $$

for a constant $e(n)>0$ depending only on $n$ .

The key tool to prove this is a recent result of Cluckers et al, on effective Hilbert’s Irreducibility Theorem, via the determinant method.

#### Theorem 2.14 ([CDH+23, Theorem 1.10]).

Let $F(T,X_{1},...,X_{m})\in\mathbb{Z}[T,X_{1},...,X_{m}]$ be irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[T,X_{1},...,X_{m}]$ with $d=\deg_{\mathbf{X}}(F)\geq 1$ . For each integer $B\geq 1$ define

$$ R_{T}(F,B)=\{t\in\mathbb{Z}\cap[-B,B]:\text{$F(t,X_{1},\ldots,X_{m})$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{m}]$}\}. $$

Then there is a constant $h(m)>0$ depending only on $m$ such that for all $B\geq 1$ ,

$$ R_{T}(F,B)\ll_{m}2^{h(m)d}d^{h(m)}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{h(m)}B^{1/2}. $$

#### Remark 2.15.

Note that the hypotheses of the theorem do not require that $\deg_{T}(F)\geq 1$ . Indeed, if $\deg_{T}(F)=0$ , then the hypothesis that $F(T,X_{1},\ldots,X_{m})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ requires that $F(X_{1},\ldots,X_{m})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , independent of specializing $T=t$ to any value $t$ . Thus the set $R_{T}(F,B)$ is empty for all $B$ , and the theorem is vacuously true. The theorem also does not require $F$ to be monic in $T$ .

To deduce Theorem 2.13, we start by observing that, since $\deg_{Y}(F)\geq 2$ ,

$$ \#\{\bfx\in[-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}:\text{$F(Y,\bfx)=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Z}$}\}\\
\leq\#\{\bfx\in[-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}:\text{$F(Y,\bfx)=0$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y]$}\}. $$

Observe that Theorem 2.13 holds immediately if $\deg_{Y}(F)\geq 2$ but $\deg_{\{X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}\}}(F)=0$ , since then the set on the right-hand side of (2.5) must be empty. For in such a case, $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ for any fixed $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ , so if $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ is reducible then $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is reducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , which contradicts the hypothesis that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is irreducible. Thus from now on we may assume $\deg_{\{X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}\}}(F)\geq 1$ .

If $n=1$ , then by Theorem 2.14 applied to $F(Y,X_{1})$ with $t$ playing the role of $x_{1}$ , then

$$ \#\{x_{1}\in[-B,B]\cap\mathbb{Z}:\text{$F(Y,x_{1})=0$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y]$}\}\ll_{D}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{h(1)}B^{1/2}. $$

From now on, let $n\geq 2$ , and we proceed by induction on the number $n$ of variables. Let us now assume that for any polynomial $G\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1}]$ that is irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1}]$ of degree $\deg_{Y}(G)\geq 2$ and $\deg_{\{X_{1},\ldots,X_{n-1}\}}(G)\geq 1$ , the following inductive hypothesis holds:

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in[-B,B]^{n-1}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}:\text{$G(Y,\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=0$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y]$}\}\\
\ll_{n,\deg G}(\log(\|G\|+2))^{e(n-1)}B^{(n-1)-1/2}, $$

for some $e(n-1)$ .

Suppose $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 2.13. We split up our count according to those $x_{n}$ such that $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})$ is reducible/irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n-1}]$ . We now apply Theorem 2.14 with $t$ playing the role of $x_{n}$ . (It may be that $\deg_{X_{n}}F=0$ , but note that by Remark 2.15, Theorem 2.14 is also applicable in this case.) This leads to:

$$ \#\{x_{n}\in[-B,B]\cap\mathbb{Z}:\text{$F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n-1}]$}\}\\
\ll_{n,D}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{h(n)}B^{\frac{1}{2}}. $$

Now if $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n-1}]$ , then $F(Y,x_{1},...,x_{n-1},x_{n})$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y]$ for any choice of $x_{1},...,x_{n-1}$ , so we count these trivially. Hence the overall contribution to (2.5) of the $x_{n}\in[-B,B]\cap\mathbb{Z}$ such that $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})$ is reducible is bounded by

$$ \ll_{n,D}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{h(n)}B^{(n-1)+\frac{1}{2}}\ll_{n,D}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{h(n)}B^{n-\frac{1}{2}}, $$

which is acceptable.

On the other hand, suppose $x_{n}\in[-B,B]\cap\mathbb{Z}$ is fixed and $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n-1}]$ . To apply the inductive step, we must ensure that

$$ \deg_{Y}F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})\geq 2,\qquad\deg_{\{X_{1},\ldots,X_{n-1}\}}F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})\geq 1. $$

The first property holds since $F$ has constant-leading-coefficient in $Y$ , and we assumed initially that $\deg_{Y}(F)\geq 2$ . Second, suppose that $\deg_{\{X_{1},\ldots,X_{n-1}\}}F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})=0,$ in which case $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y]$ while also being irreducible (in the case we currently consider). Then for all choices of $\mathbf{X}^{\prime}=\mathbf{x}^{\prime}$ , $F(Y,\mathbf{X}^{\prime},x_{n})=F(Y,\mathbf{x}^{\prime},x_{n})$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y]$ , and so no contribution to (2.5) occurs.

Now we may suppose $x_{n}\in[-B,B]\cap\mathbb{Z}$ is fixed, and that $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n-1}]$ , and (2.6) holds. We can apply the inductive hypothesis, obtaining

$$ \#\{\bfx^{\prime}\in[-B,B]^{n-1}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}:\text{$F(Y,\bfx^{\prime},x_{n})$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y]$}\}\ll_{n,D}(\log(\|F_{x_{n}}\|+2))^{e(n-1)}B^{n-1-\frac{1}{2}}. $$

Here $\|F_{x_{n}}\|$ denotes the norm of the polynomial $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})$ and satisfies that $\log(\|F_{x_{n}}\|+2)\ll_{n,D}\log(\|F\|+2)+\log(B)$ . The number of $x_{n}$ which lead to this case is trivially at most $\ll B$ , so the overall contribution from all $x_{n}$ for which $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n-1},x_{n})$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n-1}]$ is $\ll_{n,D}(\log(\|F\|+2)+\log(B))^{e(n-1)}B^{n-\frac{1}{2}}$ .

In total, this argument has proved that for all $B\geq 1$ ,

$$ \#\{\bfx\in[-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}:\text{$F(Y,\bfx)=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Z}$}\}\ll_{n,D}(\log(\|F\|+2)+\log(B))^{e(n)}B^{n-\frac{1}{2}} $$

with $e(n)=\max\{h(n),e(n-1)\}.$ This completes the proof of Theorem 2.13.

## 3. Genericity and key properties

In this section we begin with a theorem that $(1,n)$ -allowable and strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomials are generic. We then prove several key properties of these classes of polynomials, which we will call upon later.

Notation: To work with these classes of polynomials, we define the following notational conventions. For a given subset $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ , we denote $\mathbf{X}_{I}=(X_{i})_{i\in I}$ . For example, if $I=\{2,\ldots,n\}$ then $\mathbf{X}_{I}=(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})$ , so that $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X}_{I})=\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})$ , and a polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ can depend on $Y$ and $X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}$ but not $X_{1}$ . With a slight abuse of notation with respect to the ordering of variables, we indicate by $F(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{I})$ , for a given $\mathbf{x}_{I}\in\mathbb{Q}^{|I|}$ , that $X_{i}$ is evaluated at $x_{i}$ for each $i\in I$ . We will also denote $(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})$ by $\mathbf{X}^{\prime}$ .

In this section, we denote by $\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ the closed irreducible subset of the moduli space of polynomials in $\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ that are monic in $Y$ and satisfy $\deg_{Y}(F)=D$ and $\deg_{X_{i}}(F)\leq k_{i}$ . For a given integer $m|D$ , we denote by $\mathcal{Y}_{n}^{m}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})\subset\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ the subset of polynomials that take the form (1.1).

#### Theorem 3.1 (Genericity).

Fix integers $D\geq 2$ and $k_{1},\ldots,k_{n}\geq 1$ . There exists a finite collection of polynomials $\tilde{h}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{h}_{s}$ in the coefficients of $F\in\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ , not all identically zero on $\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ , such that if $F\in\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ is not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable, then $\tilde{h}_{1}(F)=\cdots=\tilde{h}_{s}(F)=0$ .

Let $\mathcal{M}\subset\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ be a closed irreducible subset. Moreover, assume that there exists $P\in\mathcal{M}$ such that $P$ is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable. Then strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomials are generic in $\mathcal{M}$ .

Fix an integer $m\geq 1$ with $m|D$ . The polynomials $\tilde{h}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{h}_{s}$ are not all identically zero on $\mathcal{Y}^{m}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ . Let $\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathcal{Y}_{n}^{m}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ be a closed irreducible subset, and assume that there exists $P\in\mathcal{Y}$ which is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable. Then strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomials are generic in $\mathcal{Y}$ .

The key conclusions of the theorem are contingent on the existence of at least one explicit example in $\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},\ldots,k_{n})$ , $\mathcal{M}$ , $\mathcal{Y}_{n}^{m}(D,k_{1},\ldots,k_{n})$ , or $\mathcal{Y}$ that confirms the polynomials $\tilde{h}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{h}_{s}$ are not all identically zero on the relevant set. We reserve the construction of these examples to §8, and summarize here the consequences, as two corollaries.

#### Corollary 3.2.

Fix integers $D\geq 2$ and $k_{1},\ldots,k_{n}\geq 1$ . Then strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomials are generic in $\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ . Furthermore, polynomials that are not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable have density zero in $\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ , in the sense that

$$ \frac{\#\{F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n}),\|F\|\leq T:F\text{ is not strongly $(1,n)$-allowable})\}}{\#\{F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n}),\|F\|\leq T\}}\ll\frac{1}{T} $$

for all $T\geq 1$ . For each $m|D$ , the above results hold for $\mathcal{Y}_{n}^{m}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ as well.

#### Proof of Corollary 3.2.

For the first claim, it is enough to observe that $\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ is irreducible and that the polynomial

$$ P=Y^{D}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}^{k_{i}}, $$

is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable, which is verified in Example 8.6 of §8. Then by Theorem 3.1, it follows that strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomials are generic in $\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ .

For the next claim of the corollary, recall that at least one among the polynomials $\tilde{h}_{1},...,\tilde{h}_{s}$ (provided by Theorem 3.1) is not identically zero over $\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ . Let us suppose $\tilde{h}_{1}$ is not identically zero over $\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ . Then the left-hand side of the claim is bounded above by

$$ \frac{\#\{F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n}),\|F\|\leq T:\tilde{h}_{1}(F)=0\}}{\#\{F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n}),\|F\|\leq T\}}\ll\frac{1}{T}. $$

This is because $\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},\ldots,k_{n})$ is isomorphic to affine space $\mathbb{A}^{M}$ (for an appropriate dimension $M$ depending on $n,D,k_{1},\ldots,k_{n}$ ), so that a trivial estimate (Lemma 2.1) saves at least one variable in the count recorded in the numerator. The argument for $\mathcal{Y}_{n}^{m}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ is analogous, since if $D=md$ then the example $P$ lies in $\mathcal{Y}_{n}^{m}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ , and again $\mathcal{Y}_{n}^{m}(D,k_{1},\ldots,k_{n})$ is isomorphic to affine space (of an appropriate dimension). ∎

#### Corollary 3.3.

Fix integers $D\geq 2$ and $k_{1},\ldots,k_{n}\geq 1$ and denote

$$ \mathcal{S}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})=\{P\in\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})\text{: }P\text{ is singular}\}. $$

Then strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomials are generic in $\mathcal{S}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ .

#### Proof of Corollary 3.3.

By Theorem 3.1, it is enough to show that $\mathcal{S}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ is irreducible and that there exists $P\in\mathcal{S}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ that is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable. The fact that $\mathcal{S}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})\subset\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ is a closed irreducible subset follows from [EH16, Proposition $7.1$ , pages $245-246$ ]. By Example 8.8 of §8 there is a polynomial $P\in\mathcal{S}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ which is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable. ∎

### 3.1. Proof of Theorem 3.1

Consider $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},...,k_{n})$ . Assume that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable; this occurs if and only if there exists a linear change of variables $\sigma\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ , some subset $I\subsetneq\{1,...,n\}$ , and an irreducible polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ with $\deg_{Y}G\geq 2$ , such that

$$ \mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/F_{\sigma}(Y,\mathbf{X})\supset\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})\supsetneq\mathbb{Q}(\bfX), $$

in which $F_{\sigma}(Y,\mathbf{X}):=F(Y,\sigma(\mathbf{X}))$ . Without loss of generality, we may suppose that $1\not\in I$ , so that $G$ is independent of $X_{1}$ . In what follows, we denote $M=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/F_{\sigma}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ and $N=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ . Note that $[N:\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})]\geq 2$ . Furthermore,

$$ \deg_{Y}F_{\sigma}=[M:\mathbb{Q}(\bfX)]=[M:N][N:\mathbb{Q}(\bfX)]. $$

Since $[N:\mathbb{Q}(\bfX)]\geq 2$ this implies that $[M:N]<\deg_{Y}F_{\sigma}$ , so $F_{\sigma}$ cannot be irreducible over $N$ . (For later reference, observe that $N=N^{\prime}(X_{1})$ for $N^{\prime}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},...,X_{n})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}))$ , so $F_{\sigma}$ factorizes over $N^{\prime}$ as well.) Now let us decompose $F_{\sigma}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ as

$$ F_{\sigma}(Y,\mathbf{X})=\sum_{j,k}f_{1,j,k}(X_{2},...,X_{n};\sigma)Y^{j}X_{1}^{k}. $$

By Noether’s Lemma 2.6 (ii), there exists a form $G_{R}$ in the coefficients of the expansion (3.2) such that $F_{\sigma}(Y,X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})$ (for a fixed choice of $x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}$ ) is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ or has strictly lower degree than $F_{\sigma}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ , if and only if

$$ G_{R}(\{(f_{1,j,k}(x_{2},...,x_{n};\sigma)\}_{j,k})=0. $$

(While the lemma produces a system of forms, by taking a sum of appropriate powers of these forms, one can construct one such a form $G_{R}$ .) Since $F_{\sigma}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is reducible over $N$ (and hence $N^{\prime}$ as observed above), it follows that for any $x_{2},...,x_{n}$ , $F_{\sigma}(Y,X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})$ is reducible over $\mathbb{Q}[Y]/(G(Y,x_{2},...,x_{n}))\subset\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Thus it follows that

$$ G_{R}(\{(f_{1,j,k}(X_{2},...,X_{n};\sigma)\}_{j,k})\equiv 0. $$

Note that for each $j,k$ the coefficients $f_{1,j,k}(X_{2},...X_{n};\sigma)$ depend polynomially on the entries of $\sigma$ , so that this function is itself a polynomial in $X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}$ , and the entries of $\sigma$ . Thus we may write

$$ G_{R}(\{(f_{1,j,k}(X_{2},...,X_{n};\sigma)\}_{j,k})=\sum_{\bfk\in K}g_{\bfk,F}(\sigma)\prod_{j\neq 1}X_{j}^{k_{j}}, $$

defining a system of polynomials $g_{\bfk,F}(\sigma)$ indexed by a finite set $K$ of multi-indices $\bfk\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n-1}$ of bounded order (depending only on $n,D,k_{1},\ldots,k_{n}$ ). The argument above has shown that if $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable, then there must exist a linear change of variables $\sigma\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $g_{\bfk,F}(\sigma)=0$ for each $\bfk\in K$ . By [Sch76, Chapter V Thm. 1A], there exists a resultant system of forms $h_{1},...,h_{s}$ in the coefficients of the polynomials $g_{\bfk,F}$ such that $\{g_{\bfk,F}(\sigma)=0,\forall\bfk\in K\}$ has a solution in $\sigma\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ if and only if $h_{1}=...=h_{s}=0.$ Moreover, the coefficients of $g_{\bfk,F}$ depend polynomially on the coefficients of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ . Thus, we find that there exists a system of polynomials $\tilde{h}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{h}_{s}$ (functions of the coefficients of $F$ ) such that if $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable then

$$ \tilde{h}_{1}(F)=...=\tilde{h}_{s}(F)=0. $$

By Example 8.7 of §8 there is a polynomial in $\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},\ldots,k_{n})$ that is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable, so we know that the polynomials $\tilde{h}_{1},...,\tilde{h}_{s}$ are not all identically zero on $\mathcal{M}_{n}(D,k_{1},\ldots,k_{n})$ .

For the next claim of the theorem, since we are assuming that there exists $P\in\mathcal{M}$ which is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable, it follows that $\tilde{h}_{1},...,\tilde{h}_{s}$ are not identically zero on $\mathcal{M}$ . Then the result that strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomials are generic in $\mathcal{M}$ follows, since we are assuming $\mathcal{M}$ to be closed and irreducible.

Finally, again by Example 8.7 (when $m|D$ ) there is a polynomial in $\mathcal{Y}^{m}_{n}(D,k_{1},\ldots,k_{n})$ that is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable, so we know that the polynomials $\tilde{h}_{1},...,\tilde{h}_{s}$ are not all identically zero on $\mathcal{Y}^{m}_{n}(D,k_{1},\ldots,k_{n})$ . In particular, if $\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathcal{Y}^{m}_{n}(D,k_{1},\ldots,k_{n})$ is a closed irreducible subset, the claim of the theorem for $\mathcal{Y}$ follows. This completes the proof of the theorem, aside from the explicit construction of Example 8.7, which we verify in §8.

### 3.2. Properties: $n$ -genuine and strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials

There is an equivalent characterization for being strongly $n$ -genuine; this in particular plays a role in §5 as well as [BPW25b].

#### Lemma 3.4.

Let $F\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be an absolutely irreducible polynomial that is monic in $Y$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ and denote $\mathcal{L}_{F}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/F$ . Then $F$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial if and only if for every $j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ ,

$$ \overline{\mathbb{Q}(X_{i})_{i\neq j}}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{i})_{i\neq j}. $$

#### Proof.

Here, for example, the notation $\mathbb{Q}(X_{i})_{i\neq 1}$ indicates $\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})$ . Recall $F$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial if and only if $\mathcal{L}_{F}$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine extension of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ . For each $j\in\{1,...,n\}$ denote $N_{j}=(\overline{\mathbb{Q}(X_{i})_{i\neq j}}\cap\mathcal{L_{F}})(X_{j})$ . By construction, $N_{j}$ is an extension of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ that is not $n$ -genuine. Now assume $\mathcal{L}_{F}$ is strongly $n$ -genuine: if for some $j$ , $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\subsetneq N_{j}\subset\mathcal{L}_{F}$ , this would be a contradiction, since $N_{j}$ is not an $n$ -genuine extension. Thus for each $j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ , $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})=N_{j}$ , and this implies $\overline{\mathbb{Q}(X_{i})_{i\neq j}}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{i})_{i\neq j}.$ In the other direction, suppose $\mathcal{L}_{F}$ is not strongly $n$ -genuine: then there exists some intermediate extension $M^{\prime}$ with $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\subsetneq M^{\prime}\subset\mathcal{L}_{F}$ , which is not $n$ -genuine. Since $M^{\prime}\subset N_{j}$ for some $j$ , we have $N_{j}\neq\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , and this suffices to show $\overline{\mathbb{Q}(X_{i})_{i\neq j}}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}\neq\mathbb{Q}(X_{i})_{i\neq j}.$ ∎

The following lemma is useful to establish whether a polynomial is $n$ -genuine or strongly $n$ -genuine, and this will play a key role in the study of $(1,n)$ -allowable and strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomials as well.

#### Lemma 3.5.

Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\ZZ[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ be an irreducible polynomial, and assume $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is not strongly $n$ -genuine (resp. not $n$ -genuine). Then we can find a non-empty subset $I\subsetneq\{1,...,n\}$ such that for every $\bfx_{I}=(x_{i})_{i\in I}\in\mathbb{Q}^{|I|}$ , the polynomial $F_{\bfx_{I}}(Y,(X_{i})_{i\not\in I})=F(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{I})$ (obtained by the specialization $X_{i}=x_{i}$ for every $i\in I$ ) is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (resp. has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ ).

Here we say that a polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Q}[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ if $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=(Y-Q(\mathbf{X}))\tilde{H}(Y,\mathbf{X}),$ in which $Q(\mathbf{X})\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[\mathbf{X}]$ and $\tilde{H}(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[Y,\mathbf{X}].$ (Suppose a non-empty subset $I\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ has been found such that the conclusion of the lemma holds. Then for every superset $S$ with $I\subseteq S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ , for every $\mathbf{x}_{S}\in\mathbb{Q}^{|S|}$ , the polynomial $F_{\mathbf{x}_{S}}(Y,(X_{j})_{j\notin S})$ has the respective property in the conclusion.)

#### Proof.

We first prove the lemma in the case that the polynomial is not strongly $n$ -genuine. Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\ZZ[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ be an irreducible polynomial that is not strongly $n$ -genuine. This means that we can find $I\subsetneq\{1,...,n\}$ and a polynomial $G\in\ZZ[Y,\mathbf{X}_{i}]$ such that

$$ \mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})\subsetneq\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/G\subset\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/F. $$

In particular, $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is reducible over $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/G$ (by the reasoning applied earlier in (3.1)). For each $\mathbf{x}_{I}\in\mathbb{Z}^{|I|}$ , let $G_{\mathbf{x}_{I}}(Y)$ denote $G(Y,\mathbf{x}_{I})$ . The result now follows since for every $\bfx_{I}\in\mathbb{Q}^{|I|}$ one has that $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}})[Y]/G_{\bfx_{I}}\subset\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}})[Y]$ and $F_{\bfx_{I}}$ is reducible over $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}})[Y]/G_{\bfx_{I}}$ .

Let us assume now that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\ZZ[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ is an irreducible polynomial that is not $n$ -genuine. This means that we can find $I\subsetneq\{1,...,n\}$ and a polynomial $G\in\ZZ[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ such that

$$ \mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/G=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/F. $$

In particular, $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/G$ . Let $Z$ be a root of $G$ , such that

$$ F(Y,\bfX)=(Y-H(\bfX,Z))R(Y,\bfX,Z). $$

For any $\bfx_{I}\in\mathbb{Q}^{|I|}$ , $G_{\bfx_{I}}(Y):=G(Y,\mathbf{x}_{I})\in\mathbb{Q}[Y]$ , thus a solution $z$ of $G_{\bfx_{I}}(Y)=0$ is in $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Hence, we obtain that for this $z\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ ,

$$ F(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{I})=(Y-H(\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{I},z)R(\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{I},z). $$

Now the result follows since $H(\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{I},z)$ and $R(\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{I},z)\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}}]$ .

∎

#### Remark 3.6.

Note in particular that if $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is not strongly $n$ -genuine (respectively, not $n$ -genuine), then we may take the non-empty subset $I\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ to be the set of variables that $G$ depends on, where $G$ is any polynomial with the property (3.3) (respectively, with the property (3.4)).

The previous lemma indicates that the property of having a linear factor in $Y$ over $\bar{\mathbb{Q}}$ will later play a role; we will require the following lemma.

#### Lemma 3.7.

If $F(Y,X_{1})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1}]$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ and is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1})$ , then

$$ F(Y,X_{1})=\prod_{j}(Y-Q_{j}(X_{1})) $$

for $Q_{j}(X_{1})\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[X_{1}]$ for all $j$ . In other words, $F(Y,X_{1})$ splits completely.

#### Proof.

Since $F(Y,X_{1})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1})$ , the automorphisms of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1})[Y]/(F(Y,X_{1}))$ act transitively on the roots of $F(Y,X_{1})$ . Since $F(Y,X_{1})$ has a linear factor over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ ,

$$ F(Y,X_{1})=\prod_{\sigma_{j}}(Y-\sigma(Q(X_{1}))) $$

for some polynomial $Q(X_{1})\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[X_{1}],$ and $\sigma_{j}$ varying over the group of embeddings of the extension $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1})[Y]/F(Y,X_{1})$ in its Galois closure. We observe that $\sigma_{j}(Q(X_{1}))\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[X_{1}]$ to complete the proof. ∎

Being $n$ -genuine is preserved by simple scaling transformations, as we will later require.

#### Lemma 3.8 (Preservation under scaling).

Let $S\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ denote a (diagonal) matrix that scales $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})$ to $(s_{1}x_{1},\ldots,s_{n}x_{n})$ , with $s_{i}\neq 0$ for each $i$ . Then $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is $n$ -genuine (resp. strongly $n$ -genuine) if and only if $F(Y,S\mathbf{X})$ is $n$ -genuine (resp. strongly $n$ -genuine).

#### Proof.

Let $S$ denote a matrix that scales $x_{i}\mapsto s_{i}x_{i}$ for $s_{i}\neq 0$ for each $i$ . Consider the extensions defined by $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ and $F(Y,S\mathbf{X})$ , namely

$$ \frac{\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]}{F(Y,\mathbf{X})}\cong\frac{\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]}{F(Y,S\mathbf{X})}, $$

and these fields are isomorphic under map $S$ . Now assume that there exists a $G(Y,\mathbf{X})$ such that $G(Y,X_{2},...,X_{n})$ is a polynomial in the variables $Y,X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}$ and that $G(Y,\mathbf{X})$ determines a subfield:

$$ \frac{\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]}{G(Y,\mathbf{X})}\subset\frac{\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]}{F(Y,\mathbf{X})}. $$

Then since subfields are preserved under isomorphism, we know that

$$ \frac{\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]}{G(Y,S\mathbf{X})}\subset\frac{\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]}{F(Y,S\mathbf{X})}. $$

However, since $S$ is a scaling matrix, $G(Y,S\mathbf{X})$ is also a polynomial in $Y,X_{2},...,X_{n}$ . Thus, we know that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is not $n$ -genuine (resp. not strongly $n$ -genuine) if and only if $F(Y,S\mathbf{X})$ is not $n$ -genuine (resp. not strongly $n$ -genuine). ∎

## 4. $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials

The main goal of this section is to prove Theorems 1.4 and 1.5. The key input is the following result:

#### Theorem 4.1.

Let $R(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be a polynomial that is $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine. Then there exists an integer $e=e(n)$ such that for every integer $d\geq 1$ and every $B\geq 1$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}\in[-B,B]\cap d^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{n}:\exists y\in\mathbb{Z}:R(y,\mathbf{x})=0\}\ll_{n,\deg R}\log(\|R\|+2)^{e}(dB)^{n-1}(\log d(B+2))^{2e}. $$

#### Deduction of Theorem 1.5.

This immediately implies Theorem 1.5, by taking $d=1$ . ∎

As explained in Remark 4.7 below, a polynomial $R$ that is $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine must have $\deg_{Y}R\geq 4$ ; similarly for a polynomial that is $(1,n)$ -allowable but not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable. To deduce Theorem 1.4 (and later Theorem 1.2), it is useful to record a corollary.

#### Corollary 4.2.

Let $F\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be given, along with a transformation $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ with all integral entries such that $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}):=F(Y,L(\mathbf{X}))\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ is $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine. Denote by $\|L\|=\max_{i,j}\|L_{i,j}\|$ , where for a rational number in lowest terms $\|a/b\|:=\max(|a|,|b|)$ . Then there exist integers $e=e(n)$ and $e^{\prime}=e^{\prime}(n)$ such that

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F}\|L\|^{e^{\prime}}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{e}B^{n-1}(\log(B+2))^{2e}. $$

#### Proof of Corollary 4.2.

For simplicity we may assume $\|F\|\geq 3$ , $\|F_{L}\|\geq 3$ , $B\geq 3$ . By Theorem 4.1, for all integers $d\geq 1$ , and for all $B\geq 3$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}\in[-B,B]\cap d^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{n}:\exists y\in\mathbb{Z}:F(y,L(\mathbf{x}))=0\}\ll_{n,\deg F}(\log\|F_{L}\|)^{e}(dB)^{n-1}(\log dB)^{2e}. $$

The set on the left-hand side identifies with the set on the left-hand side of the equivalent bound

$$ \#\{\mathbf{z}\in L([-B,B]\cap d^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{n}):\exists y\in\mathbb{Z}:F(y,\mathbf{z})=0\}\ll_{n,\deg F}(\log\|F_{L}\|)^{e}(dB)^{n-1}(\log dB)^{2e}. $$

We will next choose $d$ (and modify $B$ ) so that the values of $\mathbf{z}$ considered in this set include all integral points in a box.

#### Lemma 4.3.

Given $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ , there exist constants $1\leq c\ll_{n}\|L\|^{n^{2}}$ and $1\leq d\leq\|L\|^{n^{2}}$ such that

$$ [-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}\subset L([-cB,cB]^{n}\cap d^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{n}). $$

#### Proof.

It is equivalent to show that there exist such $c,d$ with the property that $L^{-1}([-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n})\subset[-cB,cB]^{n}\cap d^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{n}.$ Write $L^{-1}=(\det L)^{-1}M$ in which $M$ is the adjugate matrix to $L$ . By taking $d=\det L$ (so that $1\leq d\leq\|L\|^{n^{2}}$ ), it then suffices to find $c$ such that $M([-B,B]^{n})\subset[-cB,cB]^{n}$ . Such a $c$ with $1\leq c\ll_{n}\|L\|^{n^{2}}$ can be obtained by noting that each entry in the adjugate matrix is $\ll_{n}\|L\|^{(n-1)^{2}}.$ ∎

By the lemma, there exist integers $1\leq c_{L}\ll_{n}\|L\|^{n^{2}}$ and $1\leq d_{L}\leq\|L\|^{n^{2}}$ such that

$$ [-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}\subset L([-c_{L}B,c_{L}B]^{n}\cap d_{L}^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{n}). $$

We then learn from applying (4.1) (with $B$ replaced by $c_{L}B$ ) that

$$ \displaystyle N(F,B) \displaystyle\leq\#\{\mathbf{z}\in L([-c_{L}B,c_{L}B]\cap d_{L}^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{n}):\exists y\in\mathbb{Z}:F(y,\mathbf{z})=0\} \displaystyle\ll_{n,\deg F}(\log\|F_{L}\|)^{e}(c_{L}d_{L}B)^{n-1}(\log(c_{L}d_{L}B))^{2e} \displaystyle\ll_{n,\deg F}\|L\|^{e^{\prime}}(\log\|F\|)^{e}B^{n-1}(\log B)^{2e}, $$

for some $e^{\prime}=e^{\prime}(n)$ . Here we have applied that $\log\|F_{L}\|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|L\|+\log\|F\|.$ ∎

### 4.1. Deduction of Theorem 1.4

Under the hypothesis of Theorem 1.4, a given polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is $(1,n)$ -allowable but not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable.

#### Lemma 4.4.

Let $F\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be a $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomial which is not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable. Then there exists a transformation $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ with all integral entries such that $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}):=F(Y,L(\mathbf{X}))\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ and $\mathbb{Q}(\bfX)[Y]/(F_{L}(Y,\bfX))$ is $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine.

#### Proof.

By hypothesis $F$ is not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable, so there exists a transformation $L^{\prime}\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $F_{L^{\prime}}(Y,\mathbf{X}):=F(Y,L^{\prime}(\mathbf{X}))$ is $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine. Let $N$ be a positive integer such that $NL^{\prime}$ has all integral entries, and let $S=NI_{n}$ denote the corresponding scaling matrix; define the matrix $L=SL^{\prime}$ . Then by Lemma 3.8, $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine.

∎

Now, given $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ under the hypothesis of Theorem 1.4, we set $L$ to be a transformation as provided by Lemma 4.4, so that $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}):=F(Y,L(\mathbf{X}))$ is $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine. An application of Corollary 4.2 shows that $N(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F}\|L\|^{e^{\prime}}(\log\|F\|)^{e}B^{n-1}(\log B)^{2e}$ for certain $e=e(n),e^{\prime}=e^{\prime}(n)$ . The factor $\|L\|$ depends on $F$ but in an unspecified way. Thus we conclude that $N(F,B)\ll_{n,F}B^{n-1}(\log B)^{e^{\prime\prime}}$ for some $e^{\prime\prime}=e^{\prime\prime}(n),$ with unspecified dependence on $F$ in the implicit constant. This concludes the proof of Theorem 1.4.

### 4.2. Preliminaries: $n$ -genuine polynomials and linear factors

We turn to proving Theorem 4.1. Our principal results in this section are two-fold. First, we bound a count for the number of specializations of an $n$ -genuine polynomial that have a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Precisely, we say that $F(Y,X_{1})\in\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1}]$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ if

$$ F(Y,X_{1})=(Y-Q(X_{1}))\tilde{H}(Y,X_{1}), $$

where $Q(X_{1})\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[X_{1}]$ and $\tilde{H}(Y,X_{1})\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[Y,X_{1}].$

#### Lemma 4.5.
