Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be an $n$ -genuine polynomial. Then for all $B\geq 1$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in[-B,B]^{n-1}:F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\textrm{ has a linear factor in $Y$ over }\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\}\ll_{n,\deg F}B^{n-2}. $$

Second, we make a variable-reducing observation that applies to polynomials that are $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine.

#### Lemma 4.6.

Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ be absolutely irreducible, but not a strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial. Then there exists a polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ depending only $Y,\{X_{i}\}_{i\in I}$ for an index set $1\leq|I|<n$ , with the following properties:

$$ \mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})\subsetneq\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X}))\subseteq\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(F(Y,\mathbf{X})); $$

$G$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , monic in $Y$ , $\deg_{Y}G\geq 2$ , and $1\leq\deg_{X_{i}}G\ll_{n,\deg F}1$ for each $i\in I$ . Moreover, if $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ satisfies that $F(Y,\mathbf{x})=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Z}$ , then $G(Z,(x_{i})_{i\in I})=0$ is also solvable over $\mathbb{Z}$ . Additionally, we can choose $G(Y,\mathbf{X})=G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ such that $\log\|G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})\|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F(Y,\mathbf{X})\|.$

#### Remark 4.7.

In particular, if $F$ is $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine, then the right-most inclusion in (4.3) is strict, and $2\leq\deg_{Y}G$ is a proper divisor of $\deg_{Y}F$ (and thus such $F$ can only exist if $\deg_{Y}F\geq 4$ ).

### 4.3. Preparation to prove Lemma 4.5

The following lemma considers the integral closure of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})$ (omitting the variable $X_{1}$ ) in $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/F$ , and constructs a nonempty open set that will be useful for an application of Noether’s lemma.

#### Lemma 4.8.

Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be absolutely irreducible and monic in $Y$ . Consider the integral closure of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},...,X_{n})$ in $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/F$ , which we denote by $K_{\hat{1}}.$ Suppose $G(Y,X_{2},...,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}]$ is an irreducible polynomial such that

$$ K_{\hat{1}}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},...,X_{n})[Y]/G(Y,X_{2},...,X_{n}). $$

Then there exists a nonempty open set $V\subset\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}$ such that for all $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in V$ , $\mathbb{Q}[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is integrally closed in $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1})[Y]/(F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}))$ .

#### Proof.

If $\deg_{X_{1}}F=0$ , the lemma is trivially true, since we may simply take $G$ to be the polynomial $F$ , and $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(F(Y,\mathbf{X}))=K_{\hat{1}}(X_{1})$ . In general, let

$$ W_{F}=\textbf{Spec}(\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/F(Y,\mathbf{X})),\qquad W_{G}=\textbf{Spec}(\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},...,X_{n})[Y]/G(Y,X_{2},...,X_{n})). $$

The inclusion of fields gives us a morphism

$$ f:W_{F}\rightarrow W_{G}. $$

Let $V^{\prime}$ be the set of points $u\in W_{G}$ where the fiber

$$ f_{u}:W_{F,u}\rightarrow W_{G,u} $$

is geometrically integral. We claim that this contains a nonempty open set.

By [Gro66, EGA IV part 3, Theorem 9.7.7], $V^{\prime}$ is locally constructible. Since $G$ is defined so that $\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},...,X_{n})[Y]/G(Y,X_{2},...,X_{n})$ is algebraically closed in $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ , we get that the generic fiber is geometrically integral and therefore contained in $V^{\prime}$ . Hence, $V^{\prime}$ contains a nonempty open subset $V$ such that for all $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in V$ , $k(W_{G,\mathbf{x}^{\prime}})$ is integrally closed in $k(W_{F,\mathbf{x}^{\prime}})$ . (Here we use the standard notation in algebraic geometry that $k(u)$ is the residue field at $u$ .) That is to say, for all $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in V$ , $\mathbb{Q}[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is integrally closed in $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1})[Y]/(F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})).$ ∎

### 4.4. Proof of Lemma 4.5

We use Noether’s Lemma 2.6 (i) in combination with Lemma 4.8 and Lemma 3.7 to count the number of specializations $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}$ for which $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Let $F$ be given as in Lemma 4.5, with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ and $\deg_{X_{j}}F=k_{j}$ for $j=1,\ldots,n$ . In particular, each $k_{j}\geq 1$ since $F$ is $n$ -genuine. Define the multi-index $e=(1,k_{1})$ . Let $G_{L}$ denote a form provided by Lemma 2.6 for $K=\mathbb{Q}$ , which tests for any $H(Y,X_{1})\in\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1}]$ the divisibility condition $\mathcal{D}(e)$ to hold for $H(Y,X_{1})$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . (Lemma 2.6 provides a collection of forms $\{G_{1},...,G_{s}\}$ which determine when $H(Y,X_{1})$ has a linear factor, rather than a single form. We can take $G_{L}=G_{1}^{2\ell_{1}}+...+G_{s}^{2\ell_{s}}$ for appropriate powers $\ell_{i}$ to obtain a single form of degree $2\ell$ where $\ell$ is the $\mathrm{lcm}$ of the degrees of the $G_{i}$ .) Note in particular, if $H(Y,X_{1})$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ then divisibility condition $\mathcal{D}(e)$ holds for $H(Y,X_{1})$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ .

Suppose now that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ is $n$ -genuine. Denote the coefficients of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ as a polynomial in $Y,X_{1}$ by

$$ F(Y,\mathbf{X})=\sum_{i_{0},i_{1}}a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(X_{2},...,X_{n})Y^{i_{0}}X_{1}^{i_{1}}. $$

Here $a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(X_{2},...,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}]$ ; in particular $a_{\deg_{Y}F,k_{j}}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime})\equiv 1$ since $F$ is monic in $Y$ . Let $G_{L}((a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime})))\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}^{\prime}]$ denote the form specified above, so that $G_{L}((a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})))=0$ if and only if $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ satisfies divisibility condition $\mathcal{D}(e)$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (or the degree of $F$ , as a polynomial in $Y,X_{1}$ , drops). In particular, if $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , then $G_{L}((a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})))=0$ .

We aim to show that the form $G_{L}$ is not identically zero as a function of $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}=(x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})$ . Once this has been verified, it follows from the trivial bound (Lemma 2.1) that at most $\ll_{\deg G_{L}}B^{n-2}$ choices of $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in[-B,B]^{n}$ lead to $G_{L}((a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})))=0$ . Since by Lemma 2.6 (i), $\deg G_{L}\ll_{n,\deg F}1$ , this suffices for the claim in Lemma 4.5.

Now we show that $G_{L}$ is not identically zero. We first consider the integral closure of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},...,X_{n})$ in $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/F$ , which we denote by $K_{\hat{1}}.$ Then we can find an irreducible polynomial $G(Y,X_{2},...,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}]$ such that

$$ K_{\hat{1}}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},...,X_{n})[Y]/G(Y,X_{2},...,X_{n}). $$

Since $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is an $n$ -genuine polynomial, we must have $\deg_{Y}(F)>\deg_{Y}(G)$ , otherwise $G$ would provide a polynomial in $Y$ and $(X_{i})_{i\in\{2,\ldots,n\}}$ that violates the definition of $F$ being $n$ -genuine. By Hilbert’s irreducibility theorem (Theorem 2.10), we can find a dense set $U_{F,G}^{\prime}\subset\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}$ such that $F(Y,X_{1},\bfx^{\prime})$ and $G(Y,\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ are both irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ for all $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in U_{F,G}^{\prime}$ . Moreover, take the open subset

$$ V=\{(x_{2},...,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}:a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(x_{2},...,x_{n})\neq 0\text{ for all $i_{0},i_{1}$ such that $a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime})\not\equiv 0$}\}. $$

Then the set $U_{F,G}=U_{F,G}^{\prime}\cap V$ is dense in $\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}$ . Now assume for contradiction that $G_{L}=0$ on $U_{F,G}$ . Under this hypothesis, observe that for every $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in U_{F,G}$ , $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ and is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1})$ : indeed for every $\bfx^{\prime}\in U_{F,G}$ we have $\deg_{X_{1}}(F(Y,X_{1},\bfx^{\prime}))=k_{1}$ and $\deg_{Y}(F(Y,X_{1},\bfx^{\prime}))=\deg_{Y}F$ , since $U_{F,G}\subset V$ (so the degree does not drop). We also have by the assumption that $G_{L}=0$ on $U_{F,G}$ that $F=HG$ , where $\deg_{Y}(G)\leq 1$ . On the other hand, since $F(Y,X_{1},\bfx)$ is monic in $Y$ , the only possibility is $\deg_{Y}(G)=1$ .

Thus fix any $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in U_{F,G}$ , and then $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ and is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1})$ . Then by Lemma 3.7, $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ splits completely. Consequently, the splitting field of $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ over $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1})$ is of the form $R_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}(X_{1})$ for $R_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}$ a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ . Hence we can find $K_{\bfx^{\prime}}\subset R_{\bfx^{\prime}}$ such that $K_{\bfx^{\prime}}(X_{1})=\mathbb{Q}(X_{1})[Y]/(F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}))$ . Observe that this implies that $[K_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}:\mathbb{Q}]=\deg_{Y}F$ . Next, we consider

$$ S_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}:=\mathbb{Q}[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\subset K_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}. $$

We know that $[S_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}:\mathbb{Q}]=\deg_{Y}(G)<\deg_{Y}(F)=[K_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}:\mathbb{Q}]$ . So, for the fixed $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in U_{F,G}$ we considered, $S_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}$ cannot be integrally closed in $K_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}$ since $S_{\bfx^{\prime}}\subset K_{\bfx^{\prime}}$ are both finite extensions of $\mathbb{Q}$ . In conclusion, if $G_{L}=0$ on $U_{F,G}$ , then for all $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in U_{F,G}$ , $S_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}$ is not integrally closed in $K_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}$ .

On the other hand, Lemma 4.8 provides a nonempty open set $V\subset\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}$ such that for every $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in V$ , $S_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}=\mathbb{Q}[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is integrally closed in $K_{\bfx^{\prime}}(X_{1})=\mathbb{Q}(X_{1})[Y]/(F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}))$ . Since $X_{1}$ is transcendental over $K_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}$ , this implies that $S_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}$ is integrally closed in $K_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}$ . This directly leads to a contradiction, since $U_{F,G}\cap V$ is a nonempty set, and for any $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in U_{F,G}\cap V$ , it would occur both that $S_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}$ is not integrally closed in $K_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}$ and $S_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}$ is integrally closed in $K_{\bfx^{\prime}}$ . In conclusion, $G_{L}$ is not identically zero on $U_{F,G}$ , and the lemma is proved.

### 4.5. Proof of Lemma 4.6

We turn to Lemma 4.6, on the variable-reducing property implied by a polynomial $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ being not strongly $n$ -genuine. Let $E$ denote the total degree of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ , and let $D=\deg_{Y}F$ . Then by definition, there exists some subextension $M_{1}$ such that

$$ \mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})\subsetneq M_{1}\subset\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(F(Y,\mathbf{X})) $$

and $M_{1}$ is not $n$ -genuine. Let us first establish some properties of any such $M_{1}$ .

Since $M_{1}$ is not $n$ -genuine, we can find a subset $I\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $G_{1}(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})\in\mathbb{Q}[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ such that $M_{1}=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}))$ . Note that $I$ is nonempty since the left-most inclusion $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})\subsetneq M_{1}$ is strict (however, the right-most inclusion need not be strict, since we do not assume that $F$ is $n$ -genuine); additionally we can take $|I|=n-1$ . For notational simplicity, assume that $I=\{2,\ldots,n\}$ and that $1\not\in I$ . Since $G_{1}(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is independent of $X_{1}$ , we can write $M_{1}=M_{I}(X_{1})$ , where $M_{I}=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X}_{I})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}))$ . Furthermore, for any element $S$ of $M_{I}$ , we note that the minimal polynomial of $S$ over $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ will not be $n$ -genuine (as it will be independent of $X_{1})$ .

Now, we return to our original extension $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(F(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ that is not strongly $n$ -genuine. Our aim is to construct a polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ such that $\log\|G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})\|\ll_{n,E,D}\log\|F(Y,\mathbf{X})\|$ and such that $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})\subsetneq M^{\prime}=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}))\subset\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(F(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ (observe that we may not construct the $M_{1}$ chosen above – $M^{\prime}$ may be a different subextension that is also not $n$ -genuine.)

Let $T$ denote a root of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ such that $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(F(Y,\mathbf{X}))=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})(T).$ Let $b(Z)\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X},Z]$ denote a polynomial in $Z$ , with coefficients $b_{i}(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}]$ that have total degree at most $B$ , of the following form:

$$ b(Z)=b_{1}(\mathbf{X})Z+\ldots+b_{D-1}(\mathbf{X})Z^{D-1}. $$

For each $b_{i}(\mathbf{X})$ , we can expand the expression as

$$ b_{i}(\mathbf{X})=\sum_{e_{1}+...+e_{n}\leq B}b_{i,\bfe}X_{1}^{e_{1}}...X_{n}^{e_{n}}. $$

We note that for $T$ as chosen above, $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})(b(T))\subset\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})(T)$ for any such polynomial $b(T)$ . Moreover, we know that if $b(Z)$ is a nonzero polynomial, then $b(T)\not\in\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ since $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is irreducible and no polynomial of degree $<\deg_{Y}F=D$ in $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]$ can have $T$ as a root; consequently, if $b(Z)$ is a nontrivial polynomial, then $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})\subsetneq\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})(b(T))\subset\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})(T)$ . We will show that there exists a polynomial, called $a(Z)\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X},Z]$ , with sufficiently small coefficient polynomials $a_{1}(\mathbf{X}),...,a_{D-1}(\mathbf{X})$ satisfying that $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})(a(T))$ is not $n$ -genuine – in particular, the minimal polynomial of $a(T)$ will be independent of $X_{1}$ .

Consider for any polynomial $b(Z)\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X},Z]$ the minimal polynomial $m_{b}(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ of the element $b(T)$ over $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ . If we write

$$ m_{b}(Y,\mathbf{X})=c_{0}(\mathbf{X})+c_{1}(\mathbf{X})Y+\ldots+c_{\deg_{Y}m_{b}}(\mathbf{X})Y^{\deg_{Y}m_{b}}, $$

then each coefficient polynomial $c_{j}(\mathbf{X})$ is a symmetric polynomial of degree $j$ in the conjugates of $b(T)$ . Note that $\deg_{Y}m_{b}\leq D.$ Hence, the coefficients of $c_{j}(\mathbf{X})$ for each $j$ (viewed as a polynomial in $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}]$ ) will be linear combinations of $(b_{i,\bfe})_{i=1,...,D-1,|\bfe|\leq B}$ ; specifically, if

$$ c_{j}(\mathbf{X})=\sum c_{j,\mathbf{e}^{\prime}}X_{1}^{e_{1}^{\prime}}...X_{n}^{e_{n}^{\prime}}, $$

then for each $j$ and $\mathbf{e^{\prime}}$ , we can write

$$ c_{j,\bfe^{\prime}}=\sum_{i=0}^{D-1}\sum_{|\bfe|\leq B}\alpha_{i,j,\bfe^{\prime},\bfe}b_{i,\bfe}, $$

where $\alpha_{i,j,\bfe^{\prime},\bfe}$ are polynomials, in the coefficients of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ , of degree $\leq j$ .

Let us ask for $c_{j,\bfe^{\prime}}$ to be zero for any $\bfe^{\prime}=(e_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,e_{n}^{\prime})$ with $e_{1}^{\prime}\geq 1$ ; in other words, $m_{b}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is independent of $X_{1}$ . We can see that this defines a linear system of equations in the variables $(b_{i,\bfe})_{i=1,...,D-1,|\bfe|\leq B}$ and the corresponding matrix has entries bounded by $\|F\|^{D}$ . We can now input our assumption that $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(F(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ is not $n$ -genuine and thus a subextension $M_{1}=M_{I}(X_{1})$ exists, as described at the start of the proof; recall that the minimal polynomial of any element of $M_{I}$ over $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ will be independent of $X_{1}$ . Further, since

$$ \displaystyle M_{1}\subset\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(F(Y,\mathbf{X})) \displaystyle=\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},...,X_{n},Y)[X_{1}]/(F(Y,\mathbf{X})) \displaystyle=\ldots=\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n-1},Y)[X_{n}]/(F(Y,\mathbf{X})), $$

we can take any such minimal polynomial to have total degree $\leq E$ . This implies that for $B:=E$ (as we fix from now on), our linear system of equations (defined above) has a nullspace with rank $\geq 1$ , as there is a nontrivial solution given by the minimal polynomial of any element of $M_{I}\setminus\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X}).$

By Lemma 4.9 (below), we can now construct a nontrivial solution to our linear system of equations, denoted as $(a_{i,\bfe})_{i=1,...,D-1,|\bfe|\leq E}$ satisfying that $\|\bfa\|=\max_{i,\bfe}|a_{i,\bfe}|\ll_{n,E}\|F\|^{C_{n,E}}$ , where $C_{n,E}$ is a constant only depending on $n$ and $E$ , the total degree of $F$ . This set of coefficients then gives us a polynomial $a(Z)\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X},Z]$ satisfying that the minimal polynomial of $a(T)$ over $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ , denoted as $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}):=m_{a}(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ , is independent of $X_{1}$ . Further, since $\|\mathbf{a}\|\ll_{n,E}\|F\|^{C_{n,E}}$ and the coefficients of $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ are given by polynomials of degree $\leq D$ in $(a_{i,\bfe})$ and the coefficients of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ , we know that $\log\|G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})\|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|.$ Further, since $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is a minimal polynomial, we know that $G$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ and $1\leq\deg_{X_{i}}G\leq E=\deg F$ for each $i$ . Additionally, $a(Z)$ is a nonzero polynomial and hence $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})\subsetneq\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})(a(T))$ , so we know that $2\leq\deg_{Y}G.$

Finally, we must check that if $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ satisfies that $F(Y,\mathbf{x})$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Z}$ , then $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})=0$ is also solvable over $\mathbb{Z}$ . Let $\sigma_{i}$ be an element of the Galois group of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ and set $T_{i}=\sigma_{i}(T)$ ; it follows that

$$ \sigma_{i}(a(T))=a_{1}(\mathbf{X})T_{i}+\ldots+a_{D-1}(\mathbf{X})T_{i}^{D-1}. $$

Moreover, since $\sigma_{i}$ preserves the elements of $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})$ , $\sigma_{i}(a(T))$ is also a root of $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ .

Now, let $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ be such that $F(Y,\mathbf{x})=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Z}$ . Consequently, for some $i\in\{1,\ldots,D\}$ , it must be that $t_{i}:=T_{i}\bmod(X_{1}-x_{1},...,X_{n}-x_{n})$ (that is, specializing each $X_{i}$ to $x_{i}$ ) is in $\mathbb{Z}$ . For this $i$ , $\sigma_{i}(a(T))\bmod(X_{1}-x_{1},...,X_{n}-x_{n})$ is a root of $G(Y,\mathbf{x}_{I})$ and

$$ \sigma_{i}(a(T))\bmod(X_{1}-x_{1},...,X_{n}-x_{n})=a_{1}(\mathbf{x})t_{i}+...+a_{D-1}(\mathbf{x})t_{i}^{D-1}\in\mathbb{Z}. $$

Thus, $G(Y,\mathbf{x}_{I})=0$ is solvable over $\mathbb{Z}$ . This completes the proof of Lemma 4.6.

#### Lemma 4.9.

Suppose $A$ is an $m_{1}\times m_{2}$ singular matrix with rank $s<\min\{m_{1},m_{2}\}$ and with each entry $a_{ij}$ an integer satisfying $|a_{ij}|\leq M$ . Then there exists a nonzero integral vector $\bfb$ in the nullspace of $A$ with $\|\bfb\|=\max_{i}|b_{i}|\ll_{s}M^{s}$ .

#### Proof.

Since $A$ has rank $s$ , all minors of size $(s+1)\times(s+1)$ vanish, while there is at least one $s\times s$ minor that is nonzero; we may assume it arises within the top left $(s+1)\times(s+1)$ submatrix of $A$ by omitting the first row and first column. Let $A^{\prime}$ denote the $m_{1}\times(s+1)$ submatrix of $A$ that takes the first $(s+1)$ columns of $A$ ; by hypothesis every $(s+1)\times(s+1)$ minor of $A^{\prime}$ vanishes. It suffices to find a nonzero vector $\bfb^{\prime}$ of length $(s+1)$ in the nullspace of $A^{\prime}$ , and then padding $\bfb^{\prime}$ with zeroes for the last $m_{2}-(s+1)$ entries will suffice to construct a nonzero vector $\bfb$ of length $m_{2}$ such that $A\bfb=\mathbf{0}$ .

Define $\bfb^{\prime}=(b_{1},\ldots,b_{s+1})$ so that for each $1\leq j\leq s+1$ , $b_{j}$ is the cofactor obtained within the top $(s+1)\times(s+1)$ block of $A^{\prime}$ by deleting the first row and $j$ -th column. By construction, $\|\bfb^{\prime}\|\ll_{s}M^{s}$ . Note also that $b_{1}\neq 0$ , by hypothesis. Now observe that for each row $\mathbf{r}_{i}$ of the matrix $A^{\prime}$ ,

$$ \mathbf{r}_{i}\cdot\bfb^{\prime}=\det\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\mathbf{r}_{i}\\
\mathbf{r}_{2}\\
\vdots\\
\mathbf{r}_{s+1}\end{array}\right)=0 $$

so that $A^{\prime}\bfb^{\prime}=\mathbf{0}$ . Indeed, if $2\leq i\leq s+1$ this determinant vanishes since the matrix depicted has two identical rows. If $i=1$ or if $i>s+1$ , this determinant vanishes since (up to sign) it is an $(s+1)\times(s+1)$ minor of $A^{\prime}$ , which by hypothesis must vanish.

### 4.6. Proof of Theorem 4.1

The main inputs to prove Theorem 4.1 are Lemma 4.5, Lemma 4.6, and Theorem 2.13, which saves essentially $B^{1/2}$ off the trivial bound for $N(F,B)$ . For simplicity we may assume in what follows that $B\geq 3$ .

As in Theorem 4.1, suppose that $R(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,\mathbf{X}]$ is an $n$ -genuine polynomial but not a strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial. By Lemma 4.6, there exists a subset $I\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and a polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ satisfying

$$ \mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\subsetneq\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}))\subsetneq\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(R(Y,\mathbf{X})), $$

and such that if $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ satisfies that there exists $y\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that $R(y,\mathbf{x})=0$ then there also exists $z\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that $G(z,\mathbf{x}_{I})=0$ . As stated in the lemma, $G$ is irreducible, monic in $Y$ , $\deg_{Y}G\geq 2$ , and for each $i\in I$ , $1\leq\deg_{X_{i}}(G)\leq[\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(R(Y,\mathbf{X})):\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})]\ll_{n,\deg R}1.$ Additionally, $\log\|G\|\ll_{n,\deg R}\log\|R\|.$ Without loss of generality, we can assume that $I\subset\{2,\ldots,n\}$ so that $G(Y,\mathbf{X})$ can be written as $G(Y,X_{2},...,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}]$ (independent of $X_{1}$ ). Let $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}$ denote $(x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})$ .

In the context of Theorem 4.1, it suffices to bound the count:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in d^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}\\
\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in[-B,B]^{n-1}\end{subarray}} \displaystyle\#\{x_{1}\in[-B,B]\cap d^{-1}\mathbb{Z},\exists y\in\mathbb{Z},R(y,x_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=0\} \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in d^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}\\
\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in[-B,B]^{n-1}\\
\exists z\in\mathbb{Z}:G(z,\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=0\end{subarray}}\#\{x_{1}\in[-B,B]\cap d^{-1}\mathbb{Z},\exists y\in\mathbb{Z},R(y,x_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=0\} \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}\\
\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in[-dB,dB]^{n-1}\\
\exists z\in\mathbb{Z}:G_{d}(z,\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=0\end{subarray}}\#\{x_{1}\in[-dB,dB]\cap\mathbb{Z}:\exists y\in\mathbb{Z},R_{d}(y,x_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=0\}, $$

in which the last identity holds with the definitions

$$ R_{d}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}):=d^{\deg(R)}R(Y,X_{1}/d,\mathbf{x}^{\prime}/d)\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1}],\quad G_{d}(Z,\mathbf{X}^{\prime}):=d^{\deg G}G(Y,\mathbf{X}^{\prime}/d)\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,\mathbf{X}^{\prime}]. $$

In particular, $R_{d}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is a polynomial with integral coefficients, and with constant-leading-coefficient in $Y$ . (Precisely, since $R$ is monic in $Y$ , $R_{d}$ has leading coefficient $d^{\deg R}$ in $Y$ .) Moreover, the polynomial $R_{d}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{X}^{\prime})$ is $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine, by Lemma 3.8. For each $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$ , $R_{d}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=0$ defines a curve in $\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{Q})$ .

Let $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$ be fixed. Observe that since the original $R(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is monic in $Y$ , if we decompose it into irreducible factors over $\mathbb{Q}$ , say

$$ R(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=\prod_{i}R^{(i)}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}), $$

then by Gauss’s lemma each factor $R^{(i)}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ has integral coefficients. For each $i$ , define $R_{d}^{(i)}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{X}^{\prime}):=d^{\deg(R^{(i)})}R^{(i)}(Y,X_{1}/d,\mathbf{X}^{\prime}/d)$ . Then the above decomposition into irreducible factors over $\mathbb{Q}$ yields a decomposition

$$ R_{d}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=\prod_{i}R_{d}^{(i)}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}), $$

with each $R_{d}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1}]$ irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ . In particular each $R_{d}^{(i)}$ has constant-leading-coefficient in $Y$ , and there are at most $\deg R$ terms in the indexing set. If for at least one index $i$ , $R_{d}^{(i)}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is linear in $Y$ , we will say below that “ $R_{d}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ has a linear factor.” In any case, by the factorization, for each fixed $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$ ,

$$ \#\{x_{1}\in[-dB,dB]\cap\mathbb{Z}:\exists y\in\mathbb{Z},R_{d}(y,x_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=0\}\\
\leq\sum_{i}\#\{x_{1}\in[-dB,dB]\cap\mathbb{Z}:\exists y\in\mathbb{Z},R_{d}^{(i)}(y,x_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=0\}. $$

So we proceed to estimate the size of this set for each irreducible factor $R_{d}^{(i)}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ .

First, suppose that $\deg_{Y}(R_{d}^{(i)}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}))=0$ so it can be written as $R_{d}^{(i)}(X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ . In this case

$$ \#\{x_{1}\in[-dB,dB]\cap\mathbb{Z}:R_{d}^{(i)}(x_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=0\}\ll\deg(R). $$

Second, suppose that $R_{d}^{(i)}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is linear in $Y$ . Then the best bound available is the trivial

$$ \#\{x_{1}\in[-dB,dB]\cap\mathbb{Z}:\exists y\in\mathbb{Z},R_{d}^{(i)}(y,x_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=0\}\ll dB. $$

Finally, suppose that $\deg_{Y}(R_{d}^{(i)}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}))\geq 2$ . We now apply Theorem 2.13 to $R_{d}^{(i)}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ in the variables $Y,X_{1}$ , which has a constant-leading-coefficient in $Y$ . This yields:

$$ \#\{x_{1}\in[-dB,dB]\cap\mathbb{Z}:\exists y\in\mathbb{Z},R_{d}^{(i)}(y,x_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=0\}\\
\ll_{\deg R}(\log(\|R_{d}^{(i)}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\|+2))^{e(1)}(dB)^{1/2}(\log(dB))^{e(1)}\\
\ll_{\deg R}(\log(\|R\|+2))^{e(1)}(dB)^{1/2}(\log(dB))^{2e(1)}. $$

for a constant $e(1)$ . Here, we have applied the fact that for $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in[-dB,dB]^{n-1}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$ ,

$$ \|R_{d}^{(i)}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\|\ll_{\deg R}d^{\deg(R^{(i)})}\cdot\|R\|\cdot(dB/d)^{\deg(R^{(i)})}\ll\|R\|(dB)^{\deg(R^{(i)})}. $$

Combining the above observations shows that (4.4) is bounded by:

$$ \ll_{\deg R}\log(\|R\|+2)^{e(1)}(dB)^{1/2}(\log(dB))^{2e(1)}\#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in[-dB,dB]^{n-1}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}:\exists z\in\mathbb{Z}:G_{d}(z,\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=0\}\\
+dB\cdot\#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in[-dB,dB]^{n-1}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}:R_{d}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\text{ has a linear factor}\}. $$

The second term is bounded by

$$ dB\cdot\#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in[-dB,dB]^{n-1}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}:R_{d}(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\text{ has a linear factor}\}\ll_{n,\deg R}dB\cdot(dB)^{n-2}, $$

by Lemma 4.5, and this suffices. To bound the first term, recall the definition $G_{d}(Z,\mathbf{X}^{\prime}):=d^{\deg G}G(Z,\mathbf{X}^{\prime}/d).$ Note that $G_{d}(Z,\mathbf{X}^{\prime})$ has integral coefficients and a constant-leading-coefficient in $Z$ (that is a power of $d$ ). We apply Theorem 2.13 again, now to $G_{d}(Z,\mathbf{X}^{\prime})$ in variables $Z,X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}$ . Thus an application of Theorem 2.13 shows

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in[-dB,dB]^{n-1}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}:\exists z\in\mathbb{Z}:G_{d}(z,\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=0\}\\
\ll_{n,\deg G}\log(\|G_{d}(Z,\mathbf{X}^{\prime})\|+2)^{e(n-1)}(dB)^{(n-1)-1/2}(\log(dB))^{e(n-1)} $$

for all $dB\geq 3$ , for a certain power $e(n-1)$ . Finally, since $\log\|G\|\ll_{n,\deg R}\|R\|$ by Lemma 4.6,

$$ \log\|G_{d}(Z,\mathbf{X}^{\prime})\|\ll\log(d^{\deg G}\|G\|)\ll_{n,\deg R}\log(d\|R\|). $$

We summarize by concluding

$$ \#\{\mathbf{x}\in[-B,B]^{n}\cap d^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{n},\exists y\in\mathbb{Z},R(y,\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=0\}\ll_{n,\deg R}\log(\|R\|+2)^{e(n)}(dB)^{n-1}(\log dB)^{2e(n)}, $$

with the constant $e(n)$ depending only on $n$ . This completes the proof of Theorem 4.1.

## 5. Strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials: second moment bound

The main goal of this section is to prove a second moment bound we will apply when treating certain terms in the polynomial sieve, namely terms that arise from irreducible components in the stratification that are degenerate (that is, lie in a proper linear subspace, see §6.3). In full generality, this relies on the complete theory of strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials. In order to make the ideas of the proof clear, we first briefly illustrate the core strategy in the setting of Theorem 1.1, which considers a special class of strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomials that exhibit cyclic structure. With Proposition 5.1 (below) in hand, a reader could directly prove Theorem 1.1 via the “power sieve” for multiplicative characters as formulated in [Mun09, HBP12], without the full theory of strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials, which is much more technical. We handle the general case of the second moment bound in §5.2, which is applied to prove Theorem 1.3 in full, of which Theorem 1.1 is a special case.

### 5.1. Illustrative special case: cyclic structure

#### Proposition 5.1 (Second moment bound: cyclic case).

Let $H(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be an absolutely irreducible polynomial such that $\deg_{X_{1}}(H)\geq 1$ . Let $d\geq 2$ and $\chi$ denote a nonprincipal character of $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}$ of order $d$ . Define

$$ S(\mathbf{u},p)=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}\chi(H(\mathbf{x}))e_{p}(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{x}). $$

Then there exists a finite set of exceptional primes $\mathcal{E}$ satisfying $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{n,\deg H}\log\|H\|/\log\log\|H\|$ such that for all $p\not\in\mathcal{E},$

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\{u_{1}=0\}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}|S(\mathbf{u},p)|^{2}\ll_{n,d,\deg H}p^{2n-1}. $$

#### Corollary 5.2.

Under the hypotheses of the proposition, suppose furthermore that there is no $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $H(L(\mathbf{X}))\in\mathbb{Z}[(X_{i})_{i\in I}]$ for a subset $I\subsetneq\{1,...,n\}.$ Then for any hyperplane $W=\{\mathbf{X}:W\cdot\mathbf{X}=0\}$ (defined by a fixed $W\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ ) there exists a finite set of exceptional primes $\mathcal{E}$ satisfying $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{n,\deg H}\log(\|H\|\|W\|)/\log\log(\|H\|\|W\|)$ such that for all $p\not\in\mathcal{E},$

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{u}\in W\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}|S(\mathbf{u},p)|^{2}\ll_{n,d,\deg H}p^{2n-1}. $$

The corollary follows by applying the proposition to $H_{L}(\mathbf{X}):=H(L\mathbf{X})$ , where $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ is a linear transformation with all integral entries such that $\{(L^{T}\mathbf{u})_{1}=0\}=W$ . By the hypothesis of the corollary, $\deg_{X_{1}}H_{L}\geq 1$ , as required. (We may assure that $L$ is invertible over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ for each $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ by ensuring that $\mathcal{E}$ includes all $p|\det L$ , of which there are $\ll_{n}\log\|W\|/\log\log\|W\|$ .)

#### Proof of Proposition 5.1.

Suppose a prime $p$ is fixed. We start by opening up the square, getting

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\{u_{1}=0\}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}|S(\mathbf{u},p)|^{2} \displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}\chi(H(\mathbf{x}))\overline{\chi(H(\mathbf{y}))}\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\{u_{1}=0\}}e_{p}(\mathbf{u}\cdot(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})) \displaystyle=p^{n-1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}\\
\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\in\{u_{1}=0\}^{\perp}\end{subarray}}\chi(H(\mathbf{x}))\overline{\chi(H(\mathbf{y}))}. $$

Since $\{u_{1}=0\}^{\perp}=\{u_{2}=\ldots=u_{n}=0\}$ , we can rewrite

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\{u_{1}=0\}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}|S(\mathbf{u},p)|^{2} \displaystyle=p^{n-1}\sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}}\sum_{x,y\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}\chi(H(x,\mathbf{t}))\overline{\chi(H(y,\mathbf{t}))} \displaystyle=p^{n-1}\sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}}\left|\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}\chi(H(x,\mathbf{t}))\right|^{2}. $$

By the Weil bound as in [IK04, Thm. 11.23],

$$ \left|\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}\chi(H(x,\bft))\right|=\begin{cases}O_{\deg H}(\sqrt{p})&\text{if $H(X,\bft)$ is not a $d$th-power over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$,}\\
p+O_{\deg H}(1)&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

(The latter case follows since if $H(X,\bft)=(R_{\bft}(X))^{d}$ over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , say, then the sum evaluates to $p-\#\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:R_{\bft}(x)=0\}$ .) Thus in order to complete the proof of the proposition it suffices to construct an appropriately small set $\mathcal{E}$ such that for all $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ , the polynomial $H(X,\bft)$ is not a $d$ th-power over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ for all but $O_{n,d,\deg H}(p^{n-2})$ choices of $\bft\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}.$

Write the polynomial

$$ H(\mathbf{X})=f_{0}(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})X_{1}^{k}+f_{1}(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})X_{1}^{k-1}+\ldots+f_{k}(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}). $$

Since $k\geq 1$ by the hypothesis of the proposition, there is a nonzero polynomial $\Delta(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})$ with $\deg\Delta\ll_{n,\deg H}1$ (the discriminant polynomial applied at the coefficient polynomials $f_{0},...,f_{k}$ ) satisfying

$$ H(X,\bft)\textrm{ is square-free}\iff\Delta(\bft)\neq 0. $$

Moreover, the above relation also holds over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . Observe that if $H(X,\bft)$ is a $d$ th-power, then it is not square-free. So it suffices to show that $p\nmid\Delta(\bft)$ for all but $O_{n,d,\deg H}(p^{n-2})$ choices of $\bft\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}$ , as long as $p$ is not in an appropriately small exceptional set $\mathcal{E}$ .

First, we establish that $\Delta(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})\not\equiv 0$ as a polynomial over $\mathbb{Z}$ . Since we are assuming that $H(\mathbf{X})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , the Hilbert Irreducibility Theorem 2.10 guarantees that we can find $t_{2},\ldots,t_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}$ where $H(X_{1},t_{2},\ldots,t_{n})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ . For this choice of $(t_{2},\ldots,t_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$ , $\Delta(t_{2},\ldots,t_{n})\neq 0$ and hence $\Delta(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})\not\equiv 0.$ With this fact in hand, as a result of the trivial Schwartz-Zippel bound (Lemma 2.1), we can moreover choose a particular tuple $\bft$ with $\Delta(t_{2},\ldots,t_{n})\neq 0$ and $\|\bft\|\ll_{\deg\Delta}1\ll_{n,\deg H}1.$ Given this tuple, define the exceptional set $\mathcal{E}:=\{p:p\mid\Delta(t_{2},\ldots,t_{n})\}$ . By the previous bound on $\bft$ , we know that $\log|\Delta(\bft)|\ll_{n,\deg H}\log\|H\|.$ Thus, $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{n,\deg H}\log\|H\|/\log\log\|H\|$ . Moreover, for each $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ , the property $p\nmid\Delta(\bft)$ shows that $\Delta(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})\not\equiv 0\;(\text{mod}\;p)$ , so that a second application of the trivial bound (Lemma 2.1) shows $\#\{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}:\Delta(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=0\}\ll_{\deg H}p^{n-2}$ , as desired. ∎

### 5.2. General case: strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials

The notion of a strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial plays a key role in our strategy to prove a second moment bound in full generality. We first state and prove a second moment bound over the hyperplane $\{u_{1}=0\}$ , and then deduce from it a second moment bound over any hyperplane. Each of these bounds requires some additional hypothesis on $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ .

In preparation, we recall from Lemma 3.4 that $F$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial if and only if for every $j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ ,

$$ \overline{\mathbb{Q}(X_{i})_{i\neq j}}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{i})_{i\neq j}, $$

in which $\mathcal{L}_{F}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/F$ . For example, for $j=1$ , (5.1) is the statement that $\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},...,X_{n})$ is integrally closed in $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n})[Y]/F$ ; equivalently, if $\theta\in\mathcal{L}_{F}$ and $\theta$ is algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},...,X_{n})$ , then $\theta\in\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},...,X_{n})$ ; equivalently, for any algebraic extension $K^{\prime}$ of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},...,X_{n})$ , $K^{\prime}\cap\mathcal{L_{F}}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},...,X_{n})$ . The next second moment bound, tailored to the hyperplane $\{u_{1}=0\}$ , is proved under the hypothesis that (5.1) holds for $j=1$ .

#### Proposition 5.3 (Second moment bound).

Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ and $F$ monic in $Y$ be absolutely irreducible. Suppose that

$$ \overline{\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}), $$

in which $\mathcal{L}_{F}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/F$ . Define for a given prime $p$ ,

$$ S(\mathbf{u},p)=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}(v_{p}(\mathbf{x})-1)e_{p}(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{x}) $$

where $v_{p}(\mathbf{x})=\#\{y\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:F(y,\mathbf{x})=0\}$ . Then there exists a finite set of exceptional primes $\mathcal{E}$ satisfying $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ such that for all $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ ,

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\{u_{1}=0\}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}|S(\mathbf{u},p)|^{2}\ll_{n,\deg F}p^{2n-1}. $$

(In particular, the conclusion holds if $F$ is strongly $n$ -genuine.)

This proposition is the main result of the section, and to prepare for its proof we gather several key lemmas.

#### Lemma 5.4.

Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ be absolutely irreducible. Suppose that

$$ \overline{\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}), $$

in which $\mathcal{L}_{F}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/F$ . Then, there exists a nonempty open set $V\subset\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}$ such that for all $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in V$ , $\mathbb{Q}$ is integrally closed in $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1})[Y]/F(Y,X_{1},\bfx^{\prime})$ . (In particular, the conclusion holds if $F$ is strongly $n$ -genuine.)

We remark that the condition of $F$ being absolutely irreducible is actually implied by the fact that we are assuming

$$ \overline{\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}), $$

Indeed, if $F$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ but not absolutely irreducible, then we can find a polynomial $H$ with coefficients in $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ which is a proper divisor of $F$ and is a minimal polynomial for some root of $F$ . Denote by $K$ the finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ which contains all coefficients of $H$ . Now let $\eta$ be a root of $H$ (and hence a root of $F$ ), $\Omega$ be the splitting field of $F$ , and consider $\tau\in\text{Gal}(\Omega/\mathbb{Q}(\bfX))$ such that $\tau(\eta)=\eta$ ; then $\tau$ needs to fix also the coefficients of $H$ since $H$ is the minimal polynomial of $\eta$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(\bfX)$ . Hence all the coefficients of $H$ are contained in $\mathcal{L}_{F}$ , i.e. $K\subset\mathcal{L}_{F}$ which implies

$$ \overline{\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}\supset K(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}), $$

a contradiction unless $H$ has coefficients in $\mathbb{Q}$ , which cannot occur since $F$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ .

#### Proof.

Consider $W=\text{Spec}\left(\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}]/F\right)$ and the morphism induced by $\mathbb{Q}[X_{2},....,X_{n}]\subset\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},...,X_{n}]/F$

$$ f:W\longrightarrow\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}}^{n-1}. $$

Let $V^{\prime}\subset\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}}^{n-1}$ be the set of $u\in\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}}^{n-1}$ such that the fiber

$$ f_{u}:W_{u}\longrightarrow\mathbb{A}_{k(u)}^{n-1} $$

is geometrically integral (i.e. $k(u)$ is integrally closed in $K(W_{u})$ ). (Here we again use the standard notation in algebraic geometry that $k(u)$ is the residue field at $u$ and $K(W_{u})$ is the field of rational functions on $W_{u}$ .) By [Gro66, EGA IV part 3, Theorem $9.7.7$ ], the set $V^{\prime}$ is locally constructible. On the other hand, the fiber on the generic point $\eta$ , say $f_{\eta}$ , is geometrically integral; this follows from the hypothesis (5.2) that $\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},...,X_{n})$ is integrally closed in $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n})[Y]/F=K(W)$ . Consequently, the generic point $\eta$ lies in $V^{\prime}$ . Hence, since it contains the generic point, $V^{\prime}$ contains an open subset $U^{\prime}$ : indeed, since $V^{\prime}$ is locally constructible we can find an open covering $\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}}^{n-1}=\bigcup_{i}V_{i}$ such that for each $i$ , $V_{i}\cap V^{\prime}$ is a constructible set, i.e. it is a finite union of sets of the type $S\cap T^{c}$ for $T,S$ open sets. Since $\eta\in V^{\prime}$ , we can find $i$ such that $\eta\in V_{i}\cap V^{\prime}$ , but then we can find $S,T$ open sets such that $\eta\in S\cap T^{c}$ . On the other hand, since $\{\eta\}$ is dense in $\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Q}}^{n-1}$ , it follows that $T=\emptyset$ . Then it suffices to set $U^{\prime}=S\subset(V_{i}\cap V^{\prime})\subset V^{\prime}$ . Finally, defining the open subset $V=U^{\prime}\cap\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}$ in $\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}$ , for every $(x_{2},...,x_{n})\in V$ , we have that $k(u)=\mathbb{Q}$ is algebraically closed in $K(W_{u})=\text{Frac}\left(\mathbb{Q}[Y,X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n}]/F(Y,X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})\right)$ . ∎

Next, we apply Noether’s Lemma 2.6 (ii) in combination with Lemma 5.4, to control how often $F(Y,X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})$ is reducible, still under the hypothesis (5.1) for $j=1$ . The following is an alternative to [Coh81, Lemma 4.2(ii)] whose proof contains a gap (see [BPW25b] for details, as well as a full correction of the gap).

#### Lemma 5.5.

Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ be absolutely irreducible. Suppose that

$$ \overline{\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n})}\cap\mathcal{L}_{F}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}), $$

in which $\mathcal{L}_{F}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/F$ . Then there exists a finite set of exceptional primes $\mathcal{E}$ satisfying $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ such that for all $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ ,

$$ \#\{(x_{2},...,x_{n})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}:F(Y,X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})\textrm{ is reducible over }\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}\}\ll_{n,\deg F}p^{n-2}. $$

(In particular, the conclusion holds if $F$ is strongly $n$ -genuine.)

#### Proof.

By Hilbert’s irreducibility theorem (Theorem 2.10), since $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , there exists a dense set $U^{\prime}\subset\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}$ such that

$$ F(Y,X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})\text{ is irreducible over }\mathbb{Q},\forall(x_{2},...,x_{n})\in U^{\prime}. $$

Denote the coefficients of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ as a polynomial in $Y,X_{1}$ by

$$ F(Y,\mathbf{X})=\sum_{i_{0},i_{1}}a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(X_{2},...,X_{n})Y^{i_{0}}X_{1}^{i_{1}}. $$

Take the open subset

$$ V=\{(x_{2},...,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}:a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(x_{2},...,x_{n})\neq 0\text{ for all $i_{0},i_{1}$ such that $a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime})\not\equiv 0$}\}. $$

(In particular, for all $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in V,$ $\deg_{Y}F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=\deg_{Y}F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{X}^{\prime})$ and $\deg_{X_{1}}F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=\deg_{X_{1}}F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{X}^{\prime})$ .) Then the set $U=U^{\prime}\cap V$ is dense in $\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}$ .

Let $G_{R}((a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime})))$ denote a form provided by Noether’s Lemma 2.6 (ii) for polynomials in $Y,X_{1}$ of degree $\leq\max\{\deg_{Y}F,\deg_{X_{1}}F\}$ over $K=\mathbb{Q}$ and the divisibility condition “reducible”, so that $G_{R}((a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})))=0$ if and only if $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ (or the degree of $F$ , as a polynomial in $Y,X_{1}$ , drops). (Lemma 2.6 (ii) provides a collection of forms $\{G_{1},...,G_{s}\}$ which determine when $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is reducible, rather than a single form. We can, however, take $G_{R}=G_{1}^{2\ell_{1}}+\cdots+G_{s}^{2\ell_{s}}$ for appropriate $\ell_{i}\geq 1$ to obtain a single form whose degree is $2r$ , where $r$ is the $\mathrm{lcm}$ of the degrees of $G_{1},\ldots,G_{s}$ .)

We will use Lemma 5.4 to show that there exists $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in U$ such that $G_{R}((a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})))\neq 0$ . Assume for contradiction that $G_{R}=0$ on $U$ . Then $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ for all $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in U$ (since by construction the degree of $F$ does not drop, as a polynomial of $Y,X_{1}$ , on $U$ ). However, by the construction in (5.3), for each $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in U$ , $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ . So, for all $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in U$ , $\mathbb{Q}$ cannot be integrally closed in $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1})[Y]/F(Y,X_{1},\bfx^{\prime})$ . On the other hand, by Lemma 5.4, there exists a nonempty open set $V\subset\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}$ such that for all $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in V$ , $\mathbb{Q}$ is integrally closed in $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1})[Y]/F(Y,X_{1},\bfx^{\prime})$ . Since $U$ is dense and $V$ is open, $U\cap V\neq\emptyset.$ Thus, we get a contradiction: if an element $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}$ exists in $U\cap V$ , $\mathbb{Q}$ would be both integrally closed and not integrally closed in $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1})[Y]/F(Y,X_{1},\bfx^{\prime})$ . Thus the supposition that $G_{R}=0$ on $U$ must be false.

Now we can complete the proof of the lemma. Since there exists a choice of $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in U$ such that $G_{R}((a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})))\neq 0$ , then $G_{R}((a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime})))$ is a polynomial in $\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}^{\prime}]$ that is not identically zero. Consequently, for all rational primes $p$ that do not divide the gcd of the coefficients of $G_{R}((a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime})))$ , the reduction of $G_{R}((a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime})))$ modulo $p$ is a polynomial in $\mathbb{F}_{p}[\mathbf{X}^{\prime}]$ , not identically zero. Denote this gcd temporarily by $g$ , and denote by $\|G_{R}\|$ the maximum absolute value of the coefficient of any monomial in $\mathbf{X}^{\prime}$ in the polynomial $G_{R}((a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(\mathbf{X}^{\prime})))$ (which will depend polynomially on the fixed coefficients defining $F$ ). Note that $g\ll\|G_{R}\|$ . By Lemma 2.6, $\log\|G_{R}\|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|$ . Upon defining the exceptional set $\mathcal{E}$ to be all $p|g$ , it follows that $|\mathcal{E}|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ , as claimed. Now suppose $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ is fixed. Again by Lemma 2.6 (ii), for a given tuple $(x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}$ , $F(Y,X_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ if and only if $G_{R}((a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})))=0$ in $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . Since this is not the zero polynomial in $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , the trivial bound (Lemma 2.1) shows that the number of $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}$ that satisfy $G_{R}((a_{i_{0},i_{1}}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})))\neq 0$ is $\ll\deg_{G_{R}}p^{n-2}$ . By Lemma 2.6 (ii), $\deg G_{R}\ll_{n,\deg F}1$ , so that this is sufficient for the claim of Lemma 5.5.

∎

### 5.3. Proof of Proposition 5.3

The main input is Lemma 5.5. Expanding the square,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\{u_{1}=0\}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}|S(\mathbf{u},p)|^{2} \displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}(v_{p}(\mathbf{x})-1)(v_{p}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})-1)\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\{u_{1}=0\}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}e(\mathbf{u}\cdot(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime})) \displaystyle=p^{n-1}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}}\left|\sum_{x_{1}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}}(v_{p}((x_{1},\mathbf{a}))-1)\right|^{2} \displaystyle=p^{n-1}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}}\left|\#\{(y,x_{1})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}:F(y,x_{1},\mathbf{a})=0\}-p\right|^{2}. $$

Under the assumption that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is monic in $Y$ , note that for all $p$ and all $\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}$ , $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{a})\not\equiv 0$ over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . By the Lang-Weil bound (Lemma 2.4), if $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{a})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[Y,X_{1}]$ is irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ , then

$$ |\#\{(y,x_{1})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}:F(y,x_{1},\mathbf{a})=0\}-p|\ll_{n,\deg F}p^{1/2}. $$

On the other hand, if $F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{a})$ is not irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}$ , the best bound available is

$$ |\#\{(y,x_{1})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}:F(y,x_{1},\mathbf{a})=0\}-p|\ll_{\deg F}p, $$

by Lemma 2.1. By Lemma 5.5, there exists a set of exceptional primes $\mathcal{E}$ satisfying $|\mathcal{E}|\ll\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ such that for all $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}:F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{a})\textrm{ is reducible over }\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}\}\ll_{n,\deg F}p^{n-2}. $$

Thus, for each such $p\not\in\mathcal{E}$ ,

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\{u_{1}=0\}}|S(\mathbf{u},p)|^{2}\ll_{n,\deg F}p^{n-1}(\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}}O(p^{1/2})^{2}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n-1}\\
F(Y,X_{1},\mathbf{a})\textrm{ reducible/}\overline{\mathbb{F}_{p}}\end{subarray}}O(p)^{2})\ll_{n,\deg F}p^{2n-1}, $$

and the proposition is proved.

### 5.4. Linear changes of variable and second moment bounds

Proposition 5.3 proves a second moment bound when $|S(\mathbf{u},p)|^{2}$ is summed over $\mathbf{u}$ lying in the hyperplane $\{u_{1}=0\}$ . We will ultimately require a more general result that sums over $\mathbf{u}$ lying in a fixed arbitrary hyperplane $V\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ . Of course any hyperplane $V$ can be mapped to the special case $\{u_{1}=0\}$ by an appropriate linear change of variables, but because in bounding $N(F,B)$ we consider integral points corresponding to a certain box $[-B,B]^{n}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ , we must consider carefully how this set of integral points is affected by a change of variables. Given $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ , denote the rows of the matrix by $L_{1},\ldots,L_{n}$ and correspondingly define $n$ linear forms by $L_{i}(\mathbf{x})=L_{i}\cdot\mathbf{x}$ .

#### Corollary 5.6.

Let $F(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ and $F$ monic in $Y$ be absolutely irreducible. Define for a given prime $p$ ,

$$ S(\mathbf{u},p)=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}(v_{p}(\mathbf{x})-1)e_{p}(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{x}) $$

where $v_{p}(\mathbf{x})=\#\{y\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:F(y,\mathbf{x})=0\}$ . Let $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ be given, with all integer entries, and let $\|L\|$ denote the maximum of the absolute value of the entries in $L$ . If the polynomial $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}):=F(Y,L_{1}(\mathbf{x}),\ldots,L_{n}(\mathbf{x}))$ satisfies the condition (5.1) for $j=1$ , then there exists a set $\mathcal{E}_{L}$ with

$$ |\mathcal{E}_{L}|\ll\log(\|F\|\|L\|)/\log\log(\|F\|\|L\|) $$

such that for all $p\not\in\mathcal{E}_{L},$

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\{(L^{T}\mathbf{u})_{1}=0\}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}|S(\mathbf{u},p)|^{2}\ll_{n,\deg F}p^{2n-1}. $$

(In particular, the conclusion holds if $F(Y,L_{1}(\mathbf{x}),\ldots,L_{n}(\mathbf{x}))$ is a strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial.)

#### Proof.

Let $L$ be given. By assumption, $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ satisfies the hypotheses of Proposition 5.3 and $\|F_{L}\|\leq\|F\|\|L\|$ , so there exists a set $\mathcal{E}^{\prime}_{L}$ with $|\mathcal{E}^{\prime}_{L}|\ll\log(\|F\|\|L\|)/\log\log(\|F\|\|L\|)$ such that for all $p\not\in\mathcal{E}^{\prime}_{L},$

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\{u_{1}=0\}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}|S_{L}(\mathbf{u},p)|^{2}\ll_{n,\deg F}p^{2n-1}, $$

in which

$$ S_{L}(\mathbf{u},p):=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}(v^{L}_{p}(\mathbf{x})-1)e_{p}(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{x}) $$

where $v^{L}_{p}(\mathbf{x})=\#\{y\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:F(y,L_{1}(\mathbf{x}),\ldots,L_{n}(\mathbf{x}))=0\}$ . We will require that $p\nmid\det L$ , so that furthermore $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ ; this excludes at most $\ll_{n}\log\|L\|/\log\log\|L\|$ further primes, and we enlarge the set $\mathcal{E}^{\prime}_{L}$ to a set $\mathcal{E}_{L}$ that includes these further primes as well. Now suppose $p\not\in\mathcal{E}_{L}$ and write the matrix inverse as $M$ so that $ML=LM=\mathrm{Id}$ over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . Note that for each $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle v^{L}_{p}(M\mathbf{x}) \displaystyle=\#\{y\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:F(y,L_{1}(M\mathbf{x}),\ldots,L_{n}(M\mathbf{x}))=0\} \displaystyle=\#\{y\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:F(y,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=0\}=v_{p}(\mathbf{x}). $$

Consequently

$$ S_{L}(\mathbf{u},p)=\sum_{M\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}(v^{L}_{p}(M\mathbf{x})-1)e_{p}(\mathbf{u}\cdot M\mathbf{x})=\sum_{M\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}(v_{p}(\mathbf{x})-1)e_{p}((M^{T}\mathbf{u})\cdot\mathbf{x}), $$

where we have applied $(\mathbf{u}\cdot M\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{u}^{T}(M\mathbf{x})=(M^{T}\mathbf{u})^{T}\mathbf{x}$ . Since $\mathbf{x}$ ranges over $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}$ as $M\mathbf{x}$ ranges over $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}$ , that is to say

$$ S_{L}(\mathbf{u},p)=\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}(v_{p}(\mathbf{x})-1)e_{p}(M^{T}\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{x})=S(M^{T}\mathbf{u},p). $$

We can conclude that for all $p\not\in\mathcal{E}_{L},$

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\{u_{1}=0\}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}|S(M^{T}\mathbf{u},p)|^{2}\ll_{n,\deg F}p^{2n-1}. $$

Finally, we set $\mathbf{v}=M^{T}\mathbf{u}$ (and so $\mathbf{u}=(M^{T})^{-1}\mathbf{v}=L^{T}\mathbf{v}$ ), so that this statement is equivalent to

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{v}\in\{\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}:(L^{T}\mathbf{v})_{1}=0\}}|S(\mathbf{v},p)|^{2}\ll_{n,\deg F}p^{2n-1}. $$

∎

## 6. Application of the stratification to the polynomial sieve

We turn to the proof of Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.3 (which we recall immediately implies Theorem 1.1 by Example 8.7). The main claim in this section is Theorem 6.4, which is the main outcome of the polynomial sieve in this paper. For simplicity we may assume throughout that $\|F\|\geq 3$ .

### 6.1. Initiation of the polynomial sieve

The strategy is to use a polynomial sieve to control a smoothed version of the counting function $N(F,B)$ . Let $w:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ be an infinitely differentiable function that is $\geq 1$ on $[-1,1]^{n}$ and compactly supported in $[-2,2]^{n}$ . For each fixed $B\geq 1$ , let $W(\bfx)=w(\bfx/B)$ . By construction,

$$ N(F,B)\leq S(F,B):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
F(Y,\mathbf{x})=0\text{ is solvable in $\mathbb{Z}$}\end{subarray}}W(\bfx). $$

The polynomial sieve relies on understanding the local counting function

$$ v_{p}(\mathbf{x})=\#\{y\;(\text{mod}\;p):F(y,\mathbf{x})=0\;(\text{mod}\;p)\} $$

for sufficiently many primes $p$ in a sieving set $\mathcal{P}$ . The version we employ is as follows:

#### Lemma 6.1 ([BP24, Lemma 1.2]).

Let $m\geq 2$ and $d\geq 1$ be integers. Consider a polynomial of the form

$$ F(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{md}+f_{1}(\mathbf{X})Y^{m(d-1)}+...+f_{d}(\mathbf{X}), $$

in which $f_{d}(\mathbf{X})\not\equiv 0$ and $f_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ have degrees $k_{j}$ (possibly zero), respectively. Let $\mathcal{P}\subset\{p\text{ prime}:p\equiv 1\;(\text{mod}\;m)\}\cap[P,2P]$ be a set of primes. Suppose that $|\mathcal{P}|\gg P/\log P$ and that

$$ |\mathcal{P}|\gg_{\deg f_{d}}\max\{\log(\|f_{d}\|,\log B)\}. $$

Then

$$ S(F,B)\ll_{\deg F}\sum_{f_{d}(\mathbf{x})=0}W(\mathbf{x})+\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}W(\mathbf{x})+\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p,q\in\mathcal{P}\\
p\neq q\end{subarray}}\left|\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}(v_{p}(\mathbf{x})-1)(v_{q}(\mathbf{x})-1)W(\mathbf{x})\right|. $$

This formulation of the polynomial sieve introduces the requirement that $m\geq 2$ ; this guarantees that for a positive proportion of primes (namely those $p\equiv 1\;(\text{mod}\;m)$ ), $v_{p}(\bfx)>0$ implies that $v_{p}(\bfx)>1$ so that $(v_{p}(\bfx)-1)\neq 0$ . The version stated here is a small modification of [BP24, Lemma 1.2], which was stated in the setting that the polynomials $f_{j}$ are homogeneous, with degree constraints of the form $\deg f_{j}=m\cdot e\cdot j$ ; then $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=0$ defines a hypersurface in weighted projective space $\mathbb{P}(e,1,\ldots,1)$ for a given integer $e\geq 1$ . The proof given for [BP24, Lemma 1.2] did not depend on homogeneity of the polynomials $f_{j}$ , and repeating it line-by-line immediately leads to the result stated above, so we do not repeat the proof.

In our present work, we also allow $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ to have the form (1.1) with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ and $m=1$ , and for this case we apply the conditional version of the sieve lemma:

#### Lemma 6.2 ([BP24, Remark 1.3, §3.2]).

Lemma 6.1 holds for $m=1$ and $d\geq 2$ , conditional on GRH, with $\mathcal{P}$ a set of primes in $[P,2P]$ with $|\mathcal{P}|\gg P(\log P)^{-1}$ , and (6.1) replaced by $P\gg_{m,d,\deg f_{d}}\max\{(\log\|F\|)^{\alpha_{0}},(\log B)^{\alpha_{0}}\}$ for any fixed $\alpha_{0}>2$ .

For clarity, we note that [BP24, Remark 1.3, §3.2] was also stated in the case where the polynomials $f_{j}$ are homogeneous, but the proof given there did not depend on homogeneity, and repeating it line-by-line immediately leads to the result stated above. (The dependence of Lemma 6.2 on GRH can be weakened somewhat; see Remark 7.2.)

Assume that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ with $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ is any absolutely irreducible polynomial of the form (1.1) for a fixed $m\geq 1$ . (In particular, since $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is absolutely irreducible, it must be that $f_{d}(\mathbf{X})\not\equiv 0$ .) By an application of Lemma 6.1 (when $m\geq 2$ ) or Lemma 6.2 (when $m=1$ , assuming GRH),

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{\deg F}\sum_{f_{d}(\mathbf{x})=0}W(\mathbf{x})+\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}W(\mathbf{x})+\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p,q\in\mathcal{P}\\
p\neq q\end{subarray}}\left|\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}(v_{p}(\mathbf{x})-1)(v_{q}(\mathbf{x})-1)W(\mathbf{x})\right|. $$

Here the sieving set $\mathcal{P}$ is assumed to satisfy $\mathcal{P}\subset\{p\text{ prime}:p\equiv 1\;(\text{mod}\;m)\}\cap[P,2P]$ and we assume $P\gg_{\deg F}\max\{(\log\|F\|)^{\alpha_{0}},(\log B)^{\alpha_{0}}\}$ for a fixed $\alpha_{0}>2$ . (The condition $p\equiv 1\;(\text{mod}\;m)$ denotes primes in an arithmetic progression modulo $m$ if $m\geq 2$ ; if $m=1$ it imposes no restriction.) We will state the precise choice of $\mathcal{P}$ in §6.7, and confirm that $|\mathcal{P}|\gg P/\log P$ . For the remainder of the paper, whether $m\geq 2$ or $m=1$ will no longer play any role in the argument.

An application of the trivial bound (Lemma 2.1) shows that

$$ \sum_{f_{d}(\mathbf{x})=0}W(\mathbf{x})\ll_{\deg f_{d}}B^{n-1}. $$

Trivially,

$$ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}W(\mathbf{x})\ll_{n}\frac{B^{n}}{|\mathcal{P}|}. $$

Hence to bound $N(F,B)$ from above, it remains to understand the third, main sieve, term.

To bound the main sieve term, we first fix a pair $(p,q)\in\mathcal{P}^{2}$ such that $p\neq q$ . After an application of Poisson summation,

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}W(\mathbf{x})(v_{p}(\mathbf{x})-1)(v_{q}(\mathbf{x})-1)=\frac{1}{(pq)^{n}}\sum_{\bfu\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}\hat{W}(\bfu/pq)S(\bfu,pq), $$

where

$$ S(\bfu,pq)=\sum_{\bfa\;(\text{mod}\;pq)}(v_{p}(\bfa)-1)(v_{q}(\bfa)-1)e_{pq}(\bfu\cdot\bfa). $$

Accordingly, for a prime $p$ define

$$ S(\bfu,p)=\sum_{\bfa\;(\text{mod}\;p)}(v_{p}(\bfa)-1)e_{p}(\bfu\cdot\bfa). $$

The sum is multiplicative: for primes $p\neq q$ ,

$$ S(\bfu,pq)=S(\overline{q}\bfu,p)S(\overline{p}\bfu,q), $$

in which $\overline{p}p\equiv 1\;(\text{mod}\;q)$ and $\overline{q}q\equiv 1\;(\text{mod}\;q)$ . The standard result of Lemma 2.12(i) applies to bound the function $\hat{W}(\mathbf{u})$ . We define the main focus of study: for each pair of primes $p\neq q$ (for any fixed large $M\geq 1$ of our choice, to be determined later), set

$$ T(p,q;B):=\frac{B^{n}}{(pq)^{n}}\sum_{\bfu\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{pq}\right)^{-M}|S(\overline{q}\bfu,p)||S(\overline{p}\bfu,q)|. $$

In particular,

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F}B^{n-1}+B^{n}|\mathcal{P}|^{-1}+\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}\sum_{p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}}|T(p,q;B)|, $$

for $P\gg_{\deg F}\max\{(\log\|F\|)^{\alpha_{0}},(\log B)^{\alpha_{0}}\}$ for a fixed $\alpha_{0}>2$ . To control the terms $T(p,q;B)$ , the key tool we will use is a stratification result for additive character sums over a variety, with strong uniformity with respect to the variety.

### 6.2. Introducing the uniform stratification

Let $X$ be an affine scheme over $\mathbb{Z}$ of dimension $n$ and let $\varphi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbb{Z}}$ be a finite morphism. Let $p$ be a prime and $\psi:\mathbb{F}_{p}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be a nontrivial additive character. Define the following exponential sum for $\bfu\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ :

$$ S_{p,\psi}(\bfu;\varphi)=\sum_{x\in X(\mathbb{F}_{p})}\psi(\bfu\cdot\varphi(x))=\sum_{\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}\psi(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{y})r_{\varphi}(\mathbf{y}), $$

where we define $r_{\varphi}(\mathbf{y})=\#\{x\in X(\mathbb{F}_{p}):\varphi(x)=\mathbf{y}\}.$ The function $r_{\varphi}(\mathbf{y})$ is a trace function and fits into the stratification framework.

Loosely speaking, a stratification associated to this sum is a nested collection of varieties $\mathbb{A}^{n}=:Z_{0}\supset Z_{1}\supset...$ such that the tuples $\bfu$ that lie progressively deeper in this nesting sequence, have progressively worse upper bounds on $|S_{p,\psi}(\bfu;\varphi)|$ , in terms of the power of $p$ . The key is to produce lower bounds on the codimension of $Z_{j}$ for each $j$ , so that “progressively worse” $\bfu$ become “progressively sparser.” The sums $S(\bfu,p)$ we consider in (6.2) fit this paradigm: first write

$$ S(\mathbf{u},p)=\sum_{\mathbf{a}\;(\text{mod}\;p)}(v_{p}(\mathbf{a})-1)e_{p}(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{a})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(y,\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n+1}\\
F(y,\mathbf{x})=0\;(\text{mod}\;p)\end{subarray}}e_{p}(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{x})-p^{n}\mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{0}}. $$

Now let

$$ X=\{F(Y,\mathbf{X})=0\}\subset\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} $$

and $\varphi:\{F(Y,\mathbf{X})=0\}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n}$ , where $\varphi((y,\mathbf{x}))=\mathbf{x}$ , and define the additive character $\psi(a)=e_{p}(a)$ . Then for each $\mathbf{u}\neq\mathbf{0}$ , $S(\mathbf{u},p)$ is in the form of the sum $S_{p,\psi}(\mathbf{u};\varphi)$ defined above; for this particular map and choice of additive character, we define

$$ \mathbf{S}_{p}(\mathbf{u};F):=S_{p,\psi}(\mathbf{u},\varphi). $$

The existence of such a stratification has been proved by Katz and Laumon [KL85] (further explained in Fouvry [Fou00]). We require an enhanced version of the stratification, which tracks the dependence of all parameters on the scheme $X$ . We have developed such an enhanced stratification in a companion paper [BKW25] with E. Kowalski, and here we record the relevant result from that work, in the form of [BKW25, Thm. 2.3].

#### Theorem 6.3 (Uniform stratification).

Fix integers $n\geq 1$ and $D\geq 1$ , and let $F\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be a polynomial of total degree at most $D$ . Then there exist integers $C(n,D)$ and $N(n,D)$ and a stratification

$$ \mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbb{Z}}=V_{0}\supset V_{1}\supset...\supset V_{n} $$

such that $V_{i}$ is a homogeneous subvariety of codimension $\geq i$ and for all primes $p\nmid N(n,D)$ , for $\mathbf{u}\in V_{i}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\backslash V_{i+1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ ,

$$ |\mathbf{S}_{p}(\mathbf{u};F)|\leq C(n,D)p^{\frac{n+i}{2}}. $$

Moreover,

- (i) $C(n,D)\ll_{n,D}1$ ;

- (ii) $\deg(V_{i})\ll_{n,D}1$ ;

- (iii) the number of irreducible components of $V_{i}$ is $\ll_{n,D}1;$

- (iv) $N(n,D)\ll_{n,D}1$ ;

- (v) each $V_{i}=V(G_{i,1},...,G_{i,k})$ is the common vanishing set of homogeneous polynomials $G_{i,s}$ with the property that $\log\|G_{i,s}\|\ll_{n,D}\log\|F\|$ for every pair $i,s.$

We will say that such a stratification is uniform; in particular, this result follows from a statement of algebraic uniformity of the Katz–Laumon stratification, as proved in [BKW25]. Note that the first four statements are uniform in $F$ ; the impact of the last statement is that the homogeneous polynomials $G_{i,s}$ are defined over $\mathbb{Z}$ and the dependence of $\|G_{i,s}\|$ on $\|F\|$ is at most polynomial.

Let us then denote by

$$ \mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}=:V_{0}\supset V_{1}\supset V_{2}\supset\cdots\supset V_{n} $$

the stratification provided for the exponential sum $\mathbf{S}_{p}(\mathbf{u};F)$ in (6.6). Since $V_{n}$ is a homogeneous variety of codimension at least $n$ in $\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}$ , it must be that $V_{n}$ is only $V_{n}=\{\mathbf{0}\}.$ Now fix some prime $p$ in the sieving set $\mathcal{P}$ . By hypothesis $\{F(Y,\mathbf{X})=0\}$ is absolutely irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , and by the choice of sieving set made momentarily in §6.7 we may assume that for all $p\in\mathcal{P}$ the reduction remains absolutely irreducible over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . Consequently, for $\mathbf{u}\equiv\mathbf{0}\;(\text{mod}\;p)$ , by an application of the Lang-Weil bound (Lemma 2.4),

$$ S(\mathbf{0},p)=\#X(\mathbb{F}_{p})-p^{n}\ll_{n,\deg F}p^{n-1/2}. $$

Thus for each $p\in\mathcal{P}$ , as a consequence of Theorem 6.3 for $j=n-1$ applied to $\mathbf{u}\in V_{n-1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$ , and (6.8) applied to $\mathbf{u}\equiv\boldsymbol{0}\;(\text{mod}\;p)$ ,

$$ \text{$|S(\mathbf{u},p)|\ll p^{n-1/2}$ holds for \emph{all} $\mathbf{u}\in V_{n-1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$}. $$

In what follows, we thus formally re-define $V_{n}=\emptyset$ , so that any restriction of the form $\mathbf{u}\in V_{n-1}\setminus V_{n}$ can instead be read as $\mathbf{u}\in V_{n-1}$ , and this will lead to valid upper bounds due to the uniformity in (6.9).

### 6.3. Degenerate irreducible components of the stratification

For each $1\leq j\leq n-1$ decompose the stratum $V_{j}$ into irreducible components over $\mathbb{Q}$ as

$$ V_{j}=\bigcup_{s\in I_{j}}X_{j,s}. $$

By Theorem 6.3(iii), $|I_{j}|\ll_{n,\deg F}1$ . We must consider whether any stratum $V_{j}$ contains an irreducible component $X_{j,s}\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ which is contained in a proper linear subspace of $\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ ; in this case we will say the component $X_{j,s}$ is degenerate. (Recall that a variety $X\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ is said to be nondegenerate if it spans $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ , or equivalently, does not lie in any hyperplane [Har92, p. 145].) Fix a degenerate irreducible component $X_{j,s}$ ; we may in particular assume it lies in a hyperplane, say $W_{j,s}$ , defined by $\{\mathbf{u}:W^{(j,s)}\cdot\mathbf{u}=0\}\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ for a nonzero vector $W^{(j,s)}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ . By Theorem 6.3(v), $\log\|W^{(j,s)}\|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|.$ We define $L_{j,s}\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ to be a matrix with first column $W^{(j,s)}$ and all integer entries; once the first column is fixed we may choose the other entries appropriately to make the matrix in $\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ , with $\log\|L_{j,s}\|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|$ . Then in particular,

$$ \{\mathbf{u}:(L_{j,s}^{T}\mathbf{u})_{1}=0\}=\{\mathbf{u}:W^{(j,s)}\cdot\mathbf{u}=0\}. $$

Cumulatively, let $\{W_{j,s}\}_{(j,s)}$ be the finite set of (distinct) hyperplanes that contain a degenerate irreducible component $X_{j,s}$ of any stratum $V_{j}$ in the stratification $V_{0}\supset V_{1}\supset\ldots\supset V_{n}$ . By Theorem 6.3(iii), there are $\ll_{n,\deg F}1$ hyperplanes in this set (and it may be empty). Let $\mathcal{L}(F)=\{L_{j,s}\}_{(j,s)}$ denote the finite (possibly empty) set of corresponding (distinct) transformations, with $|\mathcal{L}(F)|\ll_{n,\deg F}1$ . Both Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.3 will be deduced from the following theorem, whose proof occupies the remainder of the paper.

#### Theorem 6.4.

Fix $n\geq 2$ . Let $F\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be an absolutely irreducible polynomial of the form (1.1) for an integer $m\geq 2$ . Let $\mathcal{L}(F)\subset\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ be the finite (possibly empty) set of linear transformations with integer entries, as defined above, with $|\mathcal{L}(F)|\ll_{n,\deg F}1$ and with $\log\|L\|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|$ for each $L\in\mathcal{L}(F)$ . Assume that $F(Y,L(\mathbf{X}))$ is strongly $n$ -genuine for each $L\in\mathcal{L}(F)$ . Then for $B\gg_{n,\deg F}(\log\|F\|)^{6}$ ,

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}(\log\|F\|)B^{n-1+\frac{1}{n+1}+\varepsilon}\qquad\text{for every $\varepsilon>0$}. $$

If $\deg_{Y}F\geq 2$ and the same hypotheses hold with $m=1$ , the same conclusions hold, conditional on GRH.

#### Remark 6.5.

Suppose that an absolutely irreducible polynomial $F$ of the form (1.1) has the property $(*)$ that no stratum $V_{j}$ with $j\leq n-1$ in the associated stratification $\mathbb{A}^{n}=V_{0}\supset V_{1}\supset\cdots\supset V_{n-1}\supset V_{n}$ contains an irreducible component that lies in a linear subspace. Then $\mathcal{L}(F)$ is empty, and the bound for $N(F,B)$ stated above holds (under GRH if $m=1$ ). By homogeneity, $V_{n}=\{\mathbf{0}\}$ (as remarked above), and the irreducible components of $V_{n-1}$ can be seen to be lines (as argued below in §6.11). So in particular property $(*)$ would also imply that $V_{n-1}=\{\mathbf{0}\}$ . It would be interesting to illuminate what is characterized about a polynomial $F$ if the strata satisfy property $(*)$ .

### 6.4. Deduction of Theorem 1.3

Under the hypothesis of Theorem 1.3 that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable, $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}):=F(Y,L(\mathbf{X}))$ is strongly $n$ -genuine for all $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ so certainly for each $L\in\mathcal{L}(F)$ . Thus Theorem 6.4 proves the claim in Theorem 1.3 for all $B\gg_{n,\deg F}(\log\|F\|)^{6}$ . For all $B\ll_{n,\deg F}(\log\|F\|)^{6}$ , we can apply the trivial bound

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n}B^{n}\ll_{n,\deg F}(\log\|F\|)^{6n}\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}(\log\|F\|)^{6n}B^{n-1+\frac{1}{n+1}+\varepsilon}, $$

completing the proof of the theorem for all $B\geq 1$ .

### 6.5. Deduction of Theorem 1.2

For Theorem 1.2, suppose that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is a $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomial. If $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X})=F(Y,L(\mathbf{X}))$ is strongly $n$ -genuine for each $L\in\mathcal{L}(F)$ , then Theorem 6.4 applies directly, yielding the claim of Theorem 1.2 (by the reasoning immediately above). On the other hand, suppose that for some $L\in\mathcal{L}(F)$ , say $L_{*}$ , the polynomial $F_{L_{*}}(Y,\mathbf{X}):=F(Y,L_{*}(\mathbf{X}))$ is $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine. Then we do not apply the polynomial sieve to $F$ . Instead, as a consequence of Theorem 4.1, in the form of Corollary 4.2, we know that there exist integers $e=e(n)$ and $e^{\prime}=e^{\prime}(n)$ such that for all $B\geq 1$ ,

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F}\|L_{*}\|^{e^{\prime}}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{e}B^{n-1}(\log(B+2))^{2e}. $$

By Theorem 6.3(v), $\log\|L_{*}\|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|$ , so that there exists $h=h(n,\deg F)$ for which $\|L_{*}\|^{e^{\prime}}\ll_{n,\deg F}\|F\|^{h}$ . This verifies the remaining case of Theorem 1.2.

### 6.6. Adapting the second moment bound to the setting of Theorem 6.4

In the setting of Theorem 6.4, we will apply the second moment bound proved in §5 in the following formulation. As in §6.3, let $X_{j,s}$ be a degenerate irreducible component of a stratum $V_{j}$ , with associated $L_{j,s}\in\mathcal{L}(F)$ with integer entries, which defines a hyperplane $W^{(j,s)}$ containing $X_{j,s}$ as in (6.10). By Theorem 6.3(v), $\log\|L_{j,s}\|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|$ . By Corollary 5.6, there exists an exceptional set $\mathcal{E}_{j,s}$ of primes with

$$ |\mathcal{E}_{j,s}|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log(\|F\|\|L_{j,s}\|)/\log\log(\|F\|\|L_{j,s}\|)\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|, $$

such that for all $p\not\in\mathcal{E}_{j,s},$

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}|S(\mathbf{u},p)|^{2}\leq\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in W_{j,s}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n}}|S(\mathbf{u},p)|^{2}\ll_{n,\deg F}p^{2n-1}. $$

The first inequality is by positivity, and the second is by Corollary 5.6, via the parameterization (6.10). It immediately follows that for any integer $M\geq 1$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{F}_{p}):|S(\mathbf{u},p)|\geq M\}\ll_{n,\deg F}\frac{p^{2n-1}}{M^{2}}. $$

Moreover, by the homogeneity of $X_{j,s}$ , we can deduce from this that for any $\alpha\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}$ ,

$$ \#\{\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{F}_{p}):|S(\alpha\mathbf{u},p)|\geq M\}\ll_{n,\deg F}\frac{p^{2n-1}}{M^{2}}. $$

This is the main consequence of Corollary 5.6 we will apply in §6.10 (and again in §6.12).

### 6.7. Choice of the sieving set

We now turn to the proof of Theorem 6.4, which is the main outcome of the polynomial sieve in this paper. We choose the sieving set $\mathcal{P}$ , adapted to the stratification of Theorem 6.3. Fix $N(n,\deg F)$ as in Theorem 6.3 (iv) and let $\mathcal{E}_{0}$ denote the primes $p|N(n,\deg F)$ so that $|\mathcal{E}_{0}|\ll_{n,\deg F}1$ . Let $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ denote the finitely many exceptional primes for which the reduction of $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is not irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ ; by Lemma 2.9, $|\mathcal{E}_{1}|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ .

In §6.6, for each $1\leq j\leq n-1$ , for each $s\in I_{j}$ such that $X_{j,s}$ is a degenerate irreducible component of the stratum $V_{j}$ , we have isolated a set $\mathcal{E}_{j,s}$ of exceptional primes with $|\mathcal{E}_{j,s}|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ . If (for a given $j,s$ ) $X_{j,s}$ is nondegenerate, set $\mathcal{E}_{j,s}=\emptyset.$ Define

$$ \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{deg}}=\bigcup_{1\leq j\leq n-1}\bigcup_{s\in I_{j}}\mathcal{E}_{j,s}. $$

By an application of Theorem 6.3(iii), $|\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{deg}}|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|$ .

By the Siegel-Walfisz theorem for primes in arithmetic progressions ( $m\geq 2$ ) or the prime number theorem ( $m=1$ ), $\#\{p\in[P,2P]:p\equiv 1\;(\text{mod}\;m)\}\gg_{m}P/\log P$ for all $P\gg_{m}1$ . Thus as long as

$$ P\gg_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|/\log\log\|F\|, $$

by taking (either for $m\geq 2$ or for $m=1$ ),

$$ \mathcal{P}=\{p\in[P,2P]:p\equiv 1\;(\text{mod}\;m)\}\setminus(\mathcal{E}_{0}\cup\mathcal{E}_{1}\cup\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{deg}}), $$

we still obtain $|\mathcal{P}|\gg P/\log P$ . We also assume from now on that

$$ P=B^{\rho},\qquad 1/2<\rho<1. $$

### 6.8. Separation into global and local contributions

To prove Theorem 6.4, we now bound $N(F,B)$ via the polynomial sieve; recall the main consequence of the sieve lemma stated in (6.4) with $T(p,q;B)$ defined in (6.3). We apply the stratification to the evaluation of $T(p,q;B)$ for a fixed pair $p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}$ . First, write

$$ \displaystyle T(p,q;B) \displaystyle\leq\frac{B^{n}}{(pq)^{n}}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\overline{q}\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\\
\overline{p}\mathbf{u}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\backslash V_{k+1}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\end{subarray}}|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)||S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)|\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{pq}\right)^{-M} \displaystyle=\frac{B^{n}}{(pq)^{n}}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\backslash V_{k+1}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\end{subarray}}|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)||S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)|\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{pq}\right)^{-M}. $$

The sums need only index over $j\leq n-1$ and $k\leq n-1$ by the remark (6.9) and the corresponding convention $V_{n}:=\emptyset$ . The second line is equivalent to the first since the strata $V_{j}$ are homogeneous varieties. Throughout what follows, we will repeatedly use the homogeneity of the varieties $V_{i}$ in order to impose a constraint on $\mathbf{u}$ rather than on $\overline{q}\mathbf{u}$ or $\overline{p}\mathbf{u}$ . When we next average $T(p,q;B)$ over $p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}$ , this will enable us to bring the sum over $p,q$ inside the sum over $\mathbf{u}$ . Indeed,

$$ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p,q\in\mathcal{P}\\
p\neq q\end{subarray}}T(p,q;B)\\
\ll\frac{B^{n}}{P^{2n}}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\backslash V_{k+1}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\end{subarray}}|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)||S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)|\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}. $$

To bring the sum over $p,q$ inside the sum over $j$ , we have also used the fact that the strata $V_{n-1}\subset\cdots\subset V_{1}\subset V_{0}=\mathbb{A}^{n}_{\mathbb{Z}}$ provided by Theorem 6.3 are defined over $\mathbb{Z}$ , independent of $p$ and $q$ .

We say that a vector $\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ is globally $j$ -bad if $\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{Z})$ . For such $\mathbf{u}$ , it must be that $\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ for all primes $p$ . Otherwise we say $\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ is locally $j$ -bad if $\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ for some $p\in\mathcal{P}$ , but $\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{j}(\mathbb{Z})$ . For a given pair of indices $j,k$ , the sum over $\mathbf{u}$ splits into four parts: those $\mathbf{u}$ that are globally $j$ -bad and globally $k$ -bad; those $\mathbf{u}$ that are globally $j$ -bad and locally $k$ -bad; those $\mathbf{u}$ that are locally $j$ -bad and globally $k$ -bad; and those $\mathbf{u}$ that are locally $j$ -bad and locally $k$ -bad. We first manipulate the contribution of each of these cases into a format we require in later steps.

#### 6.8.1. Preprocessing the global/global contribution

Let $j$ and $k$ be fixed. The global/global contribution to (6.14) for this $j,k$ pair takes the form

$$ S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}:=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{Z})\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash V_{k+1}(\mathbb{Z})\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\backslash V_{k+1}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\end{subarray}}|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)||S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)|\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}. $$

By the nesting of the stratification (6.7), if $\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{Z})$ and $\mathbf{u}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash V_{k+1}(\mathbb{Z})$ , then $j<k+1$ and $k<j+1$ (namely $j=k$ ). Thus we need only consider terms of the form $S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}$ for $j=k$ , $j=0,\ldots,n-1$ . In the internal sum over $p,q$ , it is equivalent (by homogeneity) to impose that $\overline{q}\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ as to impose $\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ , and similarly we may impose $\overline{p}\mathbf{u}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\backslash V_{k+1}(\mathbb{F}_{q})$ . Hence we may apply the bounds of Theorem 6.3 to the relevant factors $|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)|,$ $|S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)|$ .

It is convenient to treat the $j=k=0$ contribution to the global/global case immediately: this is the case with square root cancellation. Since $V_{0}=\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ , by an application of Lemma 2.12 (with $\kappa=n$ , $Y=P^{2}/B\gg 1$ under the assumption of (6.13)),
