$$ S_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}^{0,0}\ll C(n,\deg F)^{2}P^{n/2}P^{n/2}\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}\ll P^{n}\left(\frac{P^{2}}{B}\right)^{n+\varepsilon}. $$

(In what follows, we will allow implicit constants to depend on $n,\deg F$ and $\varepsilon$ , for an arbitrarily small $\varepsilon>0$ that may vary from line to line, without always noting this.) For each $1\leq j\leq n-1$ we now decompose the stratum $V_{j}\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ into its irreducible components, say

$$ V_{j}=\bigcup_{s\in I_{j}}X_{j,s}, $$

in which $|I_{j}|\ll_{n,\deg F}1$ by Theorem 6.3(iii). Then the global/global contribution of the term $S^{j}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}:=S^{j,j}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}$ is:

$$ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s,t\in I_{j}\\
s^{\prime},t^{\prime}\in I_{j+1}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash X_{j+1,s^{\prime}}(\mathbb{Z})\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,t}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash X_{j+1,t^{\prime}}(\mathbb{Z})\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\backslash X_{j+1,s^{\prime}}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,t}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\backslash X_{j+1,t^{\prime}}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\end{subarray}}|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)||S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)|\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}. $$

Here $X_{j,s}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\setminus X_{j+1,s^{\prime}}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ indicates $X_{j,s}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\setminus(X_{j,s}\cap X_{j+1,s^{\prime}})$ , and similarly for the other conditions on $\mathbf{u}$ . We will use this convention repeatedly in what follows. For later reference, we also note that by Theorem 6.3, we can bound the above expression by

$$ S^{j}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}\ll_{n,\deg F}\max_{p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s,t\in I_{j}\\
s^{\prime},t^{\prime}\in I_{j+1}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash X_{j+1,s^{\prime}}(\mathbb{Z})\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,t}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash X_{j+1,t^{\prime}}(\mathbb{Z})\end{subarray}}p^{\frac{n+j}{2}}q^{\frac{n+j}{2}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}. $$

The conditions place $\mathbf{u}$ in an intersection, so by positivity we only possibly enlarge the upper bound by writing this for each $1\leq j\leq n-1$ as

$$ S^{j}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}\ll|I_{j}||I_{j+1}|\max_{p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{s\in I_{j}}\sum_{s^{\prime}\in I_{j+1}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash X_{j+1,s^{\prime}}(\mathbb{Z})\end{subarray}}p^{\frac{n+j}{2}}q^{\frac{n+j}{2}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}. $$

The contribution (6.16) from the global/global case can be inserted in (6.14), recalling the diagonal condition $j=k$ , and $1\leq j\leq n-1$ .

#### 6.8.2. Preprocessing the local/local contribution

Let $j,k$ be fixed. The local/local contribution to (6.14) for this $j,k$ pair takes the form

$$ S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{loc},\mathrm{loc}}:=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{j}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{Z})\\
\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{k}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash V_{k+1}(\mathbb{Z})\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\backslash V_{k+1}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\end{subarray}}|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)||S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)|\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}. $$

We can write the conditions on the sum over $\mathbf{u}$ as $\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{j}(\mathbb{Z})$ and $\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{k}(\mathbb{Z})$ . (Otherwise, suppose $\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{j}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{Z})$ but $\mathbf{u}\in V_{j+1}(\mathbb{Z})$ ; then it would be the case that $\mathbf{u}\in V_{j+1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ for all $p$ , so the restricted sum over $p$ in the expression above would be empty, leading to zero contribution. An analogous argument holds for the second condition on $\mathbf{u}$ .) By symmetry it suffices to suppose that $j\leq k$ , so that the stronger condition is $\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{j}(\mathbb{Z})$ . We furthermore apply Theorem 6.3 to bound the sums modulo $p$ and $q$ . The local/local contribution for a given pair $j\leq k$ may thus be bounded by

$$ C(n,\deg F)^{2}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{j}(\mathbb{Z})\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\end{subarray}}p^{\frac{n+j}{2}}q^{\frac{n+k}{2}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}. $$

Furthermore, note that if $j=0$ this contribution is zero, since the condition $\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{0}(\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ makes the sum over $\mathbf{u}$ empty. In total, the local/local contribution need only consider $1\leq j\leq k\leq n-1$ , and for such indices can be represented as

$$ S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{loc},\mathrm{loc}}\ll\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}P^{n+j/2+k/2}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{j}(\mathbb{Z})\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\in\mathcal{P}\subset[P,2P]\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\end{subarray}}1. $$

We have chosen to count the number of $p$ as the innermost sum, and preserve the condition $\mathbf{u}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{F}_{q})$ in the sum over $\mathbf{u}$ (rather than reversing the roles of $p$ and $q$ ) because $V_{k}$ has higher codimension ( $j\leq k$ ).

#### 6.8.3. Preprocessing the global/local contribution

We consider one final case: the global/local contribution (the local/global contribution is equivalent, by symmetry considerations). Let $j,k$ be fixed. The global/local contribution to (6.14) for this $j,k$ pair takes the form

$$ S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}:=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{Z})\\
\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{k}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash V_{k+1}(\mathbb{Z})\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\backslash V_{k+1}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\end{subarray}}|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)||S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)|\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}. $$

We can regard the condition $\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{k}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash V_{k+1}(\mathbb{Z})$ as stating that $\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{k}(\mathbb{Z})$ , since if $\mathbf{u}\in V_{k+1}(\mathbb{Z})$ it would follow that $\mathbf{u}\in V_{k+1}(\mathbb{F}_{q})$ for all $q$ so that the sum over $q$ is empty, leading to zero contribution. Thus we consider all $\mathbf{u}$ such that $\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{Z})\setminus V_{j+1}(\mathbb{Z})$ and $\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{k}(\mathbb{Z})$ . By the nesting property (6.7), for the set of such $\mathbf{u}$ to be nonempty it must be the case that $j<k$ , and then it suffices to simply write $\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{Z})\setminus V_{j+1}(\mathbb{Z})$ . Finally, we decompose $V_{j}=\cup_{s\in I_{j}}X_{j,s}$ and $V_{k}=\cup_{t\in I_{k}}X_{k,t}$ into irreducible components, writing

$$ S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\in I_{j}\\
t\in I_{k}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{Z})\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{k,t}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\backslash V_{k+1}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\end{subarray}}|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)||S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)|\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}. $$

We will bound this contribution for all pairs of indices $j,k$ with $0\leq j<k\leq n-1$ .

Finally, we assemble the three types of cases from (6.16), (6.18), and (6.19) in (6.14), and write the result as:

$$ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p,q\in\mathcal{P}\\
p\neq q\end{subarray}}T(p,q;B)\ll\frac{B^{n}}{P^{2n}}\left(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}S^{j}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}+\sum_{1\leq j\leq k\leq n-1}S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{loc},\mathrm{loc}}+\sum_{0\leq j<k\leq n-1}S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}\right). $$

Now we will bound each of these three types of contributions, starting with the easiest case, which is the local/local case.

### 6.9. Bounding the local/local contribution

Fix a pair of indices $1\leq j\leq k\leq n-1$ and recall the expression (6.18) for the corresponding local/local contribution. Recall that $V_{j}=V((G_{j,s})_{s})$ is defined as the common vanishing set of homogeneous polynomials $\{G_{j,s}\}_{s\in I_{j}}$ as $s$ varies over a finite index set $I_{j}$ . Then if $\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{j}(\mathbb{Z})$ , it must be that $G_{j,s}(\mathbf{u})\neq 0$ for some $s\in I_{j}.$ On the other hand, since $\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ , it must be that $p|G_{j,s}(\mathbf{u})$ (indeed for all $s\in I_{j}$ ). Hence, for any $\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{j}(\mathbb{Z})$ ,

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\in[P,2P]\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{j}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\end{subarray}}1\leq\max_{s\in I_{j},G_{j,s}(\mathbf{u})\neq 0}\nu_{0}(G_{j,s}(\mathbf{u})), $$

in which the maximum is over a set with at least one element. Here $\nu_{0}(m)$ denotes the number of distinct prime divisors of an integer $m$ in the range $[P,2P]$ . Multiplying over the distinct prime divisors of the integer $G_{j,s}(\mathbf{u})\neq 0$ that lie in the range $[P,2P]$ , one sees that $(\prod p)|G_{j,s}(\mathbf{u})$ so that

$$ P^{\nu_{0}(G_{j,s}(\mathbf{u}))}\leq|G_{j,s}(\mathbf{u})|\ll_{n}\|G_{j,s}\||\mathbf{u}|^{\deg_{G_{j,s}}}, $$

and this provides an upper bound for $\nu_{0}(G_{j,s}(\mathbf{u}))$ . Consequently, applying this in (6.18) leads to

$$ S_{\mathrm{loc},\mathrm{loc}}^{j,k}\ll_{n,\deg F}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}P^{n+j/2+k/2}\deg(V_{j})\sum_{q\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\end{subarray}}\frac{\log(1+|\mathbf{u}|)+\log\|V_{j}\|}{\log P}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}, $$

in which we used positivity to omit the condition $\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{j}(\mathbb{Z})$ . We have also adopted the convention that

$$ \|V_{j}\|:=\max_{s\in I_{j}}\|G_{j,s}\| $$

so that by Theorem 6.3(v), $\log\|V_{j}\|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|$ . Also by (ii) of that theorem, $\deg V_{j}\ll_{n,\deg F}1$ . Next, we apply Lemma 2.12 to bound this smoothed sum over points of bounded height $\ll P^{2}/B$ whose reduction modulo $q$ lie in a variety of dimension at most $n-k$ in $\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q})$ . Note that for $j\leq k$ we pre-processed the local/local sum in precisely the form (6.18) so that of the two options, the highest codimension $k$ now appears in this sum. Under the condition (6.13) on the size of $P$ , $1\ll P^{2}/B=o(P)$ . By Proposition 2.2, the hypothesis (2.3) of Lemma 2.12 holds with $\kappa=n-k$ for $V_{k}(\mathbb{F}_{q})$ . We may apply the case $Y:=P^{2}/B$ in Lemma 2.12; then $Y<q^{\sigma}$ for some $\sigma<1$ since $q\in[P,2P]$ and (6.13) controls the size of $P$ . This shows

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\in V_{k}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}(\log(1+|\mathbf{u}|))\ll\left(\frac{P^{2}}{B}\right)^{n-k+\varepsilon}. $$

Finally, we sum trivially over $q$ . The conclusion is that for $1\leq j\leq k\leq n-1$ , for any $\varepsilon>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle S_{\mathrm{loc,\mathrm{loc}}}^{j,k} \displaystyle\ll_{\varepsilon,n,\deg F}(\log\|F\|)\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}P^{n+j/2+k/2}\frac{|\mathcal{P}|}{\log P}\left(\frac{P^{2}}{B}\right)^{n-k+\varepsilon} \displaystyle\ll_{\varepsilon,n,\deg F}(\log\|F\|)P^{n+k-1}\left(\frac{P^{2}}{B}\right)^{n-k+\varepsilon}. $$

By recording the second inequality, we may reduce the local/local terms to only considering the diagonal contribution from $k=j$ , which we have shown via the first inequality are the largest terms.

### 6.10. Bounding the global/global contribution, degenerate case

We next consider the global/global contribution. Let $1\leq j\leq n-1$ be fixed. Within the expression (6.16) for $S^{j}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}$ , we now further divide the irreducible components $X_{j,s}$ of $V_{j}$ into two cases. Recalling the discussion in §6.3, if $X_{j,s}$ lies in a (proper) linear subspace of $\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ , we say $X_{j,s}$ is a degenerate case, and otherwise we say that $X_{j,s}$ is a nondegenerate case. Given $j$ , we decompose

$$ S_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}^{j}=S_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}^{j,\mathrm{deg}}+S_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}^{j,\mathrm{non}}. $$

Here, $S^{j,\mathrm{deg}}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}$ (respectively $S^{j,\mathrm{non}}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}$ ) is given by the terms in the sum over $s$ on the right-hand side of (6.16) restricted to those components such that $X_{j,s}$ is a degenerate case (respectively, nondegenerate case). (This decomposition does not distinguish those $s^{\prime}$ for which $X_{j+1,s^{\prime}}$ is degenerate or nondegenerate. Also, we need only consider whether $X_{j,s}$ is degenerate over $\mathbb{Z}$ (and consequently over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ for all primes $p$ ); we do not need to handle separately any “locally degenerate” cases.) We will return to the non-degenerate contributions in §6.11; here we focus on $S_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}^{j,\deg}$ . We will apply the second moment bound from Proposition 5.3, in the form of (6.11), which is adapted to a linear transformation corresponding to the degenerate component; this specifically relies on the hypothesis of Theorem 6.4 that $F_{L}$ is strongly $n$ -genuine for each $L\in\mathcal{L}(F)$ .

As seen in the expression (6.16), the contribution of a degenerate irreducible component $X_{j,s}$ to $S_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}^{j,\mathrm{deg}}$ is at most:

$$ \displaystyle\max_{p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}}|I_{j}||I_{j+1}|^{2}\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)||S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)| \displaystyle\ll_{n,\deg F}\max_{p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq b\leq\lceil\log_{2}p^{n}\rceil\\
M_{p}=2^{b}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq c\leq\lceil\log_{2}q^{n}\rceil\\
M_{q}=2^{c}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})\\
M_{p}<|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)|\leq 2M_{p}\\
M_{q}\leq|S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)|<2M_{q}\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)||S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)| \displaystyle\ll_{n,\deg F}\max_{p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{M_{p}\nearrow p^{n}}\sum_{M_{q}\nearrow q^{n}}M_{p}M_{q}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})\\
|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)|>M_{p}\\
|S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)|>M_{q}\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}, $$

in which the sums over $M_{p},M_{q}$ denote dyadic sums, each with $\ll_{n}\log P$ summands. (We have expressed these as dyadic sums over powers of $2$ , but it would be equally possible to write them as as a $p$ -adic and $q$ -adic sum, respectively. Since $X_{j,s}\subset V_{j}$ , we do not need to take $M_{p}$ beyond $p^{(n+j)/2}$ , but the additional terms here are negligible in the dyadic sum, and similarly for $M_{q}$ .) We have also used the fact (iii) from Theorem 6.3 that the number of components $|I_{j}|\ll_{n,\deg F}1$ for all $j$ . Fix a small $\alpha>0$ (to be chosen later) and define the box

$$ C_{\alpha}=[-(P^{2}/B)^{1+\alpha},(P^{2}/B)^{1+\alpha}]^{n}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}. $$

Decompose the above expression for the contribution to $S^{j,\mathrm{deg}}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}$ from $X_{j,s}$ into two terms $\mathrm{I}+\mathrm{II}$ , denoting the contribution from summing over $\mathbf{u}\in C_{\alpha}$ and over $\mathbf{u}\not\in C_{\alpha}$ , respectively. First,

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{I} \displaystyle\ll_{n,\deg F}\max_{p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{M_{p}\nearrow p^{n}}\sum_{M_{q}\nearrow q^{n}}M_{p}M_{q} \displaystyle\qquad\cdot\#\left(\{|\mathbf{u}|\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})\cap C_{\alpha}:|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)|>M_{p}\}\cap\{|\mathbf{u}|\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})\cap C_{\alpha}:|S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)|>M_{q}\}\right) \displaystyle\ll_{n,\deg F}\log P\max_{p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{M_{p}\nearrow p^{n}}M_{p}^{2}\cdot\#\{|\mathbf{u}|\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})\cap C_{\alpha}:|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)|>M_{p}\} \displaystyle\ll_{n,\deg F}\log P\max_{p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{M_{p}\nearrow p^{n}}M_{p}^{2}\cdot\#\{|\mathbf{u}|\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{F}_{p}):|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)|>M_{p}\} \displaystyle\ll_{n,\deg F}P^{2n-1}(\log P)^{2}. $$

In the first inequality, we assume without loss of generality that we consider terms with $M_{p}\geq M_{q}$ (an analogous argument holds in the symmetric case). Then by positivity we can bound the size of the intersection by the size of the superlevel set defined with respect to $M_{p}$ (and then sum trivially over the $\ll\log P$ summands for $M_{q}$ ). In the second inequality, we use that $P=B^{\rho}$ for some $\rho<1$ by assumption (6.13). In particular, given $\rho$ , by choosing $\alpha\ll_{\rho}1$ sufficiently small, we can ensure that $(P^{2}/B)^{1+\alpha}\ll p$ (at least for $B\gg_{\rho}1$ ) so that $X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})\cap C_{\alpha}$ may be identified with a subset of $X_{j,s}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ . To achieve the last inequality, we plug in (6.11). (By the choice of the sieving set in §6.7, all primes in $\mathcal{P}$ have been chosen to avoid the possible exceptional primes for which (6.11) does not apply.)

Now we turn to the term $\mathrm{II}$ , which is bounded by

$$ \mathrm{II}\ll_{n,\deg F}P^{2n}(\log P)^{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\not\in C_{\alpha}\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}\ll P^{2n}(\log P)^{2}(P^{2}/B)^{n-\alpha(M-2)}. $$

Here we have applied that $P=B^{\rho}$ for $\rho>1/2$ so that $P^{2}/B\gg 1$ , and argued as in (2.4) of Lemma 2.12, (with $Y=P^{2}/B\gg 1$ , $A=0$ , and $\varepsilon=\alpha$ ). Recall that we may take $M$ as large as we like. Our ultimate choice of $P=B^{\rho}$ in §7 will choose $\rho=n/(n+1)$ , so that the appropriate choice of $\alpha$ above depends only on $n$ . (Any $\alpha<1/(n-1)$ will do.) Thus we may assume from now on that $M=M(n)$ is sufficiently large that $n-\alpha(M-2)<0$ . Then the contribution of $\mathrm{II}$ can be made arbitrarily small, and in particular is dominated by the contribution from $\mathrm{I}$ , for all $B\gg_{n}1$ . In total, the contribution of $X_{j,s}$ to $S_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}^{j,\mathrm{deg}}$ is dominated by (6.26). Summing over all $X_{j,s}$ in the degenerate case (at most $|I_{j}|\ll_{n,\deg F}1$ terms) leads to

$$ S_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}^{j,\mathrm{deg}}\ll_{n,\deg F}P^{2n-1}(\log P)^{2}. $$

### 6.11. Bounding the global/global contribution, nondegenerate case

We now focus on the contribution $S_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}^{j,\mathrm{non}}$ to (6.16) for each $1\leq j\leq n-1$ . First, we claim that when $X_{j,s}\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ is a nondegenerate irreducible component of $V_{j}$ , we may assume $\dim X_{j,s}>1$ (or equivalently $\codim X_{j,s}\leq n-2$ ). In other words, we claim that if $\dim(X_{j,s})=1$ , then $X_{j,s}$ must lie in a (proper) linear subspace of $\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ , and hence fall into the degenerate case. Indeed, since $X_{j,s}$ is homogeneous, the projective dimension of such $X_{j,s}$ is zero. So, when viewed projectively, $X_{j,s}$ is a finite set of points; as such, when viewed in affine space, the irreducible component $X_{j,s}$ will be a line and thus linear (and degenerate). The requirement $\codim X_{j,s}\leq n-2$ , combined with the fact from Theorem 6.3 that $\codim X_{j,s}\geq j$ , thus imposes $j\leq n-2$ from now on. Note that if $n=2$ , only $j=0$ satisfies $j\leq n-2$ , and the global/global contribution for $V_{0}$ has already been bounded in (6.15). Thus for the rest of this section, we may assume $n\geq 3$ (and if $n=2$ , the sums over $j\leq n-2$ depicted below are considered to be empty).

Second, if $X_{j,s}$ is nondegenerate, it must be that $\deg X_{j,s}\geq 2$ . Third, fix an index $j\in\{1,\ldots,n-2\}$ . Let $X_{j,s}$ be an irreducible component of the $j$ -th stratum $V_{j}$ with codimension at least $j$ in $\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ , and degree denoted $\deg X_{j,s}$ . We recall the following relation between the dimension and degree of a nondegenerate variety.

#### Proposition 6.6.

Let $W\subset\mathbb{P}^{N}$ be an irreducible nondegenerate variety of degree $e$ and dimension $m$ . Then $e>N-m$ .

We quote this from [Har92, Cor. 18.12], but we remark that it seems to have appeared originally in the note [Cor57], and soon after in Swinnerton-Dyer [SD73, Lemma 3 and Corollary]. As a result of the proposition, if $X_{j,s}$ is nondegenerate, then $\deg X_{j,s}>\codim X_{j,s}\geq j$ . Hence all that remains is to bound the contribution of $X_{j,s}$ to $S_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}^{j,\mathrm{non}}$ under the assumption that $1\leq j\leq\min\{\deg X_{j,s}-1,n-2\}.$

With these restrictions, the total nondegenerate contribution to (6.16) for a fixed $1\leq j\leq n-2$ is bounded by:

$$ S_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}^{j,\mathrm{non}}\ll_{n,\deg F}|I_{j}||I_{j+1}|^{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\in I_{j}\\
j\leq\min\{\deg X_{j,s}-1,n-2\}\end{subarray}}P^{n+j}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}. $$

We have obtained this expression by considering the nondegenerate contribution to the simplified form (6.17). We can achieve a bound that is uniform in the coefficients of the defining polynomials of $X_{j,s}$ , by applying Pila’s bound (Theorem 2.11). (See Remark 6.7 for why a more straightforward approach is not yet available.) Fix a component $X_{j,s}$ considered in the sum, and apply Lemma 2.12 to bound the smoothed sum over $\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})$ , with $Y=P^{2}/B\gg 1$ . By Pila’s bound, the hypothesis (2.2) holds with $\kappa=n-j-1+(\deg X_{j,s})^{-1}+\varepsilon$ for any $\varepsilon>0$ , and an implicit constant depending only on $n,j,\deg X_{j,s},\varepsilon$ . By Theorem 6.3 (ii), $\deg X_{j,s}\ll_{n,\deg F}1$ . Consequently,

$$ S_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}^{j,\mathrm{non}}\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}\delta_{n\geq 3}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\in I_{j}\end{subarray}}\delta_{j,\deg(X_{j,s})}P^{n+j}(P^{2}/B)^{n-j-1+(\deg X_{j,s})^{-1}+\varepsilon} $$

under the definitions $\delta_{n\geq 3}=1$ if $n\geq 3$ and vanishes otherwise, and

$$ \delta_{j,e}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if $j\leq\min\{e-1,n-2\}$ and $e\geq 2$ }\\
0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

#### Remark 6.7.

Salberger has proved the Dimension Growth Conjecture, and the uniform version of the conjecture for degree at least 4 [Sal23, Thm. 0.1, 0.3]. Let $X\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}_{\mathbb{Q}}$ be an integral projective variety defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ . Then for $\deg(X)\geq 2$ , for any $\varepsilon>0$ ,

$$ \#\{\bfx\in X(\mathbb{Z}):\|\bfx\|\leq B\}=O_{X,\varepsilon}(B^{\dim_{\mathrm{proj}}(X)+\varepsilon}). $$

For $\deg(X)\geq 4$ ,

$$ \#\{\bfx\in X(\mathbb{Z}):\|\bfx\|\leq B\}=O_{\deg(X),n,\varepsilon}(B^{\dim_{\mathrm{proj}}(X)+\varepsilon}). $$

This uniform bound was previously obtained for hypersurfaces of degree 2 in [HB02] and for geometrically integral hypersurfaces of degree 2 or degree at least 6 in [BHBS06].

In (6.29), it would be simpler to apply the truth of the Dimension Growth Conjecture, which would show that for any $\varepsilon>0$ ,

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}\ll_{X_{j,s},\varepsilon}\left(\frac{P^{2}}{B}\right)^{n-j-1+\varepsilon} $$

for any $\varepsilon>0$ . This is a better exponent than in (6.29), and leads to a bound $S_{\mathrm{global}}^{j,\mathrm{non}}\ll_{V_{j},\varepsilon}P^{n+j}(P^{2}/B)^{n-j-1+\varepsilon}$ . However, the implicit constant is only known to be uniform in the coefficients of the defining functions of $X_{j,s}$ if $\deg X_{j,s}\neq 3$ , while we cannot rule out that $\deg X_{j,s}=3$ may occur. (For $\deg(X)=3$ , the current record of [Sal23, Thm. 0.3] replaces the right-hand side of (6.31) by $O_{n,\varepsilon}(B^{\dim_{\mathrm{proj}}(X)-1+2/\sqrt{3}+\varepsilon})$ , with an exponent not strong enough for our application.) Thus we proceed with the bound (6.29), and we will use Proposition 6.6 to argue case by case that the additional $(\deg X_{j,s})^{-1}$ in the exponent is not detrimental in the proof of Theorem 6.4.

### 6.12. Bounding the global/local contribution

It only remains to bound the global/local contribution to (6.20), and this uses a combination of the above strategies. Recall the expression (6.19) for $S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}$ for each pair $j,k$ with $0\leq j<k\leq n-1$ . We will prove two bounds for $S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}$ , and choose the most advantageous depending on the pair $j,k$ of indices.

For the first bound, fix indices $s\in I_{j}$ and $t\in I_{k}$ . (By Theorem 6.3(iii) there are $\ll_{n,\deg F}1$ such tuples of indices.) The contribution of the corresponding term to $S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}$ is

$$ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{Z})\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{k,t}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\backslash V_{k+1}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\end{subarray}}|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)||S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)|\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}. $$

We apply the bounds $|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)|\ll P^{\frac{n+j}{2}}$ and $|S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)|\ll P^{\frac{n+k}{2}}$ from Theorem 6.3. Since $\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})$ , it follows that $\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{F}_{p})$ for all $p\in\mathcal{P}$ so we sum trivially over such $p$ and gain no advantage there. (It is tempting to fix $\mathbf{u}$ and use the fact that there can be few $q$ for which $\mathbf{u}$ is locally in $X_{k,t}(\mathbb{F}_{q})$ but not in $X_{k,t}(\mathbb{Z})$ , but then the remaining sum over $\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})$ is only over a set of codimension $j$ . So we currently argue a different way.) We first sum over $\mathbf{u}$ and then sum over $q$ in the remaining expression, which then is bounded above by

$$ \ll_{n,\deg F}\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}P^{\frac{n+j}{2}}P^{\frac{n+k}{2}}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{k,t}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\end{subarray}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}. $$

Here we have used positivity in order to omit all conditions on $\mathbf{u}$ except for the condition $\mathbf{u}\in X_{k,t}(\mathbb{F}_{q})$ , which we retained because $X_{k,t}$ has the higher codimension $k$ . Now for each $q$ this sum over $\mathbf{u}$ can be treated exactly as we treated the (slightly larger) sum (6.23) in the local/local case. Finally, we sum trivially over $q$ . This leads to the first upper bound

$$ S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}P^{n+j/2+k/2}\left(\frac{P^{2}}{B}\right)^{n-k+\varepsilon}. $$

This will ultimately be strong enough in two scenarios: if $j=0$ and $1\leq k\leq n-1$ , and if $1\leq j\leq n-1$ and $k\geq j+3$ .

Thus we proceed now to consider a different bound (which we will apply for all index pairs for which $1\leq j\leq n-1$ and $k=j+\kappa$ with $\kappa=1$ or $2$ ). Fix $j,k$ with $j<k$ . Now we consider whether each irreducible component $X_{j,s}\subset\mathbb{A}^{n}(\mathbb{Z})$ of $V_{j}$ is degenerate or not, and we accordingly decompose

$$ S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}=S^{j,k,\mathrm{deg}}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}+S^{j,k,\mathrm{non}}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}. $$

Suppose first that $X_{j,s}$ is degenerate: then by summing over all $p,q$ trivially, the contribution of $X_{j,s}$ to $S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}$ is bounded above by:

$$ \leq|I_{j}||I_{j+1}|^{2}\max_{p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})\end{subarray}}|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)||S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)|\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}. $$

This is recognized as (6.25) and can be dominated by $\ll_{n,\deg F}P^{2n-1}(\log P)^{2}$ , just as that expression was. (This also relies on the hypothesis of Theorem 6.4 that $F_{L}$ is strongly $n$ -genuine for all $L\in\mathcal{L}(F)$ .) Thus we can record the contribution to $S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}$ from all irreducible components $X_{j,s}$ that fall in the degenerate case as

$$ S^{j,k,\mathrm{deg}}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}\ll_{n,\deg F}P^{2n-1}(\log P)^{2}. $$

In particular, for all pairs $1\leq j<k\leq n-1$ , this contribution is dominated by the contribution (6.27) recorded for $S^{j,\mathrm{deg}}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}$ .

Now fix an $s$ for which $X_{j,s}$ is nondegenerate. By the same arguments presented at the beginning of §6.11, we need only consider the case that $1\leq j\leq\min\{\deg(X_{j,s})-1,n-2\}$ . (If $n=2$ this imposes $j=0$ , which was already handled before, so from now on we may assume $n\geq 3$ .) Fix any index $t\in I_{k}$ (of which there are $\ll_{n,\deg F}1$ choices). The contribution we must bound is

$$ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{Z})\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\backslash V_{j+1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{k,t}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\backslash V_{k+1}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\end{subarray}}|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)||S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)|\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}. $$

We apply the bounds $|S(\overline{q}\mathbf{u},p)|\ll P^{\frac{n+j}{2}}$ and $|S(\overline{p}\mathbf{u},q)|\ll P^{\frac{n+k}{2}}$ from Theorem 6.3. We again sum trivially over all $p\in\mathcal{P}$ , since $\mathbf{u}$ lies in $X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})$ . On the other hand, observe that using the local property for $q$ will preserve a savings of $|\mathcal{P}|^{-1}$ for the sum over $q$ . Recall that $X_{k,t}$ is a homogeneous irreducible component, so it is defined by some homogeneous polynomial $G_{k,t}$ . Since $\mathbf{u}\not\in X_{k,t}(\mathbb{Z})$ (since $\mathbf{u}\not\in V_{j+1}(\mathbb{Z})$ and $k>j$ ) but $\mathbf{u}\in X_{k,t}(\mathbb{F}_{q})$ , we may conclude that $G_{k,t}(\mathbf{u})\neq 0$ but $q|G_{k,t}(\mathbf{u})$ . Thus arguing as in (6.21) and (6.22) to bound the number of $q$ arising in the sum, the contribution expressed above can be bounded by

$$ \ll_{n,\deg F}\deg(V_{k})\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}P^{\frac{n+j}{2}}P^{\frac{n+k}{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\
\mathbf{u}\in X_{j,s}(\mathbb{Z})\end{subarray}}\frac{(\log(1+|\mathbf{u}|)+\log\|V_{k}\|)}{\log P}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1+\frac{|u_{i}|B}{P^{2}}\right)^{-M}. $$

By Theorem 6.3 (v), $\log\|V_{k}\|:=\max_{s\in I_{k}}\log\|G_{k,s}\|\ll_{n,\deg F}\log\|F\|.$ Furthermore, we recognize that the sum over $\mathbf{u}$ in the expression above takes the same form as the sum over $\bfu$ in (6.28) previously encountered in the global/global nondegenerate case, aside from an extra factor of $\log(1+|\mathbf{u}|)$ here. We proceed as we did to bound (6.28) by applying Pila’s bound (Theorem 2.11) as an input to the smoothed counting lemma (Lemma 2.12) with $\kappa=n-j-1+(\deg X_{j,s})^{-1}+\varepsilon$ . This shows that the contribution to $S_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}^{j,k}$ from all nondegenerate components $X_{j,s}$ is

$$ S_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}^{j,k,\mathrm{non}}\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}(\log\|F\|)\delta_{n\geq 3}\sum_{s\in I_{j}}\delta_{j,\deg(X_{j,s})}P^{n+j/2+k/2-1}(P^{2}/B)^{n-j-1+\deg(X_{j,s})^{-1}+\varepsilon}. $$

In particular, for $k\leq j+2$ , note that $P^{n+j/2+k/2-1}\leq P^{n+j}$ , in which case the summand above is dominated by the corresponding summand recorded in (6.29) of $X_{j,s}$ for $S^{j,\mathrm{non}}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}$ . But note the factor of $\log\|F\|$ here.

## 7. Combining the estimates

We now complete the proof of Theorem 6.4 via the polynomial sieve. We input the bounds for the global/global, local/local, and global/local cases into (6.20), which we summarize in the form

$$ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p,q\in\mathcal{P}\\
p\neq q\end{subarray}}T(p,q;B)\ll T_{\mathrm{loc},\mathrm{loc}}+T_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}+T_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}. $$

Recall that we consider $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ of the form (1.1) for given degree parameters $m,d,k_{1},\ldots,k_{d}$ . Inputting the bounds proved in (6.15), (6.24),(6.27), and (6.29), as well as (6.33), (6.34) and (6.35), we can summarize our conclusions as follows. For the local/local terms,

$$ \displaystyle T_{\mathrm{loc},\mathrm{loc}} \displaystyle\ll\frac{B^{n}}{P^{2n}}\sum_{1\leq j\leq k\leq n-1}S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{loc},\mathrm{loc}}\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}(\log\|F\|)\frac{B^{n}}{P^{2n}}\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}P^{n+j-1}\left(\frac{P^{2}}{B}\right)^{n-j+\varepsilon} \displaystyle\ll(\log\|F\|)P^{n-1}B^{\varepsilon}\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(B/P)^{j} \displaystyle\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}(\log\|F\|)B^{n-1+\varepsilon}. $$

In the last inequality we have used that $B/P\gg 1$ to dominate the sum by the contribution from $j=n-1$ .

For the global/global term, recall the definition of $\delta_{j,e}$ in (6.30). Under the hypotheses of Theorem 6.4,

$$ \displaystyle T_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}} \displaystyle\ll\frac{B^{n}}{P^{2n}}\left(P^{n}(P^{2}/B)^{n+\varepsilon}+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}S^{j,\mathrm{deg}}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}+\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}S^{j,\mathrm{non}}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}\right) \displaystyle\ll\frac{B^{n}}{P^{2n}}\Bigg(P^{n}(P^{2}/B)^{n+\varepsilon}+P^{2n-1}(\log P)^{2} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\;\delta_{n\geq 3}\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}\sum_{s\in I_{j}}\delta_{j,\deg X_{j,s}}P^{n+j}(P^{2}/B)^{n-j-1+(\deg X_{j,s})^{-1}+\varepsilon}\Bigg) \displaystyle\ll B^{\varepsilon}(P^{n}+B^{n}P^{-1}+\delta_{n\geq 3}P^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\in I_{j}\\
(e:=\deg X_{j,s}\geq 2)\end{subarray}}\delta_{j,e}\frac{B^{j+1-1/e}}{P^{j+2-2/e}}) \displaystyle\ll B^{\varepsilon}(P^{n}+B^{n}P^{-1}+\delta_{n\geq 3}P^{n}\Sigma), $$

say, where $\Sigma$ denotes the double sum over $j$ and $s$ . The implicit constants depend on $n,\deg F,\varepsilon$ . We now analyze the sum $\Sigma$ when $n\geq 3$ (for $n=2$ it is empty).

#### Lemma 7.1.

Suppose

$$ P=B^{\rho} n/(n+1)\leq\rho<1 $$

Then for $n\geq 3$ ,

$$ \Sigma:=\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\in I_{j}\\
(e:=\deg X_{j,s}\geq 2)\end{subarray}}\delta_{j,e}\frac{B^{j+1-1/e}}{P^{j+2-2/e}}\ll_{n,\deg F}1. $$

#### Proof.

Let $E$ denote the set of possible distinct values of $e:=\deg X_{j,s}$ that arise as $j,s$ vary over all pairs in this sum, for which $\delta_{j,e}$ is nonzero (as defined in (6.30)). Then $E$ is a finite set with $E\subset[2,\infty)$ and $|E|\leq\sum_{j}|I_{j}|\ll_{n,\deg F}1$ (by Theorem 6.3(iii)). Possibly overcounting, we can write

$$ \Sigma\leq\sum_{e\in E}\sum_{j=1}^{\min\{e-1,n-2\}}|I_{j}|\frac{B^{j+1-1/e}}{P^{j+2-2/e}}. $$

(For clarity, we observe that the condition $j\leq e-1$ may be imposed here because otherwise $\delta_{j,e}=0$ (and the underlying reason is due to Proposition 6.6).) For each $e\in E$ , the inner sum over $j$ is bounded above by the contributions of its upper and lower endpoints, so we check the contribution at $j=1$ , at $j=e-1$ (only if $e-1\leq n-2$ ) and at $j=n-2$ (only if $e-1\geq n-2$ ). The contribution at $j=1$ is

$$ \frac{B^{2-\frac{1}{e}}}{P^{3-\frac{2}{e}}}\ll 1\Longleftrightarrow P\gg B^{\frac{2e-1}{3e-2}}. $$

Note that $\frac{2e-1}{3e-2}$ is a decreasing function of $e\geq 2$ and evaluates to $3/4$ when $e=2$ , so the relation above will hold as long as $\rho\geq 3/4$ (which we note holds in particular for $\rho=n/(n+1)$ , for all $n\geq 3$ ). The contribution at $j=e-1$ (which we only consider if $e-1\leq n-2$ ), is

$$ \frac{B^{e-\frac{1}{e}}}{P^{e+1-\frac{2}{e}}}\ll 1\Longleftrightarrow P\gg B^{\frac{e-\frac{1}{e}}{e+1-\frac{2}{e}}}=B^{\frac{e+1}{e+2}}. $$

Since the function $\frac{e+1}{e+2}$ is increasing as a function of $e\geq 2$ and $e-1\leq n-2$ , the relation above will hold as long as $\rho\geq n/(n+1).$ Finally, the contribution at $j=n-2$ (which we only consider if $e-1\geq n-2$ ) is

$$ \frac{B^{n-1-\frac{1}{e}}}{P^{n-\frac{2}{e}}}\ll 1\Longleftrightarrow P\gg B^{\frac{n-1-\frac{1}{e}}{n-\frac{2}{e}}}=B^{\frac{e(n-1)-1}{en-2}}. $$

Since the exponent on the right-hand side is decreasing as a function of $e\geq 2$ (for $n\geq 3$ ) and since we may assume $e-1\geq n-2$ (as follows from Proposition 6.6), it follows that the relation above will hold if $\rho\geq\frac{(n-1)^{2}-1}{(n-1)n-2}=\frac{n}{n+1}$ . ∎

And finally, we have proved

$$ \displaystyle T_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}} \displaystyle\ll\frac{B^{n}}{P^{2n}}\sum_{0\leq j<k\leq n-1}S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}} \displaystyle\ll\frac{B^{n}}{P^{2n}}\left(\sum_{1\leq k\leq n-1}S^{0,k}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq j<k\leq n-1\\
k\geq j+3\end{subarray}}S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq j<k\leq n-1\\
k\leq j+2\end{subarray}}S^{j,k}_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}\right) $$

As previously remarked below (6.34) and (6.35), the total contribution to $T_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}$ from the last sum over $j,k$ (with $k\leq j+2$ ) is dominated by quantities we have already bounded when treating $T_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{glo}}$ , up to an additional factor $(\log\|F\|)$ . Precisely, this sum contributes $\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}(\log\|F\|)B^{\varepsilon}(B^{n}P^{-1}+P^{n})$ to $T_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}$ . The remaining consideration is to apply (6.33) to each term in the first two sums, which shows these two sums yield a total contribution to $T_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}$ of at most

$$ \displaystyle\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}\frac{B^{n}}{P^{2n}}\left(\sum_{1\leq k\leq n-1}P^{n+k/2}\left(\frac{P^{2}}{B}\right)^{n-k+\varepsilon}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq j<k\leq n-1\\
k\geq j+3\end{subarray}}P^{n+j/2+k/2}\left(\frac{P^{2}}{B}\right)^{n-k+\varepsilon}\right) \displaystyle\ll B^{\varepsilon}\left(P^{n}\sum_{1\leq k\leq n-1}\left(\frac{B}{P^{3/2}}\right)^{k}+P^{n}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq j<k\leq n-1\\
k\geq j+3\end{subarray}}P^{(j-k)/2}\left(\frac{B}{P}\right)^{k}\right). $$

We claim this is $\ll(P^{n}+B^{n-1})B^{\varepsilon}$ . In the first sum, it suffices to observe that $B/P^{3/2}\ll 1$ , which holds for all $n\geq 2$ under our current hypothesis (7.1) on the size of $P$ . In the second sum,

$$ P^{n}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq j<k\leq n-1\\
k\geq j+3\end{subarray}}P^{(j-k)/2}\left(\frac{B}{P}\right)^{k}\ll_{n}P^{n}\sum_{2\leq k\leq n-1}P^{-3/2}\left(\frac{B}{P}\right)^{k}\ll P^{n-3/2}(B/P)^{n-1}\ll B^{n-1}. $$

The penultimate inequality uses $B\gg P$ , and the last inequality is an over-estimate, but suffices. In total, under the hypothesis (7.1),

$$ T_{\mathrm{glo},\mathrm{loc}}\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}(\log\|F\|)(B^{n}P^{-1}+P^{n})B^{\varepsilon}. $$

### 7.1. Conclusion of the proof of Theorem 6.4

We have shown that if $P=B^{\rho}$ with $n/(n+1)\leq\rho<1$ and $n\geq 2$ , then under the hypotheses of Theorem 6.4,

$$ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p,q\in\mathcal{P}\\
p\neq q\end{subarray}}T(p,q;B)\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}(\log\|F\|)(B^{n}P^{-1}+P^{n})B^{\varepsilon}. $$

Inserting this in (6.4) and taking the optimal choice $P=B^{\frac{n}{n+1}},$ the conclusion is that for any $\varepsilon>0$ :

$$ N(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}(\log\|F\|)B^{n-1+\frac{1}{n+1}+\varepsilon}. $$

This consequence of the polynomial sieve has been shown under the conditions from Lemma 6.1 if $m\geq 2$ (or Lemma 6.2 if $m=1$ ), and the lower bound (6.12) for $P$ when constructing the sieving set. These are all satisfied if

$$ P\gg_{n,\deg F}\max\{(\log\|F\|)^{3},(\log B)^{3}\}. $$

With $P=B^{n/(n+1)}$ , the latter condition is satisfied for all $B\gg_{n,\deg F}1$ . The former condition is satisfied if $B\gg_{n,\deg F}(\log\|F\|)^{6}$ , so (7.3) holds for all such $B$ . This completes the proof of Theorem 6.4.

#### Remark 7.2 (Dependence on GRH).

The conditional version of the polynomial sieve stated in Lemma 6.2 for $m=1$ assumes that GRH holds for a large collection of Dedekind zeta functions (each associated to some $\bfk\in[-2B,2B]^{n}$ , in the proof provided in [BP24, §3.2]). As $B\rightarrow\infty$ , this formulation of Lemma 6.2 assumes GRH for the Dedekind zeta functions of potentially infinitely many fields.

However, an inspection of the proof in [BP24, §3.2] shows that the following average statement (7.4) (weaker than assuming GRH for all Dedekind zeta functions) suffices to prove Lemma 6.2 in the following form (which would also imply its consequences in this paper, namely the $m=1$ case of all the main theorems in this paper). Let $G(Y,\mathbf{X})$ be monic in $Y$ and write $G(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{D}+f_{1}(\mathbf{X})Y^{D-1}+\cdots+f_{d}(\mathbf{X})$ for some $D\geq 2$ . Following the notation of [BP24, §3.2], fix any $\bfk\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ with $G(Y,\bfk)=0$ solvable and $f_{d}(\bfk)\neq 0$ . Let $g_{\bfk}(y)$ be an irreducible factor of the polynomial $\tilde{g}_{\bfk}$ defined by $G(Y,\bfk)=(Y-y_{0})\tilde{g}_{\bfk}(Y)$ . Let $F_{\bfk}$ denote the splitting field of $g_{\bfk}(Y)$ and $G_{\bfk}$ the Galois group of $F_{\bfk}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ , and $\pi_{\bfk}(Q)$ the number of primes in $[Q/2,Q]$ that split completely in $F_{\bfk}$ . Suppose it is known that for a sufficiently small constant $c_{D}$ ,

$$ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bfk\in[-2B,2B]^{n}\\
f_{d}(\bfk)\neq 0\\
G(y,\bfk)=0\text{ solvable in $\mathbb{Z}$}\end{subarray}}\left|\pi_{\bfk}(Q)-\frac{1}{|G_{\bfk}|}\frac{Q}{\log Q}\right|\\
\\
\leq c_{D}\frac{Q}{\log Q}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bfk\in[-2B,2B]^{n}\\
f_{d}(\bfk)\neq 0\\
G(y,\bfk)=0\text{ solvable in $\mathbb{Z}$}\end{subarray}}1, $$

for all $Q\gg B^{\kappa}$ (for a given $1/2\leq\kappa\leq 1$ ) and $B\geq 1$ . Then for $\mathcal{P}$ a set of primes $p\in[Q,2Q]$ with $|\mathcal{P}|\gg Q(\log Q)^{-1}$ , a minor adaptation of the argument in [BP24, §3.2] proves that the smoothed count $\mathcal{S}(G,B)$ for $N(G,B)$ satisfies

$$ \mathcal{S}(G,B)\ll_{n,\deg G}B^{n}Q^{-1}\log Q+\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|^{2}}\sum_{p\neq q\in\mathcal{P}}\left|\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}(v_{p}(\mathbf{x})-1)(v_{q}(\mathbf{x})-1)W(\mathbf{x})\right|, $$

for all $Q\gg_{\deg G}\max\{(\log\|G\|)^{\alpha_{0}},B^{\kappa}\}$ , for a choice of $\alpha_{0}>2$ . Here as usual, for each $p$ , $v_{p}(\mathbf{x})=\#\{y\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:G(y,\mathbf{x})=0\}$ is the local count. If, as in this paper, the upper bound for the second term on the right-hand side of the sieve inequality is on the order of $\ll Q^{n+\varepsilon}$ , the relevant power is $\kappa\approx n/(n+1)$ . Note that (7.4) is weaker than requiring GRH on average; it only requires that on average over $\bfk$ in the relevant set, the possible Siegel zeroes of the Dedekind zeta functions $\zeta_{F_{\bfk}}(s)$ do not contribute to the error term in the Chebotarev density theorem in an uncontrolled way (see [BP24, Eqn. (3.6)]).

## 8. Construction of examples

In this section, we construct examples necessary to verify genericity in §3, examples of classes of polynomials to which each main theorem applies, and examples that verify this paper recovers nearly all the previous literature on these problems.

### 8.1. Examples: $n$ -genuine and strongly $n$ -genuine polynomials

To gain some intuition, we provide the following examples: $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},X_{2},\sqrt{X_{1}+X_{2}})$ is a 2-genuine extension of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},X_{2})$ ; $Y^{2}-X_{1}-X_{2}$ is a $2$ -genuine polynomial. Next, $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3},\sqrt{X_{3}+\sqrt{X_{1}+X_{2}}})$ is a 3-genuine extension of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3})$ but not a strongly 3-genuine extension; $(Y^{2}-X_{3})^{2}-X_{1}-X_{2}$ is $3$ -genuine polynomial but not a strongly $3$ -genuine polynomial.

Being $n$ -genuine imposes that $F$ has at least degree 2 in $Y$ : for if $\deg_{Y}F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})=1$ then $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ is not an $n$ -genuine polynomial, since $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})[Y]/F(Y,\mathbf{X}))=\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ is not an $n$ -genuine extension of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ (since it is trivial). Concordantly, if $\deg_{Y}F(Y,\mathbf{X})=1$ then trivially $B^{n}\ll N(F,B)\ll B^{n}$ , since $F(Y,\mathbf{x})=0$ is solvable for all $\mathbf{x}\in[-B,B]^{n}$ .

#### Example 8.1 (Composita).

Let $1\leq j<n$ . Let $K$ be a $j$ -genuine extension of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{j})$ and $K^{\prime}$ be a $(n-j)$ -genuine extension of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{j+1},...,X_{n})$ . Define $L=KK^{\prime}$ to be the compositum of fields. Then $L$ is an $n$ -genuine extension but not strongly $n$ -genuine extension of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{n})$ .

#### Proof.

Since $K(X_{j+1},...,X_{n})\subset L$ is a subfield of $L$ generated by a polynomial in only $Y,X_{1},...,X_{j}$ , we know that $L$ cannot be strongly $n$ -genuine. It remains to show that $L$ is $n$ -genuine.

Assume for contradiction that $L$ is not $n$ -genuine, so there exists a polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ for some index set $I\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that

$$ L=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}). $$

Assume without loss of generality that $G$ does not depend on $X_{1}$ (that is, $I\subset\{2,\ldots,n\}$ ). (If instead, $G$ does not depend on some $X_{i}$ with $i\in\{j+1,\ldots,n\}$ , the following argument would be applied with $K^{\prime}$ in place of $K$ .) Then we can write $L=L^{\prime}(X_{1})$ , where

$$ L^{\prime}=\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},...,X_{n})[Y]/G(Y,X_{2},...,X_{n}). $$

Now, we note that $L\cap\overline{\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{j})}=K=L^{\prime}(X_{1})\cap\overline{\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},...,X_{j})}.$ Thus, this implies that $K=(L^{\prime}\cap\overline{\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},...,X_{j})})(X_{1})$ ; in other words, $K$ is of the form $M(X_{1})$ for $M$ an extension of $\mathbb{Q}(X_{2},...,X_{j})$ . This implies that $K$ is not $j$ -genuine and gives a contradiction. ∎

The next example produces classes of polynomials to which Theorem 1.5 applies.

#### Example 8.2 ( $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine).

Let $G(\mathbf{X}_{I})\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ and $H(\mathbf{X}_{J})\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}_{J}]$ , where $I$ and $J$ partition $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ nontrivially. Assume that $\deg_{X_{i}}G(\mathbf{X}_{I})\geq 1$ for all $i\in I$ and $\deg_{X_{j}}H(\mathbf{X}_{J})\geq 1$ for all $j\in J$ . First, we claim that for $e\geq 2$ , $Y^{e}-G(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is an $|I|$ -genuine polynomial. Indeed, $Y^{e}-G(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ generates the extension $\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})(\sqrt[e]{G(\mathbf{X}_{I})})$ and there is no polynomial in fewer than $|I|$ variables for which $\sqrt[e]{G(\mathbf{X}_{I})}$ is a root. Similarly, we see that for $f\geq 2$ , $Y^{f}-H(\mathbf{X}_{J})$ is a $|J|$ -genuine polynomial.

Assume that $e\geq 2$ , $f\geq 2$ , and that $\gcd(e,f)=1$ . Consider the compositum field:

$$ K=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})(\sqrt[e]{G(\mathbf{X}_{I})},\sqrt[f]{H(\mathbf{X}_{J})}). $$

We saw in Example 8.1 that $K$ is an $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine extension. Thus, if $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is a polynomial satisfying that

$$ K=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/F(Y,\mathbf{X}), $$

then $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is an $n$ -genuine but not strongly $n$ -genuine polynomial. Finally, we construct such a polynomial $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ . Consider the field

$$ K^{\prime}=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})(\alpha),\qquad\text{for $\alpha=\sqrt[e]{G(\mathbf{X}_{I})}(1+\sqrt[f]{H(\mathbf{X}_{J})}.$} $$

Since $\gcd(e,f)=1$ , we can see that $\alpha^{e}\in K^{\prime}$ implies that $\sqrt[f]{H(\mathbf{X}_{J})}\in K^{\prime}$ . So, we immediately deduce that $\sqrt[e]{G(\mathbf{X}_{I})}\in K^{\prime}$ . Thus, $K^{\prime}\subset K$ . However, $[K:\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})]=ef=[K^{\prime}:\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})].$ So, $K^{\prime}=K$ . So, we can take $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ to be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ .

Recall from Lemma 3.8 that being $n$ -genuine is preserved by scaling. But being $n$ -genuine is not, in general, preserved by isomorphism of fields. For example, the field $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},X_{2},\sqrt{X_{1}+X_{2}})$ is a 2-genuine extension, but $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},X_{2},\sqrt{2X_{1}})$ is not. However the first field is isomorphic to the second, under the map $X_{1}\mapsto X_{1}-X_{2}$ , $X_{2}\mapsto X_{1}+X_{2}$ . This motivates defining the stronger notion of a $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomial, which we turn to next.

### 8.2. Examples: $(1,n)$ -allowable and strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomials

First we provide some non-examples, to distinguish these two properties.

#### Example 8.3 (Linear is not allowed).

$F(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{D}-L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ for $D\geq 2$ and $L$ a linear form is not $(1,n)$ -allowable for $n\geq 2$ .

#### Proof.

A linear change of variables $Z_{1}=L(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ shows that $F$ can be expressed as a function of only two variables $Y,Z_{1}$ and is hence not $n$ -genuine. Thus $F$ is not $(1,n$ )-allowable. Concordantly, as in [Ser97, Ch. 13], $M=\{\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}:\text{$x_{1}$ is a square}\}$ is an affine thin set, but has $\gg B^{n-1/2}$ integral points of height at most $B$ . Restricting attention to $(1,n)$ -allowable polynomials rules out such cases from the settings of our main theorems. Similarly, note that the case in which $H(\mathbf{X})$ is linear is ruled out by the hypothesis of Theorem 1.1. ∎

#### Example 8.4 ( $(1,n)$ -allowable is stronger than having no change of variables).

If $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is $(1,n)$ -allowable then there does not exist a change of variables $\mathbf{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Z}$ in $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $F(Y,\mathbf{Z})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,Z_{2},...,Z_{n}]$ . (In particular, if $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is weighted-homogeneous so that the hypersurface $F(Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})=0$ lies in weighted projective space $\mathbb{P}(e,1,\ldots,1)$ , then this condition imposes that it is not contained in a hyperplane.) Yet being $(1,n)$ -allowable is stronger than having no such change of variables: for example, $F(Y,X_{1},X_{2},X_{3})=(Y-X_{1}^{2})^{2}+X_{2}^{2}+X_{3}^{2}$ is not $(1,3)$ -allowable. (To see this, note that $F(Y,X_{1},X_{2},X_{3})$ generates the extension $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3},X_{1}^{2}+\sqrt{X_{2}^{2}+X_{3}^{2}})=\mathbb{Q}(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3},\sqrt{X_{2}^{2}+X_{3}^{2}})$ , which is not 3-genuine.) But it also has the property that there is no change of variables $\mathbf{X}\rightarrow\mathbf{Z}$ in $\mathrm{GL}_{3}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $F(Y,\mathbf{Z})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,Z_{2},Z_{3}]$ .

We next construct a class of polynomials for which Theorem 1.4 applies.

#### Example 8.5 ( $(1,n)$ -allowable but not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable).

Let $I,J$ be a nontrivial partition of $\{1,...,n\}$ , and let $H(\mathbf{X}_{I})\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ , $G(\mathbf{X}_{J})\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}_{J}]$ be two irreducible homogeneous polynomials such that there is no $L_{I}\in\text{GL}_{|I|}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $H(L_{I}(\mathbf{X}_{I}))\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}_{I^{\prime}}]$ with $I^{\prime}\subsetneq I$ , and there is no $L_{J}\in\text{GL}_{|J|}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $G(L_{J}(\mathbf{X}_{J}))\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}_{J}^{\prime}]$ with $J^{\prime}\subsetneq J$ . Then for each $d\geq 2$ and $e\geq 2$ ,

$$ F(Y,\mathbf{X})=(Y^{d}+H(\mathbf{X}))^{e}+G(\mathbf{X})=(Y^{d}+H(\mathbf{X}_{I}))^{e}+G(\mathbf{X}_{J}) $$

is $(1,n)$ -allowable but not $(1,n)$ -strongly allowable.

#### Proof.

Throughout, we may write $H(\mathbf{X})=H(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ and $G(\mathbf{X})=G(\mathbf{X}_{J})$ , even if each variable only depends nontrivially on certain coordinates. We start by recording a simple observation: suppose a homogeneous polynomial $M(\bfX)\in\mathbb{Z}[\bfX]$ is given. Let a subset $B\subsetneq\{1,...,n\}$ be fixed. Let $M^{B}(\mathbf{X}_{B})$ be the component of $M(\mathbf{X})$ containing monomials only in terms of $X_{b}$ for $b\in B$ ; that is, $M^{B}(\mathbf{X}_{B})=\left.M(\mathbf{X})\right|_{X_{a}=0,a\not\in B}$ . Suppose $\tau\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ is a linear transformation such that its associated matrix does not have any zeros on the diagonal. (That is, if $\tau_{i}$ represents the $i$ -th row of $\tau$ then $\tau_{i}\cdot\mathbf{X}$ contains $X_{i}$ ; that is to say $X_{i}$ is mapped to a linear combination that includes $X_{i}$ .) Then there exists $\tau^{B}\in\text{GL}_{|B|}(\mathbb{Q})$ acting on $\mathbf{X}_{B}$ such that

$$ M_{\tau}(\bfX)=M^{B}_{\tau^{B}}(\mathbf{X}_{B})+M_{1}(\bfX), $$

where $\left.M_{1}(\mathbf{X})\right|_{X_{a}=0,a\not\in B}\equiv 0$ . (That is, every monomial in $M_{1}$ contains a factor $X_{a}$ for some $a\in\{1,...,n\}\setminus B$ . On the other hand, $M^{B}_{\tau^{B}}$ depends only on $X_{b}$ for $b\in B$ .) Here we use the notation $M_{\tau}(\mathbf{X})=M(\tau\mathbf{X})$ and similarly for $M_{\tau^{B}}$ .

To verify the example, we first show that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is $(1,n)$ -allowable. By contradiction, assume we can find $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}):=F(Y,L(\mathbf{X}))$ is not $n$ -genuine. By reordering the columns of the matrix representing $L$ , we may assume that there are no zeroes on the diagonal. (That is, if $L_{i}$ represents the $i$ -th row of $L$ then $L_{i}\cdot\mathbf{X}$ contains $X_{i}$ ; that is to say $X_{i}$ is mapped to a linear combination that includes $X_{i}$ .) By Lemma 3.5, there exists a nonempty subset $K\subsetneq\{1,...,n\}$ such that

$$ \mathbf{x}_{K}\in\mathbb{Q}^{|K|} F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}_{K^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{K}) Y \overline{\mathbb{Q}} $$

We aim to contradict this. Let $G_{L}(\mathbf{X})=G(L(\mathbf{X}))$ . We claim that if $\ell\not\in K$ , then $\deg_{X_{\ell}}G_{L}=0$ . Otherwise, by the Hilbert Irreducibility Theorem, there exists some $\mathbf{x}_{K}\in\mathbb{Q}^{|K|}$ such that $G_{L}(\mathbf{X}_{K^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{K})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ . Since we are assuming $\ell\not\in K$ , then $\deg_{X_{\ell}}G_{L}(\mathbf{X}_{K^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{K})\geq 1$ , i.e. $G_{L}(\mathbf{X}_{K^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{K})$ is not constant. In particular, this implies that $G_{L}(\mathbf{X}_{K^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{K})$ is separable, so that it is not an $e$ -power over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . In turn, this implies that

$$ F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}_{K^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{K})=(Y^{d}+H_{L}(\mathbf{X}_{K^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{K}))^{e}+G_{L}(\mathbf{X}_{K^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{K}), $$

is irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , hence contradicting (8.2). Thus $\deg_{X_{i}}G_{L}=0$ for all $i\not\in K$ . Observe that this furthermore implies that $J\subset K$ . On the other hand, by the fact (8.1), we can find $L^{K}\in\text{GL}_{|K|}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that

$$ G_{L}(\bfX)=G^{K}_{L^{K}}(\mathbf{X}_{K})+G_{1}(\bfX), $$

where $\left.G_{1}(\mathbf{X})\right|_{X_{i}=0,i\not\in K}\equiv 0$ and $\deg_{X_{i}}G_{L}=0$ for every $i\not\in K$ . Taking these two facts in combination, it follows that

$$ G_{L}(\bfX)=G^{K}_{L^{K}}(\mathbf{X}_{K}). $$

Thus,

$$ F_{L}(Y,\bfX)=(Y^{d}+H_{L}(\bfX))^{e}+G^{K}_{L^{K}}(\mathbf{X}_{K}). $$

Next, by Remark 3.6 we know that we can find a polynomial $P\in\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X}_{K})[Y]$ such that

$$ \mathbb{Q}(\bfX)[Y]/F_{L}=(\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X}_{K})[Y]/P)(\mathbf{X}_{K^{c}}). $$

This implies that for every $\sigma\in\text{GL}_{|K|}(\mathbb{Q})$

$$ \mathbb{Q}(\bfX)[Y]/F_{\sigma\circ L}=(\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X}_{K})[Y]/P_{\sigma})(\mathbf{X}_{K^{c}}), $$

so that $F_{\sigma\circ L}$ is also not $n$ -genuine. (While $\sigma$ initially acts on $\mathbf{X}_{K}$ , we have extended the definition of $\sigma$ to act on $n$ variables by setting $\sigma(X_{i})=X_{i}$ for all $i\not\in K$ ; thus $\sigma\circ L$ is well-defined.) We claim that we can find some $\sigma\in\text{GL}_{|K|}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $G_{\sigma\circ L}=G$ and $\sigma\circ L$ has no zeroes on the diagonal. To verify this, first recall that $G_{L}(\mathbf{X})=G^{K}_{L^{K}}(\mathbf{X}_{K})$ , and by the hypothesis of the example, the polynomial depicted on the right-hand side depends nontrivially on $X_{k}$ for each $k\in K$ . Moreover $L^{K}$ is invertible when acting on $\mathbf{X}_{K}$ , so we can simply take $\sigma=(L^{K})^{-1}$ and then extend it to act on $n$ variables by nominally setting $\sigma=\begin{pmatrix}(L^{K})^{-1}&0\\ 0&I\end{pmatrix}$ (assuming temporarily for notational simplicity that $K=\{1,\ldots,|K|\}$ ); this verifies the first part of the claim. Second, we claim that $\sigma\circ L$ does not have any zeroes on the diagonal. This is true since $\sigma\circ L$ acts as the identity on $\mathbf{X}_{K}$ , and on the other variables, it acts by $L$ , which has no zeroes on the diagonal.

Consequently, by replacing $L$ by $\sigma\circ L$ , from now on we may assume that $L$ is such that

$$ F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X})=(Y^{d}+H_{L}(\mathbf{X}))^{e}+G(\mathbf{X}), $$

and $L$ has no zeroes on the diagonal. Here we note that $G$ is not modified by $L$ . Again by the fact (8.1) we can find $L_{I}\in\text{GL}_{|I|}(\mathbb{Q})$ acting on $\mathbf{X}_{I}$ such that

$$ H_{L}(\bfX)=H^{I}_{L^{I}}(\mathbf{X}_{I})+H_{1}(\bfX), $$

where $\left.H_{1}(\mathbf{X})\right|_{X_{j}=0,j\in J}\equiv 0$ . Thus after restricting to $X_{j}=0$ for every $j\in J$ , the homogeneity of $G$ implies that

$$ \left.F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X})\right|_{X_{j}=0,j\in J}=(Y^{d}+H^{I}_{L^{I}}(\mathbf{X}_{I}))^{e}. $$

Now let $i\not\in K$ ; since $J\subset K$ this implies $i\in I$ . By hypothesis we know that $\deg_{X_{i}}H^{I}_{L^{I}}\geq 1$ . First suppose that $|I|=1$ . Then under the hypothesis that $H(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , $H^{I}_{L^{I}}(\mathbf{X}_{I})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , hence separable, hence not a $d$ -power over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Next, if $|I|\geq 2$ , then by the Hilbert Irreducibility Theorem, we can find $\mathbf{x}_{I\setminus\{i\}}=(x_{\ell})_{\ell\neq i}\in\mathbb{Q}^{|I|-1}$ such that $H^{I}_{L_{I}}(X_{i},x_{\ell})_{\ell\neq i}$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , hence separable, and hence not a $d$ -power over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . In either case, this shows the polynomial $F_{L}(Y,X_{i},X_{\ell}=x_{\ell},X_{j}=0)_{\ell\in I\setminus\{i\},j\in J}$ does not have a linear factor over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ , contradicting the conclusion of Lemma 3.5 recorded in (8.2). (Indeed, recalling the comment after Lemma 3.5, it contradicts the conclusion for specialized variables with indices in a superset of $K$ .)

Finally, we show that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable. Since $\mathbb{Q}(\bfX)[Y]/(Y^{e}+G(\bfX))$ is a subextension of $\mathbb{Q}(\bfX)[Y]/(F(Y,\bfX))$ and $G\in\ZZ[\mathbf{X}_{J}]$ for a proper subset $J\subsetneq\{1,...,n\}$ , it follows that $\mathbb{Q}(\bfX)[Y]/(F(Y,\bfX))$ is not strongly $n$ -genuine, hence $F$ is not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable. ∎

We next verify the properties of six final classes of polynomials; these examples demonstrate that our general theorems recover nearly all previous literature on the topic. The first of these examples has been applied in the derivation of Corollary 3.2.

#### Example 8.6 (Diagonal structure).

Fix integers $d\geq 2$ and $k_{j}\geq 2$ for $j=1,...,n.$ Then the polynomial

$$ F(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{d}-\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_{j}^{k_{j}} $$

is $(1,n)$ -allowable.

#### Proof.

Consider the vanishing set $V(F)\subset\mathbb{A}_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}^{n+1}$ ; this variety has an isolated singularity at the vector $\mathbf{0}$ and hence $\dim_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(\sing(V(F)))=0.$ Assume for contradiction that there exists $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $F(Y,L(\mathbf{X}))$ is not $n$ -genuine, so $F(Y,L(\mathbf{X}))$ generates the same extension as a polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ in which $|I|<n$ . Without loss of generality, we may suppose $G(Y,\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}]$ . Then $\{y=0\}\cap\{x_{i}=0,i=2,...,n\}$ is contained in the singularity of $V(F(Y,L(\mathbf{X})))$ , which implies that $\dim_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(\sing(V(F)))=\dim_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(\sing(V(F(Y,L(\mathbf{X})))))>0$ , which is a contradiction. ∎

The next example confirms that Theorem 1.3 immediately implies Theorem 1.1. It has also been applied (twice) in the proof of Theorem 3.1 to verify that the polynomials $\tilde{h}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{h}_{s}$ are not all identically zero on the relevant moduli space.

#### Example 8.7 (Cyclic structure).

Let $H(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be an irreducible polynomial of total degree at least 2 and define for a fixed $d\geq 2$ ,

$$ F(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{d}-H(\mathbf{X}). $$

Suppose there is no $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $H(L(\mathbf{X}))\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ for some set $I\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ . Then $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable.

#### Proof.

We first remark that $F$ is absolutely irreducible, since $Y^{d}-H(\mathbf{X})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ if and only if $H(\mathbf{X})$ is an $\ell$ -power over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ for some $\ell|d$ with $\ell>1$ . Such a factorization $H(\mathbf{X})=(G(\mathbf{X}))^{\ell}$ for some $G\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[\mathbf{X}]$ cannot occur under the hypothesis, since then for every $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}$ , $H(X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=(G(X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}))^{\ell}$ . But by the Hilbert Irreducibility Theorem, there exists some $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}$ such that $H(X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , hence separable, hence certainly not an $\ell$ -power over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ .

Assume for contradiction that $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable, so there exists $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}):=F(Y,L(\mathbf{X}))$ is not strongly $n$ -genuine. Then there exists a polynomial $G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I})$ for some set $I\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ , such that

$$ K:=\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(F(Y,L(\mathbf{X})))\supset\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X})[Y]/(G(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I}))\supsetneq\mathbb{Q}(\mathbf{X}). $$

Without loss of generality, we may suppose $I=\{2,\ldots,n\}$ . Let $H_{L}(\mathbf{X})$ denote $H(L(\mathbf{X}))$ . By hypothesis, $\deg_{X_{1}}H_{L}(\mathbf{X})>0$ , hence by the Hilbert Irreducibility Theorem we can find $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}=(x_{2},...,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n-1}$ such that $H_{L,\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}(X_{1}):=H_{L}(X_{1},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ . On the other hand, $Y^{d}-H_{L,\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}(X_{1})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ if and only if $H_{L,\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}(X_{1})$ is an $\ell$ -power for some $\ell>1$ with $\ell|d$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ but this is not possible since $H_{L,\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}(X_{1})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ (hence $H_{L,\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}(X_{1})$ is separable, and certainly not an $\ell$ -power). Thus under the assumption that such a change of variables $L$ exists, we have produced an index set $I=I(L)$ (depending on $L$ ) with $|I|<n$ , for which there is some $\mathbf{x}_{I}\in\mathbb{Q}^{|I|}$ for which $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{I})$ is not reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . By Lemma 3.5 this yields a contradiction. For by that lemma, since $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is not strongly $n$ -genuine then there exists a nonempty subset $J=J(L)\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}_{J^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{J})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ for all choices of $\mathbf{x}_{J}\in\mathbb{Q}^{|J|}$ . Indeed, by Remark 3.6, the conclusion of Lemma 3.5 holds for $J=I$ , and this yields a contradiction.

∎

The next example has been applied in the derivation of Corollary 3.3.

#### Example 8.8 (Cyclic structure, singular locus dimension $s$ ).

Fix $d\geq 2,m\geq 1$ . Let $H(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be a homogeneous polynomial of degree $d\cdot m$ such that the projective hypersurface $V(H)\subset\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ defined by the vanishing of $H$ has $\dim(\sing V(H))=s$ , where this denotes the projective dimension in $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ , $-1\leq s\leq n-1$ . Moreover, suppose there is no $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $H(L(\mathbf{X}))\in\mathbb{Z}[\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ with $|I|<n$ . Then $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=Y^{d}-H(\mathbf{X})$ is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable.

#### Proof.

This follows immediately from Example 8.7, upon choosing $H$ with the desired dimension of the singular locus. ∎

#### Example 8.9 (Projective smooth hypersurfaces).

Let $G(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[Y,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be a homogeneous nonsingular polynomial that is monic in $Y$ and of degree at least 2. Then $G$ is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable.

#### Proof.

By contradiction, assume we can find $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $G_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}):=G(Y,L(\mathbf{X}))$ is not strongly $n$ -genuine. By Lemma 3.5 this would imply that there exists $I\subsetneq\{1,...,n\}$ such that for every $\bfx_{I}\in\mathbb{Q}^{|I|}$ , the polynomial $G_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{I})$ is reducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ . Without loss of generality we may assume $I=\{2,...,n\}$ . Consider the morphism

$$ \pi:\begin{matrix}V(G_{L})&\rightarrow&\mathbb{P}^{n-2},\\
[y:x_{1}:...:x_{n}]&\mapsto&[x_{2}:...:x_{n}].\end{matrix} $$

The linear transformation $L$ preserves the nonsingularity of the polynomial, and the geometric fiber $\pi^{-1}(\eta)$ is smooth (here $\eta$ is the generic point in $\mathbb{P}^{n-2}$ ). (Indeed, smoothness is preserved by base change [Gro67, EGA IV, Proposition (17.3.3) (iii), p. 61].) It follows that we can find $[x_{2}:...:x_{n}]$ such that $G_{L}(Y,X_{1},x_{2}T,...,x_{n}T)$ is a smooth curve. But this implies that $G_{L}(Y,X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})$ is irreducible over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ for this choice of $[x_{2}:\cdots:x_{n}]$ , which yields a contradiction. Thus it must be that $G_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is strongly $n$ -genuine for all $L$ , and hence $G$ is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable. ∎

The next example confirms that Theorem 1.3 recovers the main result of [BP24].

#### Example 8.10 (Nonsingular weighted projective hypersurface).

Fix integers $d,e,\geq 1$ and $m\geq 2$ . Let $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})$ be a polynomial of the form (1.1) in which for each $j=1,\ldots,d$ the polynomial $f_{j}$ is homogeneous of degree $m\cdot e\cdot j$ . Thus $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=0$ defines a hypersurface in weighted projective space $\mathbb{P}(e,1,\ldots,1)$ , and we assume in particular that $V(F(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ is nonsingular. Then $F$ is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable.

#### Proof.

To verify this, suppose for contradiction that $F(Y,X_{1},...,X_{n})$ is not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable; then $F(Z^{e},X_{1},...,X_{n})$ is not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable. But by hypothesis $V(F(Y,\mathbf{X}))$ is nonsingular, and as shown in [BP24, §3.3] since $m\geq 2$ it follows that $V(F(Z^{e},X_{1},...,X_{n}))\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}$ is also nonsingular. Thus $V(F(Z^{e},X_{1},...,X_{n}))$ is a smooth variety and by Example 8.9, $F(Z^{e},X_{1},...,X_{n})$ is strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable, showing the desired contradiction. ∎

#### Remark 8.11.

The main result of [BP24] states that $N(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}B^{n-1+\frac{1}{n+1}+\varepsilon}$ with an implicit constant independent of $F$ . In fact, the argument presented in that paper only shows polylog dependence on $\|F\|$ , proving $N(F,B)\ll_{n,\deg F,\varepsilon}(\log(\|F\|+2))^{e}B^{n-1+\frac{1}{n+1}+\varepsilon}$ for some $e=e(n)$ ; Example 8.10 shows this is recovered by the present work.

The next example demonstrates that our main theorems recover many cases of [Bon21, Thm. 1.1].

#### Example 8.12 (Separation of variables).

Fix $d\geq 2,m\geq 2$ . Let $P(Y)\in\mathbb{Z}[Y]$ be a monic polynomial of degree $d$ and let $G(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]$ be an irreducible homogeneous polynomial of degree $m$ such that there is no $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $G(L(X_{1},...,X_{n}))\in\mathbb{Q}[\mathbf{X}_{I}]$ with $|I|<n$ . Then $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=P(Y)-G(\mathbf{X})$ is $(1,n)$ -allowable.

#### Remark 8.13.

The result [Bon21, Thm. 1.1] proves $N(F,B)\ll_{F,\varepsilon}B^{n-1+1/(n+1)+\varepsilon}$ for all $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=P(Y)+G(\mathbf{X})$ in which $P$ is a polynomial of degree at least 2 and $G$ is a nonsingular homogeneous polynomial. Theorem 1.4 recovers this for all such $F$ that are $(1,n)$ -allowable but not strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable; Theorem 1.3 recovers this unconditionally for all such $F$ that are strongly $(1,n)$ -allowable and $P(Y)$ is a polynomial in $Y^{m}$ for some $m\geq 2$ ; otherwise Theorem 1.3 only recovers this with the additional hypothesis of GRH.

#### Proof.

We begin with a preliminary observation. Under the hypothesis that $G$ is irreducible, for every $a\in\mathbb{C}$ the polynomial $G(\bfX)-aT^{m}$ in $n+1$ variables is absolutely irreducible since $G$ is not an $m$ -power. Thus, the affine variety $\{G-a\}$ , obtained by intersecting the projective variety associated to $G(\bfX)-aT^{m}$ with the open set $\{T\neq 0\}$ is absolutely irreducible. Hence, for every $a\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}$ , $G(\bfX)-a$ is an absolutely irreducible polynomial. In particular, this implies that for every $y$ with $P(y)\neq 0$ , $G(\bfX)-P(y)$ is absolutely irreducible, hence $F(Y,\mathbf{X})=P(Y)-G(\bfX)$ is absolutely irreducible.

Now we verify the example. To seek a contradiction, suppose that we can find $L\in\text{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{Q})$ such that $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}):=F(Y,L(\mathbf{X}))$ is not $n$ -genuine. By Lemma 3.5 we know that there exists a nonempty subset $I\subsetneq\{1,...,n\}$ such that

$$ \mathbf{x}_{I}\in\mathbb{Q}^{|I|} F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X}_{I^{c}},\mathbf{x}_{I}) Y \overline{\mathbb{Q}} $$

Without loss of generality we may assume $I=\{2,...,n\}$ . For a given root $\alpha$ of the derivative $P^{\prime}(Y)$ , let $S_{\alpha}=\left\{G(\bfX)-P(\alpha)=\frac{\partial G}{\partial X_{1}}=0\right\}$ . By the preliminary observation, $G(\mathbf{X})-P(\alpha)$ is irreducible so in particular it shares no common factor with $\frac{\partial}{\partial X_{1}}(G(\mathbf{X})-P(\alpha))=\frac{\partial G}{\partial X_{1}}$ ; consequently $\dim S_{\alpha}=n-2$ . In what follows, given $(x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}$ , we denote the line

$$ H_{x_{2},...,x_{n}}:=\{X_{2}-x_{2}=...=X_{n}-x_{n}=0\}. $$

We claim that we can find a nonempty open set $U_{\alpha}\subset\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}$ such that $S_{\alpha}\cap H_{x_{2},...,x_{n}}=\emptyset$ over $\mathbb{C}$ for every $(x_{2},...,x_{n})\in U_{\alpha}$ . We first observe that $H_{x_{2}...,x_{n}}\cap S_{\alpha}\neq\emptyset$ if and only if the resultant vanishes, namely

$$ \text{Res}\left(G(\bfX)-P(\alpha),\frac{\partial G}{\partial X_{1}},X_{2}-x_{2},...,X_{n}-x_{n}\right)=0, $$

which gives a polynomial relation in the coefficients $x_{2},...,x_{n}$ . Next, we prove that we can find some choice of $(x_{2},...,x_{n})\in\mathbb{Q}^{n-1}$ such that $S_{\alpha}\cap H_{x_{2},...,x_{n}}=\emptyset$ , so that this resultant polynomial is not identically zero; this suffices to show such an open set $U_{\alpha}$ exists. Since for all $x_{2}\in\mathbb{Q}$ the hyperplanes $\{X_{2}-x_{2}=0\}$ are all parallel, for every irreducible component of $S_{\alpha}$ , say $V$ , there exists at most one value of $x_{2}$ such that $V\subset\{X_{2}-x_{2}\}$ . Thus, $V\cap\{X_{2}-x_{2}\}$ has dimension $n-3$ for all but one value of $x_{2}$ . Since $S_{\alpha}$ has finitely many irreducible components, it follows that $S_{\alpha}\cap\{X_{2}-x_{2}\}$ has dimension $n-3$ for all but finitely many choices of $x_{2}\in\mathbb{Q}$ . Pick now $x_{2}$ such that $S_{\alpha}\cap\{X_{2}-x_{2}\}$ has dimension $n-3$ . We can iterate the same argument and find $x_{2},...,x_{n}$ such that $\dim(S_{\alpha}\cap H_{x_{2},...,x_{n}})=n-2-(n-1)=-1$ , i.e. $S_{\alpha}\cap H_{x_{2},...,x_{n}}$ is empty.

Now take $U=\cap_{\alpha}U_{\alpha}$ to be the intersection over the roots $\alpha$ of $P^{\prime}(Y)$ . By the preliminary observation, $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is absolutely irreducible, hence $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ is absolutely irreducible, so by the Hilbert Irreducibility Theorem there exists a choice of $(x_{2},...,x_{n})\in U$ such that $F_{L}(Y,X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ . Observe that for such a choice of $(x_{2},...,x_{n})$ the curve defined by $F_{L}(Y,X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})=0$ is smooth on the affine plane. Indeed, the Jacobian for $F(Y,X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})=P(Y)-G(X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})$ is

$$ (F(Y,X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n}),P^{\prime}(Y),\frac{\partial G}{\partial X_{1}}(X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})). $$

If there is a singular point, so that the Jacobian vanishes, then there exists a root $\alpha$ of $P^{\prime}$ such that the system

$$ G(\bfX)-P(\alpha)=\frac{\partial G}{\partial X_{1}}=X_{2}-x_{2}=...=X_{n}-x_{n}=0 $$

has a solution, which is impossible, since $(x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})$ lies in $U_{\alpha}$ for all $\alpha$ .

We will now use (8.3) to construct a singular point of $F_{L}(Y,X_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})$ in $\mathbb{A}^{2}$ , thus obtaining a contradiction. Since we are assuming that $F_{L}(Y,X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})$ has a linear factor in $Y$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ and it is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ , it follows from Lemma 3.7 that

$$ F_{L}(Y,X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})=\prod_{\tau\in H}(Y-\tau(Q(X_{1}))), $$

where $H$ is the Galois group of the extension $\mathbb{Q}(X_{1})[Y]/F_{L}(Y,X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})$ , meaning, the group of embeddings of the extension in its Galois closure). We claim that $Q(X_{1})$ cannot be of the form

$$ Q(X_{1})=X_{1}R(X_{1})+\beta, $$

for some $R\in\mathbb{Q}[X_{1}]$ ; that is, the polynomial $Q\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[X_{1}]$ cannot have only its constant term lie in $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ . For if $Q$ had this form, then

$$ \Tr(Q(X_{1}))=\Tr(X_{1}R(X_{1}))+\Tr(\beta)=dX_{1}R(X_{1})+\Tr(\beta)\neq 0, $$

which would be a contradiction. (By construction $F(Y,\mathbf{X})$ has separation of variables, so $F_{L}(Y,\mathbf{X})$ does as well, which would be violated via the factorization (8.4) if $\Tr(Q(X_{1}))\neq 0$ .) We conclude that there is some nonconstant term in $Q$ with a coefficient in $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ , so that we can find $\tau\neq\text{Id}$ , such that $\deg_{X_{1}}(Q(X_{1})-\tau(Q(X_{1})))>0$ . This implies that $F_{L}(Y,X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})$ has singular points on the affine plane since

$$ \{Y-Q(X_{1})=Y-\tau(Q(X_{1}))=0\} $$

is not empty in $\mathbb{A}^{2}$ . This contradicts the earlier conclusion that the curve defined by the equation $F_{L}(Y,X_{1},x_{2},...,x_{n})=0$ is smooth on the affine plane. ∎
